Switch between CA and NY editions here.

One year ago, the world watched a starving young man dig what Hamas told him would be his own grave. His body had been reduced to skin and bone, and he could barely lift the shovel in his hands.

For millions of people, it was a horrifying video that appeared on their screens and then ended. For Ilay David, it was something else entirely. It was his older brother, Evyatar, and all Ilay could do was watch helplessly from home.

A few days after the video was released, the David family tried to reach President Trump through the pages of this newspaper. Evyatar appeared on the cover with the headline, “STARVED OF HUMANITY.”

“At the time, neither of us knew if Evyatar would survive long enough to read those words,” Ilay told The Post.

Today, one year later, Evyatar is home.

“When I wrote that appeal,” said Ilay, “I was trying to save my little brother’s life, but I was also trying to hold myself together. For almost two years, I had traveled wherever I believed someone might be able to help. I spoke in television studios and public squares, in Congress and at the White House.

“I told politicians, diplomats, journalists and anyone else who would listen about Evyatar. I needed them to understand that he was not simply a face on a poster or another name on a list of hostages. He was my little brother. Who loves music, makes people laugh and has an entire life waiting for him.”

When Hamas released the video, Ilay saw for the first time what captivity had done to his brother.

“I had imagined hunger, fear and darkness. But nothing prepared me for the sight of his slim body. I studied his face, searching for the brother I knew inside the person Hamas had starved. His eyes were still his, but the rest of him seemed to be disappearing.”

Recounting the episode, Evyatar tells the Post that Hamas made him and his fellow captive Guy Gilboa-Dalal remove their clothes. The terrorists then chose Evyatar to appear in the video, “Because I looked worse,” he said.

“As they led me toward the place where they wanted to film, I passed a room where I could smell tea and cake. I could hear my captors eating while I walked beside them, starving. I remember thinking that I had become a skeleton walking past men with food who had decided I did not deserve any.”

The kidnappers brought Evyatar into a small tunnel, handed him a shovel, and pointed to a narrow pit. He began to dig.

“My body had almost no strength left, and every movement made me feel as though I might faint. Still, I dug because there was a gunman watching me.”

Ilay described his feelings as he watched the video: “Every instinct I had as his older brother told me to protect him,” said Ilay. “Instead, all I could do was stare at a screen while he struggled to lift a shovel. I wanted to reach through it, take the shovel from his hands and put my arms around him. I wanted to give him food and tell him that we had never stopped fighting for him.”

But he could do none of those things. So, instead, what he did was make sure the world looked at him and understood how little time was left — even when he worried it might already be too late.

Then, on October 13, 2025, Evyatar was freed and the brothers reunited.

“After more than two years of seeing his face on posters, screens and newspaper pages, he was standing in front of me,” said Ilay. “I could touch him. I could hear his voice. For so long, I had been afraid to imagine that moment too clearly. My little brother had come home.

“There is no language big enough for the relief of getting him back. In those first moments, all the fear I had carried collided with a kind of joy I had never known before. I held him and did not want to let go.”

Ilay knows that the years stolen from Evyatar can never be returned, and his brother cannot be protected from the memories of the horrific events.

“I once believed bringing Evyatar home would be the end of our nightmare. I understand now that returning home is the beginning of learning how to live again. It can be painful and complicated, but it is also filled with moments we once feared we would never have.”

“When people speak to me now,” said Evyatar, “they sometimes talk as though I have returned from the dead. I know they mean it with love, but I find it difficult to hear because I was alive every second. Even when my body was failing, I wanted to live more than I had ever wanted anything.”

I thought about my family constantly. I pictured their faces and tried to imagine what they were doing. I wondered whether they knew where I was and whether they understood how little time I might have left.”

When asked whether he ever thought about what his family was up to while he was captive, Evyatar said, “I had no idea that he had put his own life aside and was traveling around the world saying my name.

“My captors told me that nobody cared and that Israel had forgotten us. Only after I came home did I begin to understand how hard my brother had fought and how many doors he had knocked on for me. While I was trying to find the strength to survive one more day, Ilay was making sure the world did not become comfortable with leaving me there.”

The scars are still fresh. “I am free now, but freedom has not erased captivity. There are nights when I close my eyes and find myself back inside the tunnel. The young man holding the shovel is still part of me, but he is not and will never be the only part of me. I am also the person who came home, returned to the people I love and began making plans again.

He’s learning that recovery is not simple. It is a process. “It is eating with my family, listening to music and laughing with my brother and sister again. It is discovering that life continued to wait for me, even when I was not sure I would live to return to it.”

The two brothers know they cannot go back to the people they were before October 7. “What happened will always be with us,” Ilay says, “but so will the love that carried us through it and the life we still have ahead of us.”

Perhaps the clearest image of that life came at Ilay’s wedding on August 6. The young man whom Hamas had forced to dig his own grave was standing beside his brother with a guitar, escorting him as he went to be married. Surrounded by family, friends, music and joy, celebrating a new beginning.

That is the image the brothers want the world to remember.

Not the grave Hamas forced Evyatar to dig, but the life they failed to take from him. Not two brothers separated by captivity, but two brothers walking forward together.

Topic:The Greens

Jordon Steele-John has made a statement addressing allegations against him. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Greens senator Jordan Steele-John has addressed allegations of inappropriate conduct towards women.

In a public statement on social media, he denied any wrongdoing and blamed the public fallout from the allegations against him on party "factionalism".

Senator Steele-John says he is not on leave and the matter is now subject to an internal Greens investigation.

Greens senator Jordon Steele-John has denied allegations of inappropriate conduct raised in a letter to the Greens, which he says included false allegations of sexual assault, and blamed the public fallout from the allegations against him on party "factionalism".

The Greens have been in crisis management since the existence of a 47-page dossier surfaced about how the WA Greens would manage media coverage of allegations made about Senator Steele-John.

It was previously reported Senator Steele-John had taken leave from the party room last week after a letter from seven party members was sent to the office of Greens leader David Shoebridge.

According to media reports the letter alleged the writers were aware of "multiple allegations" about his behaviour in the presence of women, although none of the writers was said to have direct knowledge of "the matters involved", according to Senator Shoebridge.

In a public statement on social media, Senator Steele-John said, among the false allegations made against him, was an allegation of sexual assault, which police had investigated and made no adverse findings against him, with a finding of no charges.

He said that, with respect to that complaint, he had faced abuse and threats before the original complaint to police was made.

Senator Steele-John addressed several other allegations which he said were put to him by a journalist, which are now the subject of an internal Greens investigation.

Jordon Steele-John says false allegations have been made against him. (ABC News: David Sciasci)

He said a nickname others used to refer to him, "Feels on wheels", had grown from its original meaning to something "more sinister".

"Other parties started using [the name] to refer to me after I became emotional early in my career while giving speeches about the Royal Commission into Violence, Abuse, Neglect and Exploitation of Disabled People," he said.

The senator said his experience as a victim of abuse had collided with "political games", and denied he had taken leave after the allegations surfaced.

"I had hoped to be able to share all of this when I was ready, but because of a political clique in Greens WA and a leader facing his first serious test of leadership, I feel that the silence of self-protection will be [and has been] perceived as the silence of guilt," he said.

The senator claimed an "unofficial faction" of the Greens WA branch had released a letter detailing the allegations against him.

"This is not accountability. It is factionalism, and it has no place in the Greens," he said.

In a statement, a Greens WA party spokesperson said they were "putting together an independent process to assess the allegations".

"To ensure the integrity of that process, we will not be commenting further at this time," the spokesperson said.

David Shoebridge has big ambitions for the Greens, but his party is still wrestling with how to turn voter disillusionment into greater support.

Senator Steele-John said he had asked Senator Shoebridge "not to announce that I had requested leave" as it would appear to validate the allegations against him.

"I had expected him to recognise that absent any specific allegations, there was no procedural need for me to take leave of any kind," Senator Steele-John said.

"It was a bad call from David. We've all made those in politics.

"So, to be clear, I am not on leave and did not agree to the inclusion of that line within David's statement."

Senator Shoebridge's office has been contacted for comment.

Federal judges meeting in Boston heard tech industry warnings that AI-generated images and video are becoming nearly impossible to verify, as a judiciary committee considers whether courts need new rules for evidence that may be deepfakes instead of the real thing.

Reuters reports that the U.S. Judicial Conference’s Advisory Committee on Evidence Rules has spent three years, since 2023, studying how courts should handle evidence that may have been faked or altered using artificial intelligence. At Thursday’s meeting, representatives from OpenAI and Meta told the panel that detecting such fakes is only going to get harder.

“AI images are only getting better, and I do not think that there will be a scientific way going forward to detect them,” said Shira Anderson, OpenAI’s policy counsel.

Devin Norder, Meta’s director of product management, told the committee that the latest generation of AI models produces media that people simply cannot tell apart from the real thing. “Media generated from frontier models, at least in the last few generations, are indistinguishable by humans from authentic or AI-generated media,” Norder said. He added that producing convincing fakes no longer takes much effort or money: “And the cost and the time it takes to create this media really are quite trivial at this point.”

Both companies have built tools meant to verify whether visual content is authentic, and lawmakers have started moving the same way. California and the European Union have each passed laws requiring “watermarking” designed to flag AI-generated material. But Anderson cautioned that no single system can catch everything, since different companies’ tools don’t talk to each other. “My guess is that this absolutely will continue to get better. I do not think it’ll ever be bulletproof,” she said.

Despite the warnings, the committee has found little evidence that deepfakes are actually showing up in courtrooms. A survey released in March by the Federal Judiciary Center, the judiciary’s research arm, polled 931 judges and found that only 15 had handled a case in which someone challenged evidence as a deepfake. US District Judge Jesse Furman of Manhattan, who chairs the committee, pointed to that gap between prediction and reality. “There’s a lot of academic commentary and other commentary predicting that courts will be dealing with deepfakes, but we haven’t actually seen a whole lot of that yet,” Furman said.

That gap has split the committee over whether courts need an AI-specific evidence rule at all. Manhattan US District Judge Valerie Caproni argued that courts already have what they need and don’t have to reinvent it for AI. “We’ve dealt with bad actors presenting fake evidence since Cain and Abel. That’s a longstanding problem,” Caproni said.

AI Deepfakes are causing problems for regular Americans through their usage in fraud schemes. Wynton Hall explains this threat in his New York Times best seller Code Red: The Left, the Right, China, and the Race to Control AI.

As Hall explained during a Newsmax appearance:

“They can now mine your social media and then they build a detailed dossier on your life, and then they use the AI to mimic a loved one so convincingly that your instincts will tell you that it’s real,” the author said.

“These tools are now becoming democratized so that they’re cheap, they’re easy to use, and that means they’re accessible at a mass scale,” Hall added.

AI-related scams accounted for more than 22,000 complaints in 2025, and nearly $893 million in losses, according to the FBI.

Interceptors have been unable to stop Russian strikes due to speed restrictions imposed by Starlink, according to President Zelenskyy. (Reuters: State Emergency Service of Ukraine)

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said the country's interceptor systems are ineffective due to speed restrictions imposed by Starlink.

He said when used in EU territory, the system worked at higher speeds.

It comes as US President Donald Trump pauses incoming sanctions against Russia, after agreeing to purchase diesel from the country.

Ukraine is now unable to use its interceptor systems against Russian drone attacks because of a Starlink speed restriction, president Volodymyr Zelenskyy says.

He said any restrictions would have been set by the US military and US President Donald Trump.

Mr Zelenskyy told reporters in a WhatsApp media chat Ukrainian officials had been told the restrictions were linked to technical issues, adding he was discussing it with US officials.

He said Ukraine had tested Starlink on European Union territory and encountered no such problems there, with the system operating at higher speeds.

Earlier this week Ukraine experienced similar issues, with Starlink owner Elon Musk responding by insisting his firm had nothing to do with the speed limits.

Starlink is a vital battlefield communications tool and determine the speed at which some of Ukraine's weapons can travel. (Reuters)

President Zelenskyy said Moscow had carried out a massive strike on Ukraine's energy infrastructure, targeting more than 15 sites across the country.

"The sheer scale and unrelenting pace of Russia's strikes, specifically against our energy sector, are unfortunately having severe consequences," he said.

Ukraine's air force said Russian forces launched four cruise missiles and 332 attack drones overnight.

Mr Zelenskyy previously said Ukraine wasn't receiving forewarning of ballistic missile strikes from intelligence partners. (Reuters)

All of the missiles and 289 of the drones had been suppressed or destroyed, it said.

Russia's heavy bombardment of the power grid ahead of winter has been an annual feature of the war, aimed at wearing down Ukraine's appetite for the fight by denying civilians heat and running water.

Ukrainian officials have warned that Russia is stockpiling ballistic missiles for more attacks in the coming months.

President Zelenskyy has also urged supporters to speak out in defence of new US sanctions against Russia, hours after Mr Trump signed an executive order pausing a sweeping package of restrictions targeting the Russian economy.

The White House decision has further raised fears Ukraine could be left exposed to Moscow's escalating assaults.

The relationship between Ukraine and the US has been strained following the announcement the US would buy diesel from Russia. (AP: Julia Demaree Nikhinson)

Mr Zelenskyy described Mr Trump's move to put sanctions on hold as unfortunate, but did not directly criticise the US leader despite deepening tensions between Ukraine and Washington in recent days.

Ukraine is worried the road bridge could be used to conceal military personnel and weapons in vehicles, rather than a trade route.

"A decision was unfortunately made in America to completely disregard the Lindsey Graham Act, which was supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia to bring this war to an end," Mr Zelenskyy wrote.

He also expressed hope that the new sanctions could be revived.

"This Act could have helped enormously — and still can! But it needs to actually work, and every voice in support of it matters," he said.

Named after late South Carolina Senator Lindsey Graham, the legislation had sought to clamp down more quickly on the flow of financial resources fuelling Russia's against Ukraine.

The bill had sought to sanction Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers that keeps Russian energy moving.

President Trump personally signed the legislation last month, two days before a deadline set in the law itself for its implementation.

The president told Congress that the pause was in the national interest but gave no further details.

Senator Richard Blumenthal, who co-drafted the bill, said in a statement Mr Trump was turning his back on "the majority of Americans, their representatives in both houses of Congress, and our European allies."

Mr Trump's unexpected decision comes a week after he stunningly said the US had agreed to purchase diesel from Russia to try to bring down global energy prices, despite that potentially hurting Ukraine in its war with Russia.

It is hard to see Donald Trump's shifting position on Ukraine as a clear strategic change, and not one driven principally by soaring fuel prices ahead of the US mid-term elections.

Mr Trump said Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter".

The decision has been pilloried by Republicans and Democrats alike who say it will help Russia execute its war against Ukraine — without making a difference to global fuel prices, which are elevated mostly due to Mr Trump's war on Iran.

Welcome to the Boo Apple.

In the midst of spooky season, Halloween-themed bars are scaring up monster business timed to Halloween, with lines out the door for the chance to sip on an array of chilling cocktails while taking in some over-the-top frights.

From a tiki bar serving up tropical delights to a gothic spectacle crawling with goblins — the Big Apple’s watering holes are going all out to give customers a frightfully good time.

And New Yorkers are cashing in on the action, one witch-tastic cocktail at a time.

“Halloween bars are fun because they are, by definition, limited edition,” Mandy Naglich, cocktail expert and author of the book “How to Taste: A Guide to Discovering Flavor and Savoring Life,” told The Post.

“In a world where it’s on-trend to sip clarified pina coladas, minimalist margaritas, and extra-refined martinis, it’s fun to know you’ll be getting a tiki drink made with fake vampire blood. Let us have fun! It’s a bar!”

Behind the ghoulish fun is a seasonal business, as NYC bars invest in elaborate decor, enticing menus and captivating experiences to draw crowds — and keep them coming back.

From haunted underwater worlds to witchy rooftop escapes, these limited-run concepts are proving there’s money to be made in a little Halloween havoc.

“October is easily our busiest time of year,” Kavé Pourzanjani, the owner and general manager of the spooky East Village bar Paradise Lost, told The Post.

Boasting a Tiki-horror theme with eye-popping interiors, Pourzanjani opened the year-round bar in 2023 as an upscale tropical cocktail oasis.

It’s inspired by B horror films, the spirit of punk rock and the work of EC Comics, the latter being the publisher behind the “Tales from the Crypt” series.

“We had a love for the nonsensical world of Tiki, and were hoping to get away from a lot of the usual trappings you see in Tiki bars and instead focus on its less-explored aspects,” Pourzanjani said, noting there’s usually a long wait list on the weekends with guests thirsting for an array of frightful libations.

Paradise’s beast of a menu boasts 25 bespoke cocktails, plus an extra eight available exclusively for October and November. Each one has fewer than 12 ingredients “in true Tiki fashion,” according to Pourzanjani.

Among them is a crowd favorite, The Pumpkin Pie Tie, a stand-out made with a blend of Ron Del Barrilito 2 Star, Jamaican, Venezuelan and Martinique rums, along with pumpkin spice, Sichuan peppercorn and a brown butter maple gardenia.

“My hope is to always keep Halloween open to the public, never charge a cover or ticket fee, and make certain it’s one helluva good time.”

A short walk on from Paradise lies The Haunting on E 9th Street, a spooktastic spectacle that has taken over The Cabinet Mezcal Bar.

For this month only, the bar has traded its usual look for one crawling with ghosts and goblins — complete with spooky cocktails, including a mezcal-based ‘clown pear-anoia’ and a whiskey ‘poison apple,’ some even served in skull-shaped glasses.

“Halloween resonates everywhere, and I think that bodes well for building a destination around it,” Joann Spiegel, the Vice President of Miracle Inc., told The Post of her viral pop-up company, which completely takes over a former concept for the holidays.

This year, Miracle is taking over 40 bars all over the US. That includes another Haunting concept over in Bushwick, in the usual home of Vacations.

The ghoulish operation traces its roots to NYC in 2014, when founder Greg Boehm — an NYC cocktail star behind acclaimed bars including Mace, Katana Kitten and Super Bueno — was opening a stand-alone bar that was delayed due to construction

“It wasn’t cosmetically ready, so his mother said, ‘Why don’t you just hide everything behind Christmas decorations?’ They didn’t know what they were creating at the time, but it became absolute insanity; people couldn’t get enough of it.”

Eventually, the viral bar became the holly jolly-themed Miracle, their global Christmas pop-up. That holiday concept then expanded to Halloween, with the Christmas version opening its doors shortly after The Haunting ends.

Fun decor and festivities aside, running a ghoulish pop-up is not for the faint of heart.

“It’s like opening a brand new restaurant in an extremely-shortened timeline,” said Spiegel, who noted that planning takes years.

“The entire aesthetics of these bars change, from the hand soap to the beverage napkins, both outside and inside, let alone the menu,” she says, noting a mad scramble to switch everything as quickly as time allows, which usually takes a grueling four days.

Spiegel declined to disclose how much the massive makeover costs.

At The Haunting, the witchy cocktails are just as festive as its surroundings, including the Widow’s Whisper, a frightful, flavor-packed blend of vodka, chocolate, melon, lychee, matcha, yuzu, cardamom and rose, finished with a dash of absinthe.

For the bars they transform, the payoff is worth the scramble, according to Spiegel.

“Everybody comes back again and again because it does increase business; they cut through the noise to give people a destination to celebrate,” she said.

“We get bigger every year.”

But a booming business can bring its own set of headaches.

“With a pop-up you’re not flying completely blind, but you do have moments like; ‘Oh, my God, we already sold all of our mugs after two weeks,” Erin Hayes, co-founder of another Halloween hideaway, The Black Lagoon, told The Post.

This month, The Black Lagoon has taken over Boerum Hill’s Someday Bar, one of 34 bars across the country being transformed by the company for 2026. The result is a kitschy horror fever dream brought to life.

Inside, Someday is transformed into a spooky underwater haunted seabed, complete with a cast of custom sea monsters who haunt the space dreamed up by designer Kasira Hill. They include an octopus-witch named Abyssia.

The original concept began on a smaller scale.

“For our first one, we rented out a little space and just went for it with a three-week pop-up and the reception was insane,” recalls Hayes.

“We had people lined up around the block every night of the week,” she says, noting their busiest days are Fridays and Saturdays. To alleviate any sell-outs of custom goodies like ornate mugs, the company stores a backlog of merch ready to ship at a moment’s notice.

Cocktail creation, meanwhile, remains at the heart of the operation. Hayes and co-founder Kelsey Ramage consider it one of their “first loves,” spending months developing gourmet twists on classic drinks.

“Our favorite from the very beginning was Abyssia’s Obsession, which I would describe as a Pumpkin Spice Pina Colada,” Hayes muses of the creamy orange libation.

It includes a deliciously unsettling mixture of pumpkin-infused Kraken Rum, along with fruity pineapple and coconut, and Lustau Sherry “to dry it out a touch, so it’s not so in your face.”

But for Hayes, it’s more than just elaborate décor and festive drinks

“Things in this world are so heavy right now, so Halloween itself is a time to let go of the shackles of being a grown-up and let out your inner child a bit.”

“I’ve been to Black Lagoon the last two years and there’s a lot to love about it,” said the aforementioned Naglich.

“Even though the cocktail presentations here are a bit extreme, the flavors of the drinks are dialed in and balanced. You can tell there are veteran bartenders behind the event, not just people trying to cash in.”

Letting go of your inhibitions is also the eerie ethos at Midtown’s towering Dark Magic Hour, located on the 18th floor of the Moxy Times Square.

Normally the home of Magic Hour Rooftop Bar and Lounge, which boasts sweeping skyscraper-accented vistas, the space’s seasonal concept is inspired by horror films, including “Practical Magic,” right down to a Midnight Margarita on the menu, which was famously featured in the film.

“We approached it almost like building a movie set,” Christian Parker, Director of Marketing at TAO Group Hospitality, told The Post of the space, which features floating candles and tarot cards, all revolving around a massive ‘Wishing Willow’ tree; the result of a collaborative process between the company’s design and production partners.

“We wanted it to feel cinematic and nostalgic.”

Guests are also invited to make a wish at the centerpiece tree, while Dark Magic Hour’s menu includes a luscious Bloody Chocolate Fondue, which features a black cauldron of creamy strawberry chocolate alongside graham crackers and marshmallows.

“In New York, people are always looking for an experience that feels immersive and transportive,” said Parker.

“Halloween gives us an opportunity to completely transform a familiar space and create something guests can experience beyond just going out for a drink or dinner.”

A 7-year-old disabled girl is battling for her life after she was callously targeted by mass shooter Griffin J. John II and shot in the face — but loved ones say the student has always been a “fighter.”

Little Saylor Graham is in serious but stable condition in the wake of the tragedy, which claimed the lives of three other students and a teacher, Central Oregon Daily reported.

She was already well known in the community for her bubbly personality and her pink glasses, and as the high school’s adopted “Sparrow” — meaning the teenagers helped raise money to fund her medical expenses.

“Saylor is the definition of light and joy. And one of those kids that, you know, when she’s in the room. You can’t think of anything else other than what Saylor’s doing; ‘I need to get to know her,'” Matt Sampson, Sparrow USA’s executive director, told the outlet.

“She’s just very inspirational, very joyful, very courageous, and inspirational.”

Saylor was adopted by Bend Senior High School as part of the nationwide program in the 2024-25 academic year.

According to a 2024 announcement, the “sweet, happy, adorable, and resilient” girl battles CASK, a gene mutation that impacts her physical and cognitive development, as well as dysphagia, a disorder that makes it difficult for her to swallow food and drink.

At the time, she was a 5-year-old Kindergartener at Silver Rail Elementary School, the same school where John, 17, would unleash the bloodshed years later.

She was also nonverbal and frequently used a wheelchair, though was able to walk on her own.

As part of the Sparrow program, the high schoolers were encouraged to “earn money for Saylor through sponsored community service, supporting her and cheering her on as her family continues to navigate her medical journey.”

“Saylor was the Sparrow catalyst for Bend High School when she was a Sparrow, and the little girl was used to teach kids things that many of us probably couldn’t have taught them without her,” Sampson told the newspaper.

“She’s a fighter, and we’re praying that she fights through this and her family. I want to express to her family how much we love them and how valuable they are to us,” he continued.

“We’re here for them in whatever way we can be. They’re fighters, and they’ll need a lot of support. I’m so glad this community is giving it to them, but they’re fighters, and I believe in them.”

In a Facebook post by the Central Oregon Daily sharing the story, Kaylub Giamanco, the hero father who fatally shot John during the attack, wrote that he was hoping to connect with the little survivor.

“I would really like to reach out to this family and this beautiful little girl,” Giamanco wrote.

Community members have expressed their prayers for Saylor  — and a community fundraiser by a local restaurant is planned for the Sunday.

“We’re coming together for 7-year-old Saylor as she bravely heals from unimaginable tragedy,” Portello Lounge said in a flyer.

Saylor and teacher Becky Drury, 54, are the only two shooting victims who survived — but both remain in serious condition. Saylor was reportedly struck in the face, NBC News reported.

Three students, 5-year-old Rhoam Summer, an 8-year-old, and an 11-year-old, and teacher Megan Lambert, 25, were killed.

Investigators say John stormed into the Oregon elementary school’s special education classroom Thursday and fired at least 15 shots before a teacher tackled him to the ground. That’s when Giamanco rushed in and fatally shot him.

Police are still probing what John’s motive for the horrifying attack was, but cops say he went to extreme lengths to carry out the bloodshed.

John’s weapon had been legally purchased by his mother, Shauntai Nickerson, around the time of his August birthday, sources said.

Geoscience Australia registered a 3.0-magnitude earthquake aftershock in south-eastern Victoria on Saturday afternoon. (Reuters - file image)

A 3.0-magnitude earthquake aftershock has been recorded in south-eastern Victoria, three weeks after an initial late-night quake woke thousands.

Geoscience Australia said the quake hit at a shallow depth of 5 kilometres just after 2pm, and the epicentre was at Kardella South, near Korrumburra.

There were no reports of injuries or damage due to the quake.

A 3.0-magnitude earthquake aftershock has been recorded near the Victorian town of Korumburra, three weeks after an initial late-night quake woke thousands.

Geoscience Australia said the quake hit at a shallow depth of 5 kilometres just after 2pm, and the epicentre was at Kardella South, near the Gippsland town, which is about 135km south-east of Melbourne.

The federal agency's website cited more than 200 felt reports in the area — far fewer than the October 3 initial quake. There have been no reports of injuries or damage.

Respondents to Geoscience Australia registered felt reports close to the epicentre between 2pm and 3.30pm Saturday, as well as the Latrobe Valley and suburban Melbourne. (Geoscience Australia)

Monash University's School of Earth, Atmosphere and Environment earthquake geologist Dee Ninis said aftershocks were often registered some time after an earthquake.

"Aftershocks are felt hours, days, even weeks after an initial earthquake. Because it occurred in the same area as the earthquake earlier this month and was of a lower magnitude than the initial earthquake, it is an aftershock," Dr Ninis said.

"Often there's hundreds of aftershocks after an earthquake and the majority are usually too small to be felt.

"The Gippsland Basin is a region of heightened seismic activity relative to some other regions. Back in 2009, there was a magnitude 4.7 which was followed by a similar magnitude earthquake about two weeks later. There was also a magnitude 4.4 quake in the Gippsland basin in 2011."

Dee Ninis says aftershocks are often felt some time after the initial quake. (Supplied)

Dr Ninis said the October 3 and 17 Gippsland tremors were "unrelated seismic events" to the 2021 Woods Point earthquake, which rattled greater Melbourne five years ago.

The magnitude 5.9 earthquake, which struck in September 2021, was centred near the tiny town near Mansfield, about 130 kilometres north-east of Melbourne.

Although it caused only minor damage, the earthquake was larger than the 1989 Newcastle earthquake, which killed 13 people.

The 2021 quake caused some damage to buildings in Melbourne, including on the famous Chapel Street shopping strip in South Yarra.

Nine of 13 people killed in the Newcastle earthquake were inside the city's Workers Club that collapsed when the earthquake hit on December 28, 1989.

South Gippsland Shire mayor Nathan Hersey said he hadn't personally noticed the latest aftershock but added that seismic activity remained a hot topic of conversation locally.

"People are still talking about the initial earthquake and there's been several aftershocks since," Cr Hersey said.

"I was at a community breakfast in Arawata, which is the town at the epicentre of the initial earthquake, and people are still talking about it weeks down the track. Earthquakes are a fascinating topic."

More than one in four Americans cannot pay all of their monthly bills, according to a concerning new survey.

A troubling 27% of adults surveyed by Pew Research Center admitted they can only pay some of their monthly dues or make partial payments — a slight uptick from the share who said the same during COVID in 2020.

Twenty-four percent of Americans surveyed in April 2020 said they couldn’t make all their monthly bills, according to the pollsters.

Meanwhile, the majority of Americans (60%) said they don’t currently have enough income to lead the kind of life they want — while 53% said they don’t have emergency funds to cover expenses for three months.

The survey was conducted on more than 5,000 adults on Aug. 24-30, 2026.

Around a third (32%) said they worry nearly every day about the cost of healthcare and the amount of debt they have.

“We asked Americans a series of questions about their financial stability and security, their ability to afford basic necessities, and their general outlook on their personal financial situation,” Pew said in the report.

“The survey, conducted in August, finds that many Americans are not on solid financial footing.”

Overall, roughly 44% said they have had trouble paying for at least one basic necessity, including rent, mortgage and transportation, in the past year.

And forget fun expenses.

A total of 70% of US adults said they had to cut back on spending money on extras — including eating out, streaming services and other entertainment — in the past year, according to the survey.

Roughly 54% also said they have not been able to save money for the future.

For the study, researchers asked Americans questions about rent and mortgages, whether they’ve been laid off recently, and if they’ve needed to take out a loan, and more.

A New York-based dairy company recalled one lot of raw milk cheddar cheese that was distributed to a slew of states — including the Empire State — due to E. coli contamination concerns.

Family Farmstead Dairy pulled a batch of Raw Milk Cheddar Cheese that has a best-by date of July 22, 2027 on Thursday that was distributed to stores in New York and New Jersey, according to a company announcement shared by the US Food and Drug Administration.

The batch of raw cheddar cheese may potentially be contaminated with E. coli, the company shared.

The potentially plagued cheese was also recalled in Pennsylvania, Connecticut, Maryland, Virginia and Massachusetts — but may have been distributed to other states through downstream distributors, the announcement said.

The Worcester-based dairy company distributes a variety of their products to grocers across the country, including Whole Foods Market and Fresh Direct, according to its website.

No other Family Farmstead Dairy products have been affected by the recall.

Family Farmstead Dairy said the issue was discovered after a sample in Maryland isolated two strains of a toxin producing E. coli in two samples of the cheddar cheese.

No illnesses or allergic reactions related to the recalled cheese had been reported at the time the company made its announcement Thursday.

“We sincerely apologize to our customers, retail partners, and consumers for the inconvenience caused by this recall,” Family Farmstead Dairy said in its recall announcement.

“Product quality is an utmost priority here at Family Farmstead so we are committed to identifying the cause of this issue and taking all necessary corrective actions to ensure the continued safety and quality of our products.”

E. coli can cause diarrhea, often with bloody stools but most healthy adults can completely recover in a week.

Some people, however, can develop a form of kidney failure — Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS) — which can lead to severe kidney damage and possibly death.

HUS is most likely to occur in young children and elderly people.

The Post reached out to Family Farmstead Dairy for comment.

A Texas Democratic congressional candidate’s campaign reported more than $4,300 in spending on cookies, Mexican restaurant purchases and beer and wine earlier this year, according to federal election records, drawing renewed attention after a heated debate in which she apologized for a remark about her Republican opponent “making fun of Nazis.”

Katy Padilla Stout, the Democrat nominee for Texas’ 23rd Congressional District, reported expenditures totaling $4,338.14 in five transactions in March and April, according to spending details cited in an August report by RedState and records attributed to the Federal Election Commission (FEC).

The reported purchases included $675 for cookies for a campaign event, $1,289.22 at Total Wine and $2,373.92 at Las Guitarras Cocina Mexicana.

The expenditures have also become a line of attack for Republican Brandon Herrera, whose campaign website showcases the cookie purchase and accuses Stout of using donor funds to pay for the treats.

According to the spending details, the campaign reported a $675 payment dated March 30 with the stated purpose “COOKIES FOR EVENT.” Herrera’s website identifies the payee as Denise Gamboa Zelle and categorizes the expense as a campaign event expenditure.

Additional transactions included $1,089.08 at Total Wine on April 21 and $200.14 the following day, both described as “BEER AND WINE.”

The campaign also reported payments of $2,027.52 and $346.40 to Las Guitarras Cocina Mexicana on April 27 and April 28, respectively, according to the transaction details.

In a statement to Fox News Digital, Stout said the disbursements “were for campaign and fundraising events which were attended by our supporters.”

“Sugar cookies, particularly Texas-shaped ones, hold a special place in Texan culture,” she said. “We bought ours at a local bakery because we believe in supporting small businesses.”

The filings establish that the campaign reported the expenditures but do not establish whether the purchases were improper, whether any were for personal use or how many people attended the associated events.

The spending has attracted criticism from Herrera’s campaign, which maintains an opposition website, The Real Katy Stout.

Under a section labeled “Cookie gate,” the site highlights the $675 expenditure and displays the reported purpose, “COOKIES FOR EVENT.”

The website also criticizes Stout’s positions on immigration, taxes and other issues.

The spending questions come as the two candidates compete for a congressional seat representing one of the country’s largest districts along the southern border. During Tuesday’s televised debate in San Antonio, Stout also drew attention for an unusual exchange involving Herrera’s online videos.

“He made millions of dollars after making jokes online, making fun of Nazis, making fun of all of these things that we know he does not need to be doing,” Stout said in a heated moment during the debate.

Herrera responded, “And here I thought making fun of Nazis was a good thing.”

Stout later apologized and clarified her criticism after closing remarks.

“I apologize, I did misspeak,” she said. “He chooses to goose-step on YouTube for clickbait and money so that he can promote that type of ideology. He chooses to shame women.”

The exchange was part of a debate hosted by WOAI/KABB, during which the congressional candidates also sparred over gun rights, immigration and the cost of living.

Stout told Fox News Digital “mocking Nazis is fine, and that is not what I objected to, nor is that what my opponent does.”

“I object to content that trivializes veteran suicide, rape, child murder, women’s bodies and the Holocaust, the type of content he churns out,” she added. “You can hear his disgusting commentary straight from his own mouth at HeReallySaidThat.com.

“Do I think he promotes Nazi imagery? Yes. In a video posted 5/24/22, he goose-steps to ‘Erika,’ and touts an MP-40 machine gun. In another video posted 6/23/20, he said ‘for the fatherland’ before firing a Nazi-made STG 44, calling it ‘like a religious experience.’

“Calling it a joke doesn’t change what it is: giving a platform to Nazi symbols and weaponry for clicks and money. In my view, the ‘I’m only joking’ defense is a familiar tactic among neo-Nazi and antisemitic content creators. His content has attracted bipartisan condemnation, including the Republican Jewish Coalition, which called my opponent ‘a goose-stepping extremist who pals around with online Nazis.'”

Stout, a former teacher and child welfare attorney, has emphasized affordability and corruption as central themes of her campaign.

Herrera, a firearms manufacturer and online personality who has adopted “Let’s Go Brandon” as his campaign slogan, has campaigned on border law enforcement, tax reductions and Second Amendment protections.

The two are vying to replace former Republican Rep. Tony Gonzales, who resigned earlier this year after acknowledging an affair with a staffer.

Texas’ 23rd Congressional District stretches from the San Antonio area toward El Paso and includes hundreds of miles of the US-Mexico border. Early voting begins Oct. 19, with Election Day scheduled for Nov. 3.

The campaign for Brandon Herrera did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital’s request for comment.

The 5-year-old Queens girl battered to death by her mother suffered gruesome injuries to her heart, eyes, lungs, and brain, prosecutors revealed Friday — as the confessed killer was held without bail.

The disturbing details emerged as Francis Cabello, who chillingly told a 911 operator, “I killed my daughter,” was arraigned in Queens Criminal Court on second-degree murder charges.

First responders discovered the youngster, Fabiana Cabello, in her South Richmond Hill home just before 7 p.m. Wednesday after her 32-year-old mother made the harrowing confession.

Franklin Cabello, the grandfather of the victim, told reporters outside court in Spanish, “As a family, we feel mentally and physically destroyed. We can’t think [clearly] but we put our confidence in God.”

“She was very respectful, quiet, and she always treated me like a father, she treated me with respect… She loved her daughter… She wasn’t in control. She didn’t make this decision in her right mind. She was under some kind of influence”

“I forgive my daughter,” he said with tears in his eyes.

When officers arrived at the family’s home, they immediately began CPR on the unconscious child.

“But given the severity of her condition, they didn’t even wait for an ambulance,” Assistant District Attorney Lindsey Ruzza said, describing how police placed the girl in a patrol car and rushed her to Jamaica Hospital, where she was pronounced dead.

Ruzza explained the mom made several statements to police “in reference to not only killing the child but wanting to have killed her child.”

The young girl was allegedly in good health and running around her home for hours before her mother brought her to a second-floor bedroom, locked the door and emerged alone 45 minutes later to call 911.

Fabiana was found by first responders face down on the floor with blood coming out of her nose.

Francis and her daughter were the only two people in the room, police said.

At the time of her arrest, Francis appeared stoic and didn’t shed a tear while she was carted away in handcuffs, according to a neighbor who identified himself as Carlos.

“She was not crying, it was like nothing happened,” he told The Post.

“It’s too much emotions together. I feel sad for the child.”

Erika Santiago, 43, a licensed practical nurse who lives across the street, said she heard “a lot of yelling” Wednesday night before the emergency response.

“I heard about this when I woke up this morning at 6 o’clock and it’s absolutely devastating, devastating,” said Santiago, who has two daughters of her own, 10 and 12.

“And it’s right across the street and they brought her to the hospital I work at. It’s so close to home.”

An autopsy conducted by Dr. Lin of the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner revealed scrapes to the child’s face, petechiae in her eyes, heart and lungs, a swollen brain, bruises to her extremities, and intramuscular hemorrhaging on her shoulder blade and lower back — findings consistent with asphyxiation, according to court documents and prosecutors.

Additional reporting by Marie Pohl

Kelly said her team immediately contacted the U.S. Capitol Police, which she said is also investigating the incident. The police force didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

The Illinois State Board of Elections evacuated its offices Thursday when it received a suspicious letter, which was taken as part of the investigation by the FBI. gen-z-trump-voters-regret:
Elena Moore

President Trump speaks at a campaign rally in San Antonio on Oct. 7. Trump made big inroads with young voters in 2024, but some of that support appears to be waning.
                
                    
                    Mandel Ngan/AFP via Getty Images
                    
                
                hide caption

Gen Z Americans were a key part of President Trump's winning coalition in 2024. Nearly two years later — and with early voting underway in multiple states for the midterms — some of that youth support has faded.

That sentiment was on display in a focus group, conducted last week, of eight Generation Z Trump voters, who reported varying degrees of unhappiness and disappointment over the state of politics, with some going as far as to say they regret supporting Trump in 2024.

The conversation was conducted virtually by Navigator Research, a left-leaning polling group. Participants ranged in age from 20 to 29 and spanned five states: Florida, Mississippi, Ohio, Texas and South Carolina — places Trump won by double digits in the last election. Two of those states, Texas and Ohio, are home to competitive races that could be key to control of the Senate.

For participants who now regret their vote for Trump, much of their frustration centers on what they see as a string of failed promises. When asked to give the president's job performance a letter grade, a majority of participants, 6 out of 8, assigned him a grade of either D or F, while two selected C.

"I just feel like nothing went correctly. I just feel like everything got worse," said John, a 29-year-old Black man from Florida. (Participants agreed to be part of the focus group on the condition that they be identified by only their first names.)

John, who identifies as a Republican and has voted for Trump since 2016, gave the president an F and said he now plans to support Democratic candidates this fall, in large part because of the strain he has felt from rising costs.

"I'm willing to give the other side a chance," he added. "I don't think they're going to make a total change. But things are just horrible right now for me. So I feel like even if they make one or two small changes, it will probably benefit me."

Though the focus group is not a nationally representative survey, the frustrations shared by participants echoed Navigator polling released in August, which found that nearly a third of Gen Zers — those under age 30 — regret voting for Trump, higher than older generations do.

Trump's rising unpopularity among young voters isn't in a vacuum. He has also lost ground with other key groups that shifted right in 2024, notably independents and Latino voters — and in a year when the Republican Party is facing political headwinds, it's unclear whether that expanded coalition from two years ago can show up at the same strength now.

While some voters, like John in Florida, do feel compelled to vote blue this cycle in response to Trump, 4 of the 8 who took part in the focus group said they still planned to back Republicans this year. Three said they'd vote for Democrats; one participant said she was still deciding.

Matthew, a 25-year-old Black man living in Texas, said he doesn't regret his support for the president and gave him a C grade.

"I feel like he's done a really good job closing the border," he said. "I also do appreciate his efforts in trying to end some of the conflicts that began under the last administration, besides the fact that the Iran conflict hasn't really worked the best, from my perspective."

He plans to vote in the midterm elections and argued that Trump will be able to carry out more of his agenda if Republicans can secure a larger majority in both the House of Representatives and the Senate, although national polls indicate that the GOP is more likely to lose seats.

But enthusiasm is a different question.

Courtney, a 20-year-old white woman based in South Carolina, said she doesn't regret her vote for Trump in 2024 and overall aligns with Republicans, but she did admit she has grown more distrustful of both major political parties, particularly on foreign policy.

"I just really do feel like we would be in this situation either way. … Education, the economy, everything else would be so much better if we weren't pumping money out into other countries that aren't ours," she said, referring to U.S. aid for Israel and the decision to go to war with Iran.

"I don't think it matters what side you vote on — that's why I voted red, because I agree with those policies more — but at the end of the day, what we do in the Middle East is going to be not at all up to [the] party [in power]," she said during the focus group.

That sense of political disaffection may underscore a growing challenge for both Republicans and Democrats moving forward as both try to repair ties with this generation.

"As we see people regret their vote for Trump, sour on the Republican Party and Republican policies, that doesn't necessarily mean that they're swinging right over to Democrats," said Melissa Toufanian, the managing director at Navigator.

Toufanian points to Navigator's own polling, which has found that even as the GOP has lost trust on economic issues, "it's not a one-for-one with Democrats gaining that trust."

"A lot of people are moving to this middle, this category that 'I don't trust either party,'" she said. "We are seeing people who are becoming increasingly pessimistic about our political parties and our political system, and they're not feeling strongly that either party can really deliver for them."

The Oregon teen who burst into an elementary school, killing three students and a teacher, used his mom’s shotgun to fire at a pickup truck before his deadly rampage, according to a report.

The unidentified 16-year-old shooter, a Bend resident, was heading towards Silver Rail Elementary School just before 1 p.m. Thursday when he was spotted by a man driving a red Toyota Tacoma pickup truck in the school’s parking lot, the Bend Source reported.

The boy was armed with a long gun, which a law enforcement source speaking on the condition of anonymity later told the Associated Press that the weapon was a pump-action shotgun his mom had bought.

The teen opened fire at the truck after the driver confronted him, shattering the rear window and leaving at least six large bullet holes in the car.

The boy then allegedly threw his weapon over a fence before jumping over onto the school’s property, while the man in the car called emergency dispatchers to report he had been “shot at multiple times by a person with a long gun.”

The shooter then picked his weapon up and fired several shots at the locks – breaking his way into the school, which serves children in kindergarten through fifth grade.

Cops arrived within three minutes of the first 911 call, but three kids, of the ages 5, 8 and 11, and a teacher were fatally shot. Another child, 7, and teacher, 54, were hospitalized in critical condition.

The boy was “shot by a community member who had seen [him] enter the school, pursued him into the school, and engaged him,” Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz told reporters at a press conference Thursday.

Authorities didn’t say if the shooter had previously attended the school, if he knew his victims or if the heroic bystander who stopped the teen had a concealed weapons permit.

The shotgun was purchased by the boy’s mom, a law enforcement source briefed on the shooting said.

In Oregon, a person must be 18 to buy rifles and shotguns and 21 to purchase a handgun. Those under 18 can possess non-handgun weapons if they have parental consent. It’s unclear if the shooter had consent to use his mom’s weapon.

Bend La Pines school district previously banned all people, including those with concealed handling licences, from carrying firearms on district property, Oregon Public Broadcasting reported in 2022.

A separate provision of state law does allow lawfully possessed guns on school grounds if they are unloaded and locked in a vehicle, the outlet reported.

Krantz has warned the investigation into the shooting will be “long” and there has been an outpouring of grief among officials.

Rep. Janelle Bynum (D-Oregon) lamented, “our kids are getting shredded.”

“The most heartbreaking thing, as the details have surfaced, is that we have a child involved in the killing of other children,” she told CNN’s Anderson Cooper Thursday.“Multiple families are being impacted. This continues to happen.”

Meanwhile, former Bend Mayor Jeff Eager said, “You can’t imagine that it happens here.”

“Bend is a place that people move to from bigger cities,” he told CNN.

“They move here because it’s relatively safe here, they move here because we have schools you can walk your kids to.”

Tina Kotek, the Oregon governor, thanked the community member who “”heroically intervened to ⁠stop further loss of life” but said no one “should have to live through this kind of day.”

“And as we learn more about the children and the adults who have been killed or injured, and their families and their ​loved ones, we are going to do a lot of crying, and we are going to cry together, and we’re probably going to cry privately,” she said.

With Post wires

Celebrating with the Chicago Bears has helped Brenda Mayfield-Anderson get through some grueling chemotherapy treatments after she was diagnosed with breast cancer.

Mayfield-Anderson, who lives in Lynwood with her husband Kenneth, was one of nine Advocate Health Care breast cancer patients to unveil a pink banner at halftime during the Chicago Bears game on Oct. 4 at Soldier Field, which ended up being a Bears victory over the New York Jets.

“It was awesome … it was amazing,” said Mayfield-Anderson. “It was really cool to be able to go out on the field and open the ribbon.

“It makes the journey a little lighter — being given this honor and feeling supported.”

Mayfield-Anderson and her family were also treated to a Halas Hall experience a few days earlier, meeting there with running back Kyle Monangai, who bestowed her and her family with gifts including a jersey. She also had the chance to customize two varsity jackets with patches, keeping one and presenting the other to Monangai, who wore it to Soldier Field the following game day.

“It makes the journey a little lighter — being given the honor and feeling supported,” she said.

The chance to share the experience with other breast cancer patients and their families also was uplifting, Mayfield-Anderson said.

She’s on her last cycle of chemotherapy at Advocate South Suburban Hospital in Hazel Crest and each dose gets that much harder, causing fatigue, nausea, vomiting and other harsh side effects. Next she’ll need a lumpectomy and another biopsy to find out how much radiation therapy will be needed.

But along the way, Mayfield has received unwavering support from her husband and five sons, as well as colleagues at Advocate Trinity Hospital in Chicago, where she’s a lead biomedical equipment technician and is known for sporting her Bears gear.

Her breast cancer diagnosis came about after a diagnostic mammogram and ultrasound she sought out after something felt off during a self-examination. Then the diagnostic mammogram and ultrasound, which can detect abnormalities in dense breast tissue, showed the cancer.

“It was shocking,” Mayfield-Anderson said. “In the beginning, it was quite overwhelming. Once you find out, you have difficulty feeling this is real. This is happening and my life is about to change.”

Dr. Barbara Krueger, medical director of breast cancer services at Advocate Christ Medical Center in Oak Lawn, who helps oversee Mayfield-Anderson’s care, said her breast cancer was a more aggressive form that required not only chemotherapy, but also monoclonal antibodies.

“This is a difficult, terrifying discussion to have with women who have just been diagnosed, often resulting in fear, resistance and denial,” said Krueger. “Brenda listened to the conversation with both Dr. Priyanka Reddy (a hematologist/oncologist at Advocate Trinity Hospital) and me, processed the information, asked extremely enlightened questions and agreed to proceed with this very effective protocol.

“She has done extremely well, and we plan an excellent outcome for her,” said Krueger.

Her supportive family, including her husband, who brings her meals in bed for several days after chemotherapy, and five sons, have helped. Four of her sons live nearby and she refers to them as Honorable 1, 2, 3 and 4.

“They started this thing for me (on) weekends before treatments,” said Mayfield-Anderson “They would come over, bring food, laugh and play cards with me.”

Though she loses her sense of taste after treatments, she’s kept her appetite up and said she loves the peach cobbler her sons bring. She’s managed to gain about 25 pounds since starting treatments.

Her husband, on the other hand, has lost about that much weight after having esophageal surgery in July.

“It’s time to take care of her now,” he said.

He was the reason she initially became a Chicago Bears fan, since he likes the team. She started watching games with him years ago.

Her faith has also been a big part of her perseverance.

“Faith over fear,” said Mayfield-Anderson, “My God is a good God, he’s ever-present, always there.”

Anderson-Mayfield still feels relieved she and her medical team caught the cancer early. She has some advice for both men and women who notice anything different in their breasts.

“If something changes, don’t wait to get it checked out because timing is everything,” she said.

Janice Neumann is a freelance reporter for the Daily Southtown.

Indonesia’s plummeting poverty rate, America’s largest wildlife bridge, and ‘a new era’ for the River Thames, plus more good news

The number of Indonesians living in extreme poverty has plummeted by almost 83% in just four decades, “impressive” new figures reveal.

While China has led the way in reducing extreme poverty in Asia – cutting it from 91% to almost zero in 40 years – Indonesia has not been far behind.

“In 1984, 86% of Indonesians lived on less than $3 (£2.26) per day; by 2025, this had fallen to less than 4%,” the nonprofit, Our World in Data, reported this week. “While it didn’t quite match China’s decline, it has still been impressive.”

Indonesia’s strong economic growth is credited with boosting living standards across the country. However, according to the World Bank, many Indonesians still live just above the poverty line and are at risk of falling into poverty.

The latest figures chime with data from Statistics Indonesia. In 2024, it put the extreme poverty rate at 9%, and suggested that some three million Indonesians had been lifted out of poverty in the last decade alone.

While such figures have been broadly welcomed, critics claim they are a result of social assistance, such as cash handouts, rather than gains in overall living standards. Nonetheless, millions of Indonesians are living more comfortably than before.

Image: benk.88

US president Donald Trump may have entered the White House on a pledge to “drill, baby, drill”, but his adventures abroad are accelerating the global shift to electric vehicles.

So finds a new report from the energy thinktank Ember. Of the 56 countries tracked by its researchers, 49 were shown to have broken records for the number of electric vehicles sold since Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz – through which a fifth of the world’s oil and gas transits – in response to US-Israeli launching air strikes on the country.

According to Ember, nations that led the way in electric vehicle adoption have insulated themselves significantly from the subsequent energy price shock, especially China. Its EV fleet, Ember says, has saved the country $14bn (£10.5bn) in oil imports since the crisis began.

Ember’s research also shows that it’s not just rich countries embracing battery powered vehicles, with the likes of Vietnam and Uruguay also rolling them out at pace. The US, meanwhile, is losing ground on other nations, it added.

“The countries that invested in electric vehicles before this crisis are now better protected, and a growing number are following,” said Euan Graham, a senior analyst at Ember. “Every electric car on the road reduces exposure to volatile oil markets.”

Image: Ake Ngiamsanguan

London’s new ‘super sewer’ has led to a “dramatic reduction” in sewage entering the River Thames, marking a “new chapter” for a waterway that was once declared biologically dead.

That’s according to a report from Thames Water, which recently took on the running of the 16-mile sewer. The beleaguered water firm, which faces re-nationalisation due to poor performance, reported an 86% decline in the amount of raw sewage entering the river since the tunnel opened.

The sewer has also prevented around 84 tonnes of litter, such as wet wipes and sanitary products, from reaching the waterway, it added. However, pollution and extreme weather still present “big challenges” for the capital, the firm warned, claiming further action was needed to prepare London for the effects of climate change.

Thames Waters’ Tess Fayers, said the report’s findings were “an important milestone for the river and a significant step towards a cleaner, healthier and more resilient Thames.”

Image: SHansche

A bridge built exclusively for wildlife has been credited with a 91% reduction in the number of animals being hit by vehicles on a busy US freeway.

The overpass in Colorado opened 10 months ago and has already been hailed a “huge success”, with elk (pictured), pronghorn and bears among the animals captured on camera using it to cross Interstate 25.

The $15m (£11.3m) bridge – North America’s largest wildlife crossing – opened last December, along with five underpasses, on a stretch of freeway that saw frequent collisions between vehicles and animals.

Not anymore. The Colorado Department of Transportation told Positive News this week that since the overpass opened, it has provided safe passage for scores of migrating animals, reducing collisions by 91%.

Image: Jaroslav Sugarek

All those walks to school and kickabouts in the park could be doing more for teenagers than previously thought, as a new study links higher step counts with better mental health.

Researchers tracked 5,515 young people in the US over a year. Participants wore Fitbits and were quizzed on their mental health using the Child Behaviour Checklist, a widely used questionnaire that measures anxiety, low mood and behavioural problems.

A link between step count and mental health emerged. Adolescents who took fewer than 5,000 steps a day were shown to have the most symptoms for poor mental health, while those hitting 12,000 or more had the fewest. Those with the highest step counts also showed thicker brain tissue in areas involved in movement and regulating emotion.

The findings add to a growing body of evidence linking physical activity with improved mental health.

“This study gives us some of the clearest evidence yet that even an everyday, low-cost, accessible measure of physical activity like daily step count is tied to how adolescent brains and mental health develop,” said Dr Divyangana Rakesh, senior lecturer in neuroscience and psychology at King’s College London, which led the research.

Image: monkeybusinessimages

Giant tortoises are “thriving” again in the Seychelles, a century after the species stood on the brink of extinction.

A survey of the Aldabra giant tortoise population on Aldabra Atoll has revealed 180,000 individuals living on the island – the highest figure ever recorded. It’s a remarkable turnaround for a population that was reduced to around 1,000 individuals in the 19th century, when the animals were persecuted to near-extinction. It means there are now more tortoises on the Seychelles than humans (135,000).

Aldabra Atoll is one of only two places where giant tortoises are found in the wild, with a smaller population living in Galápagos. The island was declared a nature reserve in 1982, and its tortoises have been subject to ongoing conservation efforts.

“More than 180,000 giant tortoises roaming freely on our atoll is proof of what long-term commitment to conservation can achieve,” said Dr Frauke Fleischer-Dogley, CEO of the Seychelles Islands Foundation. “This is wonderful news for Seychelles, for the world, and for everyone who has worked to protect Aldabra.”

Image: Chalabala

Reports of moths invading people’s homes might not sound like good news, but it’s a development welcomed by Australian scientists this week.

The sight of bogong moths swarming through the skies was once common in New South Wales as the species migrated to the mountains in summer before returning to their lowland breeding grounds in autumn.

However, the insect’s population has fallen dramatically since the 1980s due to drought and warming temperatures. In 2021, it was listed as an endangered species.

Recent weeks, however, have seen a huge resurgence in the moths. Footage posted online showed them swarming people’s homes – a phenomenon scientists think was made possible by a milder winter and more rainfall.

Prof Dieter Hochuli from the University of Sydney described the event as “one of the great animal migrations of the world”.

Image: Ken Griffiths

The share of land farmed organically in England will rise to 10% by 2036, the UK government promised this week, as it published its long-awaited organic farming plan.

It comes a week after the World Wildlife Fund warned that urgent changes to food production are required to halt biodiversity loss. That’s especially true in England, one of the world’s most nature-depleted nations, where just 3.4% of agricultural land is given over to organic farming (in France it’s 10.4%, and rising).

The UK government pledged on Wednesday to support more farmers in England to go organic. Details were thin, but public procurement and grant funding were mooted as potential levers to affect change.

The plan, said the government, “recognises how organic farmers can help maintain healthy soils, support biodiversity and produce food sustainably”. It’s also a response to growing demand for organic produce.

“More shoppers are choosing organic food and drink than a few years ago, yet the share of England’s farmland managed organically has barely moved,” the government said. “That gap is a chance for English producers.”

Related: Regenerative agriculture isn’t misty-eyed nostalgia, it’s the future

Image: WHPics

Almost five years after it was invaded by Russia, Ukraine has shown remarkable resilience in the face of war – and not just on the battlefield.

While the environment usually takes a backseat in times of conflict, Ukraine has continued with its rewilding efforts. Now, residents of one Black Sea city are taking the circular economy underground amid the threat of Russian strikes.

Chornomorsk is a hub for Ukraine’s repair movement, but has been subjected to Russian missile strikes. Ahead of International Repair Day on 17 October, organisers of Chornomorsk Repair Festival in Ukraine are relocating their event to an underground shelter.

“When we fix something broken, bring items back to life, or find new uses for them, we see the tangible results of our actions and feel that we can make a difference,” said Nataliia Pasenko, one of the organisers. “This simple experience can be especially important right now.”

Read the full story here.

Image: The Restart Project / Mark A Phillips

It’s been a culinary institution for 228 years, nourishing royals, politicians and celebrities, including Charles Dickens, who declared it his favourite restaurant.

Now, Rules of London – the city’s oldest restaurant  – looks set for another 228 years in business after it was donated to the National Trust.

The poet Sir John Betjeman, a Rules regular, famously described it as having an “invisible atmosphere just as a church frequented by praying people acquires an atmosphere”. That didn’t stop it from being threatened demolition in 1971, which it was ultimately spared from.

Now its future looks truly safe after owner, J-P Mayhew (pictured), gave the building to the trust. The charity will not run the restaurant, however, which will trade independently.

“This place is an outstanding piece of living history, with its corners where kings dined and writers and politicians plotted, and the traditions it kept alive through wars and upheaval,” said Hilary McGrady, director-general of the National Trust.

“It has defied the odds to be standing here today. Mr Mayhew’s extraordinary generosity … means this beloved place has a future measured not in years but generations.”
