As she faces up to a swathe of challenges from summer fires to West Coast Main Line reliability, GBR West Midlands Managing Director Denise Wetton says the newly integrated business is already seeing signs of welcome cultural change.

‘The blame culture, where it’s their fault or it’s their fault, or raiding the commercials of different organisations, that’s gone’, insists Denise Wetton, Integrated Managing Director of GBR West Midlands as she reflects on the near-100 day period since the West Midlands Trains business moved into public ownership under the government’s rail reforms.

Wetton has taken on the role of heading up what is now the GBR West Midlands integrated business unit, having previously led the Central Route at Network Rail for five years.

‘I’ve spent the last 90 days getting out into the business, talking to the front line and really understanding what we need to do together to improve’, she explains. But the five core principles that have shaped her career to date remain steadfast: safety, performance, making every pound matter, growing revenue and looking after her people.

Safety is a particular area of focus, amid rising concern about how safe the railway can sometimes be for its staff and passengers. ‘We work in a safety-critical environment, so getting colleagues home safe every day is fundamental to who I am’, she emphasises. As for the passengers, she recognises that the public often takes safety while travelling as a given, but ‘I think we need to really work on demonstrating how safe the railway can be’.

Speaking to Rail Business UK, Wetton reflects that her ‘big focus’ at the start was industrial relations. ‘Getting out there, talking to the front line has been key to actually changing the relationship with the front line, but also the trade unions. I think that’s been the biggest win. The close working with Network Rail Central Route and WM Trains has been brilliant; overnight, I saw the transformation happen.’

But this closer collaboration in the restructured West Midlands Integrated Business Unit was tested almost immediately when the railway between Stourbridge Junction and Hagley was severely damaged by a heatwave-related fire on August 13 that started next to the line. Wetton describes the fire as ‘one of the toughest [incidents] I’ve ever seen on the railway’, but she notes that the new entity was able to rebuild the infrastructure in just eight days.

‘Within hours, we managed to get a shuttle service from Stourbridge to Birmingham, from Kidderminster to Worcester, and have a rail replacement in the middle. We looked after the community and rebuilt a whole entire railway network in eight days, whilst looking after customers, communities and also keeping stakeholders on site. That, for me, was integration, and probably the best example I’ve seen.’

While she recognises that not all of the cultural traits of the privatised railway structure can be eradicated overnight, she is adamant that the ‘them and us’ mentality is shifting in the West Midlands already.

‘I feel that everyone wants to fix the problem, rather than saying “oh, it’s Network Rail’s fault”, which was usually the top response’, she says. The hub of the local — and arguably national — rail network is Birmingham New Street station, which she places at the vanguard of the changing culture. This is partly because New Street was an outlier in the pre-DFTO era as it was a major station where NR was responsible for all train dispatch, rather than any of the operators.

Describing it as ‘one of the pinnacle stations in the UK’, Wetton explains that ‘everyone’ working at the station knows they are there to help customers irrespective of the corporate badge they are wearing. ‘When I started in Central Route, I just made the decision that we wouldn’t put NR badges anywhere now around the station, it was the BR double arrows. Going forwards it will be GBR. So hopefully because of the structures at New Street, it’s more aligned to an integrated railway than another station that has a number of operators operating within it’, she adds.

While progress is being made on the organisational culture as track and train are brought together, the day to day challenge of running the railway remains, and Wetton is unambiguous that much work remains to be done.

Across the WM business, which covers two distinct operating brands — London Northwestern Railway serving London Euston and the West Coast Main Line, and West Midlands Railway — ‘we had a tough summer’, she admits. ‘We’ve got a lot of learnings that we’re going through’ to prepare for future hot and dry summer weather.

However, she points to ‘a real difference between WMR and LNR’, stating that ‘quite frankly, the performance on LNR is unacceptable, it is not where it needs to be, and that’s something that I’m working really hard on’. An immediate step has been to appoint Andy Boyle, previously West Midlands Trains’ Operations Director, as Service Delivery Director with particular responsibility for LNR services. ‘This is important for two reasons: one, we absolutely need to give customers a better journey, but we also need to focus on the two brands as distinctly different as well.’

But Wetton is sanguine about how far the operating environment and timetable constraints on the West Coast Main Line are a factor. ‘At the moment, I could probably eke out an 82%, 83% T3 [within three minutes of on-time measure] on a perfect day, and that’s with nothing [disruptive] happening across the network.’ But driving that metric up towards 90% will take work across numerous disciplines, she feels, including regulation, traincrew diagramming, timetabling and infrastructure resilience.

‘We need to fix the West Coast, because if we’ve got the ambition and the direction for 90% T3, there’s no chance of ever achieving that level of train performance if we don’t invest in it.’ A completely fresh timetable once GBR is established may be possible, but implementing it will not be easy or quick, she believes, with 2028 a tentative target for a recast.

Wetton confirms that for the time being the sub-brands WMR and LNR will continue to be managed as part of WM Trains; there are suggestions that eventually under GBR, LNR could become part of the West Coast business unit. ‘There’s been no firm decision yet on the future of LNR, in future we will look to ask if it is the right thing to do. In the meantime we will be able to make use of the better integration within GBR in terms of discussions about the timetable and capacity.’

With Chiltern Railways having moved into DFTO ownership on September 20, Wetton says that there is plenty of successful collaboration from previous years that GBR WM can draw upon. ‘Chiltern Railways is quite a contained railway with Network Rail. We are now able to look at how WM Trains can learn from Chiltern, and how Chiltern can learn from WM Trains.’ She says that key interfaces between the businesses exist at Stratford and Dorridge, and on the Snow Hill line. ‘When I was in my Network Rail role, we did some good work between Network Rail, Chiltern and WM Trains in 2023, where we looked at the timetable, and had a grown up conversation about what was the best solution for reliability.’

This co-operation should be easier to expand under the nascent GBR as revenue allocation between operators is much less relevant; she points to the December 2026 timetable change where Chiltern will be increasing its trains between Stourbridge Junction and London Marylebone via Birmingham, adding vital peak-time capacity through Snow Hill and Moor Street stations.

Yet as with the performance metrics, there is no shying away from the capacity constraints that exist across the West Midlands transport network. While in the medium term, the aspiration among local policymakers remains that the Midlands Rail Hub needs to be fully funded and delivered, some short term gains are in the works. Wetton highlights the return to main line use of the fourth platform at Birmingham Snow Hill station; it had been used by Midland Metro light rail services between 1999 and 2015.

‘Platform 4 is the first element of the Midlands Rail Hub, it gives us resilience’, Wetton explains, adding that an early proposal to create a bay platform facing towards Moor Street in order to accelerate the project was quickly abandoned in favour of restoring its original functionality.

Nevertheless, around New Street, spare capacity is close to being exhausted, Wetton acknowledges. The trade-offs are already being made: the introduction of two trains per hour serving the recently opened stations on the Camp Hill line have taken potential paths from the Cross-City suburban service, hindering attempts to restore that route to a six trains/h offering. Meanwhile, LNR is adding a new hourly New Street to Crewe service in December as a precursor to a May 2027 extension of this service to Manchester Airport.

‘New Street is getting to its limit in terms of operating the station itself, whether that’s through dispatch or through signalling the actual station itself’, Wetton admits. ‘If we need growth across the network, then new services would need to be reviewed on a case by case basis. We’re currently doing a study on the corridor which includes New Street to look at if there is any opportunity to get anything more in. My view at the moment is operationally there isn’t.’

However, external pressure is mounting, spurred on by investment in the wider city. The Sports Quarter development is a £3bn scheme to the east of the city that will see the construction of a new stadium for Birmingham City FC among other elements, and a £400m allocation has been made by the national government to upgrade Adderley Park Station and extend the West Midlands Metro tram lines directly into the regeneration zone. With completion expected in time for the start of the 2030-31 football season, the clock is ticking to find ways to deliver additional capacity within the capacity and financial constraints the industry faces.

‘It’s a huge investment into the UK economy’, Wetton reflects, but it needs a transport system. ‘We’re working hand-in-hand with the Combined Authority and Transport for West Midlands to ask “what does rail need to do and what does Adderley Park need to do in the new model?”’

Returning to the GBR transition, Wetton warms to her theme of cultural and people-centric change.
‘Bringing drivers and signallers together was an iconic moment for me, because that’s how we run our railway, operationally’, she enthuses. ‘I had a train planner from Network Rail sat with a driver, talking about the timetable and what the driver sees and what the train planner then puts into the system. That was priceless. I was thinking, goodness, imagine what the future can be!’

Given the constraints on the West Midlands rail network, she sees greater interaction between former NR and TOC staff as especially important. ‘We’ve done something that we’ve called Coffee Roulette — basically you put your name in a hat and you get connected to somebody in Network Rail. Then the idea was that you’d go and have a coffee and learn about what they’re doing, and it could be anybody. We’ve started to do a lot of that and had quite a lot of success, just to help with that understanding.’

The gloves were off.

Hudson Valley Rep. Mike Lawler ripped his Democratic challenger Cait Conley over her support for sanctuary state policies and portrayed her as a phony New Yorker in their final debate.

The two candidates for New York’s hotly contested 17th Congressional District came out swinging in the Wednesday night televised showdown on Pix11, trading barbs over ICE and immigration policies.

In one particularly feisty exchange, Conley accused Lawler of “mansplaining” when they were asked about the Cornell University gang rape case.

Early on in the deabte, Lawler, the Republican incumbent seeking his third term, said the high-profile ICE shooting last week in the Big Apple could have been prevented if local law enforcement were able to cooperate with federal immigration officers.

“[Gov.] Kathy Hochul’s disastrous new law — which Conley supports — prohibits cooperation,” fumed Lawler.

“We’re talking about a gangbanger who came into this country illegally,” Lawler said, referring to Oscar Begal, the Dominican Republic native and alleged Trinitarios gang member shot by ICE agents in The Bronx as he tried to evade arrest.

“You want accountability, so do I. Let’s start by actually enforcing the law in this country,” Lawler fumed.

He argued that Begal’s prior arrests on robbery charges should’ve triggered deportation proceedings, but New York’s lax bail laws paired with local and state policies that discourage law enforcement from working with ICE allow them to slip through the cracks.

He further attacked Conley, saying she “ran around” a question at their previous debate posed by the parents of Sheridan Gorman, a Yorktown Heights 18-year old college freshman killed by an illegal migrant in Chicago.

“What happened to Sheridan Gorman should never have happened,” Conley replied after Lawler repeatedly pressed her.

“He should’ve been deported. He should’ve been turned over to federal immigration officials,” Conley finally conceded, referring to Gorman’s killer.

But while she maintained that law enforcement should have the ability to cooperate with federal immigration enforcement to go after “violent” criminals, she also expressed support for Hochul’s legislation that would bar counties from entering agreements with ICE to do so.

“I do not believe that our local tax dollars funding our local law enforcement should be going to doing the federal government’s job,” Conley told reporters afterwards, dancing around getting into specifics about what anti-ICE restrictions she supports and doesn’t.

Conley repeatedly tried to connect Lawler to the president, saying he “votes with Donald Trump 100% of the time.”

Lawler countered by dismissing the 100% figure as bogus and touted bipartisan accomplishments as well as endorsements from Democrats such as outgoing Maine Rep. Jared Golden.

But Lawler unsurprisingly tried to pin Conley to her party’s respective radical bogeyman – Mayor Zohran Mamdani.

“Last debate, Cait was given four opportunities to condemn Zohran Mamdani’s antisemitism and she refused each time only for him to issue the most vile antisemitic statement on Oct. 7,” Lawler said once again demanding she condemn the lefty mayor.

Conley, who distanced herself from the Democratic Socialists of America, was bullied into denouncing Mamdani’s statement last week appearing to fault Israel for the Oct. 7, 2023 Hamas attack.

“Yes I do denounce Mamdani’s statement on October 7th,” she said.

The incumbent also tried to paint Conley — who grew up in the greater Hudson Valley, attended West Point and then moved out-of-state with the Army — as a carpetbagger.

“I know you just moved here from Virginia,” Lawler sniped during one of many snide digs the two exchanged.

Conley returned to New York after living and working in Washington, DC, in national security after serving in the Army.

Conley owns homes in Alexandria, Virginia, and Sanford, North Carolina. She now leases a house on Inningwood Road in Ossining, which is in the district.

It was just one of many quick witted attacks between the two, who came off as polished and largely unflustered amid the scrap.

The two got particularly spirited when sparring over the topic of sexual harassment – asked about the role congress could play in preventing another incident like the alleged gang rape of a woman at Cornell University in 2024.

While the two both agreed in substance that congress could address Title IX statutes to prevent breakdowns like critics allege allowed the Cornell case to go unprosecuted, Lawler tried to call Conley out for accepting donations from former Gov. Eliot Spitzer, who was caught participating in a prostitution ring, though never faced charges

“You refuse to return those funds. You refuse to denounce him in any way?”

“I don’t need you to mansplain to me what domestic abuse and sexual assault against women is and the appropriate response, don’t start, sit over there,” Conley retorted, wagging her finger at Lawler as he called her “disgraceful.”

“I do not need you to mansplain to me, Mike,” she added.

The candidates are neck and neck going into the debate, with recent polls finding them separated by a mere two points — and Conley was leading, 48% to 46%, per PIX11’s survey conducted by Emerson College.

That tight spread meant the stakes of Wednesday’s debate were higher than ever, with Emerson College Polling finding 7% of voters undecided — more than enough people to sway and tip the scales for a win in a district Lawler carried in 2024 despite it going for Kamala Harris, the Democrat.

New York’s 17th district covers Westchester County from the White Plains border as far north as Hopewell Junction as well as Rockland and Putnam Counties.

The district was tightly contested in the 2024 election, too, with Lawler winning by a close 52% to 45% — and a razor-thin 50.3% to 49.7% against then Democratic National Congressional Committee Chairman Sean Patrick Maloney in 2022.

The state of Florida won a key court decision Wednesday that allows it to enforce a ban on social media accounts for kids under 14 and other restrictions.

The law was one of the most restrictive in the U.S. on social media use by children when Gov. Ron DeSantis signed it in 2024.

The law implicates the First Amendment, an appeals court said, but “likely does so in a content-neutral manner.”

It would likely survive a full legal challenge “because it doesn’t burden substantially more speech than necessary to advance the important interest in protecting minors from social media addiction,” a panel from the 11th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals said in a 3-0 opinion.

The law bans social media accounts for Florida children under 14 and requires parental consent for use by kids who are 14 or 15.

Industry trade groups the Computer & Communications Industry Association and NetChoice sued Florida, arguing that the law violated the free-speech rights of social media providers and users.

A judge in 2025 said the law likely was unconstitutional and granted an injunction.

That injunction was put on hold while the appeals court heard the case. The lawsuit, with the injunction now overturned, will return to federal court in Tallahassee.

The appeals court noted that the law covers social media platforms “that have been determined to induce heavy use by children, and applies only to platforms that use both algorithms and one of several addictive features.”

An email seeking comment from the Florida attorney general’s office was not immediately answered. NetChoice said it was disappointed with the decision.

A&M BBQ in Sebastopol is now smoking its meat outside city limits and trucking the food back to the restaurant, a costly workaround that owner Kristopher Austin says cannot last.

The unusual arrangement follows a May 28 notice giving the restaurant 10 days to stop using its outdoor commercial smokers because they violated local zoning rules, SFGATE reported.

Rather than shut down the operation, Austin and co-owner Finn Liss have moved the equipment beyond Sebastopol’s borders and are hauling the finished barbecue back to customers.

But the logistical shuffle is taking a toll on the business.

The dispute is especially frustrating for the restaurant, which has already earned high-profile praise for its food. Fieri singled out A&M’s confit smoked oxtail at last year’s Healdsburg Wine & Food Experience, raving about the dish’s creamy, silky texture.

Austin and Liss opened the restaurant in June 2024 and are now hunting for a permanent solution that will let them expand without running afoul of city regulations.

In a mid-May Instagram statement, the owners said they had spent nearly a year searching for a location better suited to the restaurant’s growth.

But relocating a commercial smoking operation is no easy feat. Permits, infrastructure and financing can make an immediate move prohibitively difficult.

“Relocating a restaurant operation involving commercial smokers, permitting, infrastructure, and financing is a complex process that takes time, but we are committed to finding a responsible path forward,” the owners said.

City officials, meanwhile, have maintained that the smokers are not permitted at the restaurant’s Main Street location.

City Manager Mary Gourley confirmed the zoning restriction to SFGATE, which reported that officials first asked Austin to remove one of the smokers around March.

Austin put that unit into storage, but an April notice and the subsequent deadline followed.

The crackdown stems from complaints by nearby residents after A&M acquired larger commercial smokers last fall.

Dozens of complaints were filed, according to The Press Democrat, with residents raising concerns about smoke, air quality and traffic during a May 5 City Council meeting. The smokers’ towering stacks also drew objections, SFGATE reported.

Former Mayor Larry Robinson suggested high-tech filtration systems, but Austin has expressed concern about the expense.

The restaurant has also drawn a crowd of supporters as the dispute plays out.

Dozens attended a recent City Council meeting, including the president of the NAACP’s Santa Rosa-Sonoma County branch, which is representing Austin over concerns about fairness and transparency in the city’s handling of the case, The Press Democrat reported.

Russell Brand arrives at Southwark Crown Court in London on Wednesday. (Reuters: Jack Taylor)

The prosecution has made its opening statement in Russell Brand's trial for numerous sex offences.

In London on Wednesday, the court was told women were "simply a means to an end" for the entertainer.

The trial is expected to last several weeks.

A "ruthless, calculated and manipulative sexual predator". That is how the Crown Prosecutor has described British entertainer Russell Brand in her opening address at his trial for multiple sex offences on Wednesday.

For almost two decades, Brand was a stand-up comedian, popular TV and radio presenter, and eventually, a Hollywood movie star.

The 51-year-old is now in the dock at London's Southwark Crown Court, accused of three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault, and one count of indecent assault relating to six women over a 10-year period from 1999. He has pleaded not guilty to all seven charges.

Barrister Riel Karmy-Jones KC spent about two hours laying out the prosecution's case against the world-famous defendant on Wednesday morning, local time.

She told the court the women who will give evidence during the trial "did not know each other, have never met each other, and came forward independently of each other".

"Their paths all crossed the defendant's either through their employment, social events through work, or through attending gigs where he was performing," she said.

Ms Karmy-Jones told the jury of eight men and four women that each of the alleged victims' experiences occurred when Brand's career "was beginning to flourish".

She told the court Brand had met the women in different settings; one at a political conference, three in various media-industry settings (including radio stations), one at a London bar and one in the foyer of a venue where he was performing.

"Offending took place in a number of locations: a hotel room, workplaces, a toilet cubicle, in a bar, and at his home address," Ms Karmy-Jones told the court.

"Some of the women involved protested and said no, others had no opportunity to protest, but it mattered not to the defendant.

"Regardless of who they were and what they said or did, Russell Brand was not deterred. His desire, his strong desire, for some form of sexual contact was indiscriminate and voracious."

Russell Brand and his wife Laura Gallacher make their way past the cameras on Wednesday. (Reuters: Corey Rudy)

The Crown Prosecutor told the jury graphic details of the alleged sexual assaults the "demanding" and "entitled" Brand had inflicted on women who were left feeling "stupid" and "ashamed".

"To the defendant, women were simply a means to an end," Ms Karmy-Jones told the court, pointing out Brand was a much-younger man at the time of his alleged crimes.

"Over the years he may have changed both physically and as a person, however, despite that passage of time, his responsibility for wrongs done, and crimes committed at a younger age remain," she told the court.

The court heard Brand had declined to answer questions when police interviewed him about the allegations, but did provide written statements.

In these statements, Ms Karmy-Jones told the court, Brand claimed he did not remember the alleged incidents, had never engaged in non-consensual sexual activity, and that his accusers' accounts may have been "re-imagined".

The first prosecution witness called was Mark Pinheiro, who performed with Brand in cabaret shows on the sidelines of the 1999 Labour Party Conference, at which the first alleged victim claims she was raped.

Pinheiro told the court that in the car on the way from London to Bournemouth — where the conference was held — Brand had said "he hoped one day he would have slept with 5,000 girls".

Pinheiro also told the court several months after the conference, Brand told him he had sex with a woman while they were in Bournemouth and that "things got a little bit heated and a little bit out of hand".

During cross examination, Brand's barrister Ian Winter KC challenged Pinhero's evidence as inconsistent.

The trial before Mr Justice Joel Bennathan is expected to run for at least six weeks. Mr Brand's barrister Ian Winter KC will have the chance to set out the defence case later in the trial, which is the subject of significant global interest.

During proceedings Brand sat up straight in the dock and listened intently to what was being said.

Earlier, as he arrived for his trial with is wife Laura Gallacher, Brand told reporters he felt "blessed".

"I feel, of course, concerned but hopeful that this process will lead to good outcomes for everybody involved, that's my prayer," Brand said outside Southwark Crown Court.

The trial continues.

From Seattle’s chapter of National Public Radio comes the remarkable story of the kindness of strangers immortalized in an origami crane.

Published through KUOW’s “My Unsung Hero” series, the story begins with a 7-year-old in Japan who had just gotten a new bike.

Young Rika Matsuda was at first very excited because the bike was fast, much faster than her old one. Riding at the park, she was heading straight for the wall when she learned the new bicycle’s brakes didn’t work.

Into the wall she went, falling down and hurting her foot which began to turn purple before long. Seeing the incident, a man, whom Matsuda described as tall, strong, and wearing a suit, approached her. She was nervous and didn’t know if she could trust the stranger, who gave off the air of importance.

“But when he said, ‘Are you OK?’ I knew from his kind and gentle voice that he was a very nice man,” Matsuda recalled in her native Japanese to a translator, who relayed it to KUOW.

The man helped the young girl to her feet, took her to a water fountain where they washed the cut on her foot, and lent her his phone so she could call her grandfather. As they waited for the caretaker to arrive, the man took out a white piece of paper and, like a scene out of Japanese cinema, showed her how to fold an origami crane.

“He was really good at folding origami, and he taught me the right way to make a clean and beautiful crane,” she said. “Maybe he wanted me to think about the paper instead of my foot.”

When Matsuda’s grandfather arrived, the man helped get the bike and its rattled young owner back home. When parting came, the stranger handed the girl the origami crane without saying a word, before disappearing back into anonymity, and eventually, memory.

The memory lived on, though, through the white paper crane which she always kept on her desk, remembering his kindness whenever she looked at it.

A full decade later, and Matsuda was sitting in her high school English class, and the teacher, Benjamin Johnson, used NPR’s “My Unsung Hero” as a teaching workshop, asking each student to write details about an encounter with a Good Samaritan. That’s when Matsuda remembered the crane.

10 years of time had muddied the recollection, but she remembered the man and the crane, and his kindness above all. At that moment, Matsuda was seized by the urge to unfold the origami work and see if the man had written anything on the paper.

The trip home from school was done at some pace, and upon entering her room she carefully unfolded the crane to find—just as her premonition had held—a secret message.

Two characters, containing well-known Japanese idiom.

“We should treasure each time we cross paths with someone because it might never happen again,” Matsuda said, translating. More simply, she said it reminds the reader to “cherish the moment.”

“Then I realized even more how kind and how nice of a man he was,” Matsuda said—a true unsung hero.

The Iran war — among the most unpopular conflicts in modern U.S. history — has reportedly cost the average American household approximately $2,000, according to a new analysis.

Mark Zandi, the chief economist of financial intelligence firm Moody’s Analytics calculated the past eight months of war cost the American household this amount by analyzing fuel costs, interest rates, and tax dollars allotted towards the military, according to his Tuesday post to X.

Higher energy prices are contributing most to the costs. A gallon of regular goes for $4.37, up from just under $3 before the war. Diesel is above $6, and jet fuel has nearly doubled. As winter approaches, the much higher price of home heating fuel is also adding to the costs.

Energy costs contribute to the vast majority of this sum. The total consumer burden of additional gas and diesel costs since the onset of the war has amounted to over $100 billion, per a study from Brown University’s Climate Solutions Lab. The individual household bears $1,100 of these costs, according to Zandi’s calculations. In addition to car fuel, these costs also factor in home heating bills and the fuel of commercial vessels such as long-haul trucks and cargo planes.

The Department of War’s costs of the Iran conflict amount to approximately $38 billion as of Aug, 1, per the Congressional Budget Office. This price tag is forecasted to increase $3 billion per month, Reuters reported in September. This amounts to the American taxpaying household paying an extra $360 per month to cover these costs, according to Zandi. More than 250 square miles of forests at the center of Victoria state in Australia have become new national parks.

Parliament passed the law to create the parks back in November 2025, and this week they take effect, creating Mount Buangor National Park, Pyrenees National Park, and the largest: Wombat-Lerderderg National Park.

The Victoria National Parks Association (VNPA) is celebrating the event with fellow private campaigners, Wombat Forestcare and the Wilderness Society, among others.

“Today we get to see the protection these forests deserve. It’s a fantastic day for nature and for Victorians, we have three new national parks! Congratulations to the Carroll Government for getting it done,” said VNPA Executive Director Matt Ruchel in a statement to mark the occasion.

The 3 are Victoria’s first new national parks of substantial size in 15 years, and together protect hundreds of rare and threatened plants, animals, and fungi, including platypuses, greater gliders, goannas, Mount Cole grevilleas, brush-tailed phascogales, mountain skinks, and powerful Owls.

“We are delighted that the state government has officially recognized the importance of these central-west forests for their plants and animals and acted to conserve them,” said Gayle Osborne, a founding member of Wombat Forestcare, one of the groups who campaigned for the parks’ creation.

“These forests are such important habitat for so many plants, animals, and fungi. If we want our koalas, gliders, and owls to be here into the future we must protect their habitat.”

Wombat Forestcare launched a campaign in 2010, hosting a public conference in Hepburn that brought the community together around a vision for protected forests in the central west. Over the following years, its volunteers produced detailed ecological reports on the landscape zones that are now national park, work that was central to securing the government investigation that recommended their creation.

They lie on lands of the Dja Dja Wurrung, Eastern Maar, Wadawurrung, Wurundjeri, Gunaikurnai, and Taungurung peoples, who have cared for these landscapes for thousands of years.

AUSTRALIAN PROTECTED AREAS:

Parks Victoria now joins them in caring for these forests, and together they will work on management plans over the next 12 months to continue that thousand-year stewardship.

“We’re ready to help shape these plans, to make sure wildlife and people are both looked after and the parks have the resources they need to thrive,” said Ruchel.

“For years we worked with local community groups to search for threatened animals, survey rare plants and, through years of delays, kept writing letter after letter. Today that hard work becomes permanent protection.”

HONG KONG – In Nepal, a catastrophic Himalayan slope collapse in August triggered floods that killed more than 1,300 people. 2026 brought the warmest summer on record in the United States. In Hong Kong, hourly rainfall records that were once broken only every few decades have been exceeded several times in recent decades.

As extreme weather becomes more frequent and intense, policymakers face difficult choices over solutions to limit the damage. The 2015 Paris Agreement calls on countries to hold the rise in global average temperature to well below 2 C above pre-industrial levels, while pursuing efforts to limit it to 1.5 C. But what happens if the temperatures rise beyond these limits?

In early September, the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) released a report, “Limiting Overshoot - Navigating exceedance of 1.5 C and pathways towards return” to present an overview of the reality if global temperatures exceed 1.5 C. Later in the month, Debra Roberts, one of the report’s lead coordinators and authors, presented its latest findings at the Chinese University of Hong Kong.

“While exceeding 1.5 [C] now is unavoidable, how high we go and for how long it lasts is very much still … in our hands. Every day above 1.5 [C] is now going to matter,” said Debra.

An environmental scientist with 40 years of experience in climate policy and biodiversity planning, Debra Roberts has co-authored reports for the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC).  During her time with the government of Durban, a port city in South Africa, she was responsible for environmental planning and strengthening the city’s climate resilience.

Debra predicted that global warming levels will exceed 1.5 C within three to four years. This would mean increased extreme weather events, glacial melt, sea-level rise, and ecological damage. The report estimates that global food production could decline by 14% by 2050. By the end of this century, glaciers could lose more than a quarter of their mass, adding up to 12.5 cm to sea levels if warming reaches 3 C.

This does not mean action is useless. On the contrary, Debra said that we need to act immediately to cut emissions and slow the rise in temperatures.

The report proposes an “exceed, decline, stabilise” approach: after temperatures cross 1.5 C, they could be brought down through methods such as carbon dioxide removal.

The smaller the exceedance, the greater the chance of temperatures falling back to the 1.5 C level, Debra pointed out. The report’s most optimistic projection puts the peak temperature rise at 1.8 C if countries meet their current emissions-reduction commitments. Beyond 1.8 C, returning to 1.5 C would become increasingly difficult.

But here is a catch: the feasibility of carbon dioxide removal is still uncertain. The report indicates that current afforestation and forest-management methods would take 100 years to reduce warming by 0.1 C, assuming zero residual CO₂ emissions, while other novel technologies (such as bioenergy combined with carbon capture and storage, direct air carbon capture and storage, biochar, and enhanced rock weathering) only achieve one-thousandth of the effect currently. Even under the most favourable scenario, carbon dioxide removal methods would take 50 years to reduce warming by 0.25 C.

Some impacts are irreversible or could take decades to reverse. Even if global warming is stabilised at current levels, global glacial loss is projected to continue for centuries. Exceeding 1.5 C and later returning below it will lead to additional glacial loss, but less than stabilising at a higher level.

“1.5 C is actually not a safe level; it’s just less dangerous than temperatures that are higher,” Debra said. She added that countries need to develop flexible climate adaptation policies because we may live with excessive warming for decades or even millennia.

So, should adaptation start before the worst impacts arrive? Debra says yes.

Decision-makers need to examine whether existing infrastructure can withstand a warmer world. For example, by 2050, 76% of urban tree species will be at risk.

During the 2010 World Cup in Durban, South Africa, trees were planted on 580 hectares of land — an area roughly equivalent to around 700 football fields — to offset carbon emissions and enhance urban resilience. Policymakers need to identify which tree species will survive, and replace those that cannot.

Many existing policy decisions may need to be adapted to new conditions. Coastal cities (such as Durban and Hong Kong) may need to consider not only infrastructure development to protect the coastline, but also strategies to relocate from the coast, Debra said.

The Xylom previously exclusively reported how the 2022 IPCC Sixth Assessment Report criticized the highly unpopular Mumbai Coastal Road, which has nearly halved incomes and daily catch of lower-caste fishermen, as an example of “maladaptive” infrastructural intervention.

“The Mumbai Coastal Road (MCR) project aimed at reducing flood risk and protecting against [sea-level rise] will potentially cause damages to intertidal fauna and flora and local fishing livelihoods,” the authors wrote.

Jakarta’s Great Garuda sea wall project is another example of maladaptive infrastructure. While the project’s sea wall and 17 artificial islands are meant to protect the city from sea-level rise and create a huge new urban quarter, there is a strong possibility that the project will exacerbate flooding, especially for poor households.

Debra emphasised that adaptation policies should be forward-looking and flexible, rather than reactive to disasters. Such an approach can protect assets, reduce the need for emergency response and free up resources for emissions reduction and long-term planning.

The UNEP report calls for an accelerated energy transition, with renewable energy reaching 60% to 70% of global electricity generation by 2030.

Can nuclear energy, a low-carbon but controversial energy source, help bridge the gap?

“Nuclear has to be part of the mix. We don’t get to limit temperatures or reduce emissions unless nuclear is part of the mix,” Debra said. She noted that the UNEP report draws on the IPCC’s Sixth Assessment Report, whose modelled pathways all include nuclear power in the energy mix. As pressure to reduce emissions grows, she said, the share of nuclear power is likely to increase.

The IPCC’s Sixth Assessment Report describes nuclear power as an established energy source that can be deployed at scale. In pathways limiting warming to 1.5 C, nuclear energy use would need to increase by 40% between 2019 and 2030. Other less ambitious pathways would also see increases of 10% to 35%.

In fact, data on deaths and emissions per unit of electricity generated show that nuclear power is among the safest and lowest-emission sources of electricity.

Nuclear energy may not be equally accessible to all countries. Some regions in Africa may lack the experience and technology needed to manage it, Debra said. However, she emphasised that nuclear energy remains essential, pointing to France, where nuclear power supplies much of the country’s electricity.

“Renewables, obviously, are always envisaged to be the greater part. But you don’t actually get over the line unless you use absolutely every technology you have at your fingertips,” Debra said.

At the Chinese University of Hong Kong event, an attendee asked Debra if she thought there was still hope. “For me, hope is not a strategy. It doesn’t get anything done. I’m a realist. But I do believe that science and research are such important tools that can give us a sense of where we might be able to act,” she said.

Limiting warming to 1.5 C seems difficult, but before the 2015 Paris Agreement, global warming was projected to reach a 4C rise by 2100, while the current projection is 2.6 C, Debra pointed out. She said this is “still not good enough,” but shows that science, policy, and grassroots action can bend the curve.

A firm believer in translating scientific research and international frameworks into local action, Debra encouraged people to ask questions and pressure policymakers to take bold climate action.

“Now is really the time. We’ve got a very limited opportunity to try and reduce the level of temperature increase that we will experience. I think every one of us has a role now to deal with this challenge.”

The call for action comes as Hong Kong prepares to review its own climate policies. The Hong Kong Climate Action Plan 2050 is due to be updated, setting the course for the city to halve its carbon emissions from 2005 levels before 2035 and achieve carbon neutrality before 2050. The city’s emissions have already fallen by 27% from their 2014 peak, but electricity generation still accounts for 61% of total emissions, followed by transport at 18% and waste at 8%.

Renewable energy only accounted for 1% of Hong Kong’s electricity mix as of 2023, with the city’s rooftop solar incentive scheme garnering mixed results.

Americans head to the polls on 3 November to decide how the rest of Donald Trump's presidency will play out.

Thousands of races are taking place across the US, at different levels of government. But the main event for voters will be electing members of the House of Representatives and the Senate, the two chambers that make up Congress.

Both of them are currently controlled by the Republicans, the president's party. The success or failure of Trump's final two years in office could rest on the outcome.

Here's our visual guide to where the battle for power will be won and lost - from approval ratings, to key races and issues and the huge amount of money being spent.

One of the reasons the opposition Democrats have a chance to take back Congress is the president's low approval rating, which is a good indicator for how well his party could perform.

He began his second term as president with an approval rating of just over 50%, according to polling resource website Silver Bulletin, but it quickly fell into the 40s.

It was hovering around 42% when Trump decided to launch air strikes with Israel against Iran at the end of February this year but it fell below 40% shortly afterwards. It is currently sitting at about 37%.

Eight years ago, Trump's approval rating was significantly higher at this point in his first term, at 43%. Joe Biden's at the same point in his term was at 40%. In both cases, the sitting president lost control of the House in the midterms but kept hold of the Senate.

But Trump's poor ratings help explain why Democrats are hopeful of winning both chambers of Congress and why they are setting their sights on states that Republicans have won consistently in recent years.

The current Republican majority in the House of Representatives, the lower chamber, is as thin as it gets - they have 218 representatives, which is the exact number needed to have control, plus one independent who votes with them.

Members of the House serve a two-year term so all 435 seats are up for election in November.

But most districts are not considered competitive because the party that holds them has such solid support that there is only one likely winner.

The Cook Political Report, which analyses campaigns and elections, suggests that just 21 districts are "toss-ups" that could be won by either party.

Of those 21 toss-ups, 15 are currently held by Republicans and six by Democrats. If the Democrats win five of those on top of 28 districts classed as likely or leaning Democratic, they will win the House.

Historically, the midterms see a high number of seats changing hands in the House, usually in a protest against the White House. The average number lost by the president's party is 27, according to data, external going back to 1934. Of those 23 elections, the president's party has only made gains in three.

The Republicans have a slightly stronger hold on the Senate. They hold 53 of the 100 seats while the Democrats have 45 and two independents who also vote with them.

Members of the Senate serve six-year terms so roughly a third are up for election every two years.

Thirty-five seats are up for grabs in November but analysis by the Cook Political Report suggests that only seven of them are toss-ups that could go either way.

Of those toss-ups, six are currently held by Republicans and one by Democrats. The Democrats would need to win four of those seats, plus the four classed as likely or leaning Democratic, to hit 51 and take control of the Senate.

But winning a majority is no easy task for the Democrats.

They need to keep hold of their seat in Michigan, where polls suggest the race is tighter than Democrats would like between Abdul El-Sayed, a left-wing political outsider, and his Republican rival Mike Rogers, a Trump ally and former FBI agent.

And they would also need to pick up seats in states that Trump won by double-digits in 2024, including Alaska, Iowa and Ohio.

But polls suggest they have a chance, even in Texas where former teacher James Talarico could become the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in the state since 1988 if he defeats Ken Paxton, the current state attorney general and close Trump ally.

GUIDE: What are the US midterms?

EXPLAINED: What would Democratic control of Congress mean for Trump?

IN DEPTH: The Republicans walking a Trump tightrope

Trump pledged to "end inflation and make America affordable again" in his 2024 election campaign but the cost of living crisis is proving to be the key issue for voters.

The president proudly declared that gas was "now below $2.30 [Â£1.74] a gallon in most states" in his State of the Union address on 24 February. But the war with Iran began four days later, disrupting Middle Eastern energy supplies and causing gas to hit $4 (Â£3.03) in the US.

The war became increasingly unpopular as its consequences reverberated around the world and ultimately hit American consumers in the pocket. One poll carried out in August found 63% of respondents disapproved of Trump's handling of the situation.

Other issues that voters say are important to them include healthcare and immigration.

Trump has recently touted his policies around immigration as a big success, citing significantly lower border-crossing figures than in recent years.

Many Democratic candidates are focusing on the high costs of US health insurance and the impact of Trump's legislation on access to the healthcare system.

Trump wants to reduce the cost of fuel as the midterms loom - will it work?

Most signs point towards a successful midterms for the Democrats, but it wouldn't be the first time that Trump and his party have outperformed polls if they do win more seats than expected.

One of the few things in their favour is their huge financial advantage.

At the end of August, the Republican National Committee and its allied groups had more than $600m (Â£455m) cash on hand, while the Democrats had just under $400m (Â£303m).

On top of that, the Republicans also had more than $400m held by Trump's MAGA Inc group, the main fundraising and spending arm of the "Make America Great Again" political movement.

The Republicans are using that financial advantage to buy advertising.

More than $1bn worth of political ads were broadcast to US voters in September, according to research firm AdImpact, external. Republicans spent $200m more than the Democrats and outspent them in nearly all of the Senate races classed as toss-ups.

Trump will be hoping this late messaging blitz can help convince Republicans to get out and vote in November, boosting turnout and limiting the damage done to him and his party.

Whatever the result, attention will quickly turn to the next presidential election in 2028. Trump's unpopularity has dominated the midterms, but with him constitutionally unable to run for a third term the focus will shift to what the Democrats stand for, not just what they stand against.

A clinical and forensic psychologist breaking down President Donald Trump’s weekend rally in Tennessee flagged a moment he called “a really wild thing to watch”: Trump told the crowd he could say the stupidest things and they’d clap, and they did.

Dr. John Paul Garrison, known online as “Dr. G” to more than half a million YouTube subscribers, broke down the Clarksville event in a new video. Trump appeared Saturday at the F&M Bank Arena to campaign for Tennessee Republicans, including Sen. Marsha Blackburn, the GOP nominee for governor, ahead of the Nov. 3 midterms.

“When you stand up here, it’s just like the love. I could say the stupidest things and you clap,” Trump told the audience, which cheered. “You know, I love you so. That’s true.”

Garrison called it “clapping after a thinly veiled insult, basically saying that they would clap for anything.”

“You notice how at the end he said it’s true because he’s emphasizing the fact there is unconditional loyalty no matter what he says,” Garrison said. “Not surprisingly, he goes on to say that he doesn’t say stupid things, but what this does is this is using authority and dominance, and framing it as humor.”

Garrison also zeroed in on a recurring sideways shift of Trump’s jaw that appeared when the president grew animated, including as he boasted about renaming Lake Ontario “Lake America.”

“Sometimes we see that when people are either on stimulant medication or taking stimulants of some kind,” Garrison said, adding that the movement could also have a neurological cause tied to impaired motor functioning. Garrison has not examined Trump, and the White House has not disclosed that the president takes any stimulant medication.

On nights like Saturday, Garrison said, Trump appeared “more emotionally dysregulated” and “almost manic,” struggling to inhibit his own behavior.

Garrison stressed at the start of his video that his analysis “is not a psychological evaluation of any kind” and reflects his opinions. He isn’t the first mental health professional to raise alarms about Trump’s public behavior, and a former GOP strategist said one Trump rally showed he was fading.

Trump, 80, said after a May exam at Walter Reed that “Everything checked out PERFECTLY,” and his White House physician declared him “fully fit” to serve. In a February Reuters/Ipsos poll, 61% of Americans, including 30% of Republicans, said Trump has “become erratic with age.”

In October of 1769, a conservative Boston printer broadsided a bunch of the day’s leading activists. The colonies were in a furor at the time. Rioters and looters, often backwoods settlers angry about the power of gentlemanly land speculators, had grown in number and motive and became fixtures of American political life. Coastal cities were seeing new waves of migrants who’d been disfigured or dislocated in the wake of the French and Indian War, and a postwar depression in trade had brought the first period of economic hardship that many white colonists had ever known. “Mob rule” prevailed as the basic political condition in some cities, where the wealthy aimed to contain the popular energy or to channel it for their own ends—a tension that would dominate the framing of the Constitution. By the end of the 1760s, a large part of Boston’s merchant class had discovered in the mob an expedient political tool: they spent half a decade recasting Parliamentary taxation as an assault on the “liberty” of impecunious colonists, though most moderate Britons (and colonists) were aware that white people in colonial America were governed as liberally as anywhere in the European world. A superheated rhetoric won out; soon it became a patriotic duty to support boycotts of taxed goods. Those who spoke against the boycotts faced social banishment, economic ruin, assault, and humiliation from the fomented crowd.

John Mein, the Loyalist printer of the Boston Chronicle, thought that the gentlemen who whipped up the mob were hypocritical profiteers, and he set out to prove it. He published the manifests of ships owned by leading members of Boston’s merchant circle, showing that some of the loudest mouths rallying popular support for boycotts and anger against British taxes were violating the boycott themselves, using their low-priced, smuggled goods to put smaller merchants who abided by the boycotts out of business. But Mein misunderstood the temper of Boston at the time. He thought that exposing the hypocrisy of men like John Hancock, whom he called the “milch-cow of the well-disposed,” would chasten the men whipping up riots and writing inflamed pamphlets. The Patriot press and its supportive public didn’t care. They attacked Mein, calling him one of those “who have AUDACIOUSLY counteracted the UNITED SENTIMENTS of the BODY of Merchants throughout NORTH-AMERICA,” which was to say, basically, that talking about wealthy Patriots violating the boycott was more of an attack on the unity of the colonies than wantonly violating the anti-British boycotts that the unity was supposed to be in service of. Soon a throng of a thousand came for Mein, who had his head beaten with a shovel before he absconded to England by disguising himself as a British soldier. Hancock bought up Mein’s debts and shuttered his troublesome paper. The Patriots of pre-Revolutionary America did not believe in free speech or reasoned discourse.

It has always been hard for Americans to deal squarely with the fact that we had a revolution.

A quarter of a millennium later, a cadre of mostly older liberalish intellectuals and younger conservatives ignited one of our periodic internet wildfires with an open letter in Harper’s, attempting to defend cultural life against the same forces that led us into the American Revolution. “Censoriousness,” they wrote, is a spreading force in our lives—“an intolerance of opposing views, a vogue for public shaming and ostracism, and the tendency to dissolve complex policy issues in a blinding moral certainty.” The writers of the letter took pains to avoid using the phrase “cancel culture,” though that is what they were writing about, possibly because this censoriousness has become so pervasive that it already feels pointless and passé to even rail against it using the common phrase. For the right’s part, the term-of-choice for this force is “mob rule,” a timeworn expression Tucker Carlson has recently taken to using almost every night as he portrays our ritual online denunciations of the living and the destruction of monuments of our once-hallowed dead as vilely un-American. But mob rule and cancel culture are what made our Revolution, which is to say that they made the America we still, for now, live in.

It has always been hard for Americans to deal squarely with the fact that we had a revolution. The right has trouble admitting that the United States, and a soon-to-form national and social consciousness, were born out of the convulsive and bloody overturning of a social and political order. The left has always had trouble believing that the ouster of that order deserves to count as a proper revolution, since it didn’t look anything like the revolutions that leftists would later celebrate or yearn for: it had no pronounced class basis, didn’t change the basic economic structures of the country, and its leaders were never interested much in pushing the logic of freedom and the equality of humankind to their rightful conclusions. “Why is it that we hear the loudest yelps for liberty from the drivers of Negroes?” Samuel Johnson famously wondered, long before anyone on this continent was seriously hoping for a split with the British crown. Even before most people fully understood that a revolution was beginning, observers were pointing out the duplicity in the rhetoric that birthed it.

The people can have a little rioting, in the right circumstances, so long as they don’t unduly threaten the aims of the powerful.

Conservatives, in the moment before revolution, were terrified to speak out. Patriots began exposing private correspondences, leading one tremulous merchant to warn a friend to watch his language because “the temper of the people is such that misconstructions are put on the most innocent expressions,” as he put it, by “those who call themselves the Assertors of American Freedom.” Mob rule, or cancel culture, was among the forces that drove the formation of America. But it did not, for all that the papers spoke of liberty, birth an egalitarian or even an avowedly democratic America—which can hardly be a surprise, given that financial interests were what produced Revolutionary zeal; by the time George Washington, a slave-owner riding in a chariot with polished silver fittings, took up the presidency, the narrative of the new Revolutionary aristocracy as liberators and champions of the people was almost impossible to challenge. It was with this language that the Federalists soon set about tamping down popular energies and reasserting elite rule. It is a trick that elites would come to use many times in American history. And it is a trick they are using now.

In June, Amazon Studios posted a billboard on Sunset Boulevard in East Hollywood showing a black woman’s upraised fist with the caption “Amplify Black Voices.” I find this billboard irksome, perhaps because I see it a lot, perhaps because one older woman I know broke her ten-year boycott of Amazon this spring citing to me “all their support of Black Lives Matter.” Everyone, of course, has their pet example of recent corporate hypocrisy—Popeye’s Chicken tweeting out “Popeyes is nothing without Black Lives,” or Jamie Dimon taking a knee in front of an open bank vault to show Chase Bank’s support for equality and justice in America. But anyone, of any political persuasion, looking honestly at this moment can admit that it has been disorienting to watch so many companies, from Uber to Exxon to Rag & Bone, tripping to align themselves with a movement that began as an extralegal and sometimes violent revolt against the system that these companies administer. For their part, conservatives now seem genuinely shell-shocked by how quickly corporate establishments have accommodated themselves to the idea that looting and burning stores can be a legitimate form of protest—or at least to how quickly they’ve turned a blind eye. Meanwhile, the liberal punditry showed itself to be outlandishly terrified by the armed anti-lockdown protests that spread after the arrival of quarantine this spring, and horrified, too, at the way that conservative politicians and media embraced them. But these are both examples of the riotous tendency in American politics, a force that the powerful have only found dangerous when it couldn’t be brought in line with their own interests.

Yet riots were an accepted, or at least tolerated, part of British society in the eighteenth century. Britons prided themselves on having a constitutional order that provided “liberty” far greater than any of the benighted and priest-ridden societies of mainland Europe, and they took for granted that this liberty had been in part won by the threat of violence from common people. “Tho’ innocent Persons may sometimes suffer in popular Tumults,” one observer wrote in 1768, “the general Resentment of the People is principally directed according to Justice and the greatest Delinquent feels it most.” The unwritten British Constitution, a tripartite agreement between King, Parliament, and the common people, made it possible to believe that “extralegal” armed politics could, in fact, be legal when a fair point was being made and the powers-that-be weren’t unduly threatened. This was especially true in pre-Revolutionary America, which lacked the standing military force needed to quash riots. As colonial governor Thomas Hutchinson, in what now sounds like an uncanny echo of how corporations and establishment politicians have embraced contemporary protest movements, wrote in 1768: “Mobs, a sort of them at least, are constitutional.” This produced an effect that was as obvious in the founding days of the republic as it is now: in an unruly and dissatisfied country, mob politics are unavoidable. Which is to say that the people can have a little rioting, in the right circumstances, so long as they don’t unduly threaten the aims of the powerful.

The best indication of how two decades of mob politics in America would look came with the passage of the Stamp Act, which placed duties on printed matter, and more importantly sought to establish a precedent for Parliament’s right to tax Britain’s American colonies. It was passed in 1765, to go into effect on November 1 of that year. On August 14, an effigy of Andrew Oliver, who was supposed to act as the stamp distributor in Massachusetts, was discovered hanging on an elm that would later come to be known as Boston’s “liberty tree.” That evening, a crowd torched the effigy, attacked Oliver’s home, and tore down his office—this opening salvo amounted to the first short burst of the Stamp Act Riots. The mainstream media celebrated them. “Our Brethren in Boston have indeared themselves more than ever to all the colonies in America,” a letter in the New York Gazette declared, wishful that this “Noble example . . . will be unanimously followed by all the colonies.” It was.

These were not spontaneous uprisings. The August 14 “riots” were planned by the Loyal Nine, a club of well-off merchants and tradesmen who would soon morph into Boston’s chapter of the Sons of Liberty. British officials noted “respectable people” looking “decently-dressed”—sounding much like Tucker Carlson accusing Black Lives Matter protesters of being well-off liberal arts grads—and complained that the mob did not appear as a proper mobile vulgaris—which would have included the unemployed, unpropertied, and free blacks comprising the truly dispossessed of the city. British officials, at the same time, sought to convince the mobs they’d been heard. “You have no need to have recourse to VIOLENT methods any longer,” Hutchinson wrote. “The channel is now open to the ear and heart of the best of KINGS: rely upon it and he will hear you.” Even the English took a kindly view: the protests were “highly approved,” one Briton wrote, “except the acts of violence—the destruction and plunder of private property.”

Personal vituperation and baroque hyperbole became more or less the rhetorical standard for political speech.

But the still-forming intra-continental associations of Sons of Liberty found it advantageous to their mercantile interests to keep passions on medium-high, while preserving the threat of simmering violence. By November 1 of 1765, the rich were firmly in control of the rebellion: “Two Gentlemen . . . the richest merchants in the town” called the leaders of North Side and South Side mobs and hired the proto-mobster Ebeneezer Mackintosh, “with his corps to keep the Peace and prevent mischief,” as Governor Francis Bernard was quoted describing the scene in Pauline Maier’s classic study From Resistance to Revolution. Mackintosh “presided in a blue and gold uniform, wearing a gold-laced hat and carrying a rattan cane,” maintaining a crowd of two thousand, while “allegedly disorder-prone Negroes” were excluded.

After exhausting his usefulness, Mackintosh was himself cast aside by his gentlemen friends and placed in debtors’ prison. Soon enough these same patricians discovered a safer tool than riots, but one that proved just as effective at channeling a species of popular anger that traditional politics couldn’t: social ostracism and public shaming. On October 25, the freemen of Essex County, New Jersey, proclaimed that anyone who adhered to the Stamp Act should be cast out of polite society, that decent people should have “no Communication with any such Person, nor speak with them on any Occasion unless it be to inform them of their Vileness.” This was not an isolated view. One writer to a Pennsylvania paper suggested, in language typical of the time, that a man paying stamp duties should be “branded with eternal infamy and reproach,” and cast out. “Let him be alone in the world—let him wish to associate with the wild beasts of some dark loathsome cave.”

This invitation to shaming wasn’t a social affliction in the eyes of the people who encouraged it—it was deliberate and sound politics, a more controllable, pantomimed violence that placated the mob while containing the energy that led it to burn the homes of rich merchants and loot storehouses. “The central preoccupation of the Sons of Liberty and later the revolutionary movement,” Maier wrote, “was then with winning a mass base, with converting the population at large into Sons of Liberty.” What this meant, in practice, was that while Sons of Liberty groupings were springing up all along the Atlantic Seaboard, the patriotic zeal they embodied was able to appear radical without ever slipping beyond the grip of the merchants who inspired it. Again, it was highly effective: “So universal has been the resentment of the people,” John Adams wrote gleefully, “that every man who has dared to speak in favour of the stamps . . . how great soever his Abilities and Virtues had been esteemed before, or whatever his fortune, Connections, and Influence had been, has been seen to sink into universal Contempt and Ignominy.”

It was more than a decade from the passage of the Stamp Act before the flames broke out in earnest. In retrospect the path looks inexorable, but it needn’t have been. British officials and many conservatives, finding themselves suddenly part of a confused and embattled minority, struggled to assuage or even understand the anger of the mob. In 1772, the royal governor of North Carolina took action to free backcountry farmers from the yoke of corrupt if well-connected land speculators, like George Washington, who used their connections to buy up land at cut rates and rent it out in an early form of sharecropping peonage. But this shift toward the interest of the poor and landless never fully took hold—partly because conservatives did not have much genuine care for the poor or the landless, and otherwise because the poor and landless were in many places already firmly in the Patriot camp. The disenfranchised had stopped believing in the capacity of the older order to hear their protests, and the Patriot elite took full advantage.

This period was not a time of earnest appeals or reasoned discourse. Personal vituperation and baroque hyperbole became more or less the rhetorical standard for political speech. Riots and disorder calmed for a while in the early 1770s, after the repeal of the Stamp Act and the subsequent Townshend Duties led to boycotts and smuggling of the sort that lined the pockets of men like John Hancock. But a new colonial sub-elite, an entire class born, like John Adams, with an “enormous chip on his round shoulders,” as Alan Taylor put it in his American Revolutions: A Continental History, 1750-1804, was not appeased by this power structure. Engaged in a fight over control of the colonial system, they wanted a respect that had long eluded them. And so the colonies became a zone of contest between rich men, with the mob serving as a weapon, or at least an instrument. “Rather than denounce all of the rich as a predatory class,” Taylor wrote, “Patriots encouraged laboring people to focus their animus more narrowly on a few gentlemen who seemed especially menacing because of their imperial connections.”

The Stamp Act was repealed in 1766, but the politics it inaugurated had been institutionalized. The inter-colonial Continental Association was formed, and the tactics its leaders used to enforce its boycotts and political conformity now look positively Maoist. Long before the war began, the “mobs singled out suspected Loyalists, subjected them to elaborate interrogations, and urged them to sign confessions of guilt and repentance,” wrote Gordon Wood. Americans who drank British tea or spoke out against the Continental Association were forced to sign oaths of “Fidelity” in elaborate ceremonies of contrition. One observer complained that their methods were “really infamous,” and put opponents of the Association in “real danger of their lives. Their property was actually unsafe, their Signs, Doors and Windows, were daub’d over in the Night time with every kind of Filth, and one of them particularly had his person treated in the same manner.”

By the mid-1770s, the traditional aristocratic order had not been upended, but it had been sundered. Rich men who avoided the ire of Patriot diehards were paid the usual deference, which bordered on worship, offered to gentlemen of the age. But those who crossed the line were subject to almost comical extremes of social opprobrium. A Connecticut doctor, Abner Bebe, was “stripped naked & hot Pitch was poured upon him,” one friend wrote, “which blistered his Skin. He was then carried to a Hog Sty & rubbed over with Hog’s Dung. They threw the Hog’s Dung in his Face, & rammed some of it down his Throat. . . . His house was attacked, his Windows broke.” Taylor added: “Going door-to-door, committeemen urged every man and woman to sign the association or suffer the consequences. Inviting everyone to spy on their neighbors, the committees ferreted out, seized, and burned stashes of tea and conservative books while a crowd gathered at the county courthouse to hoot at the culprits. After confessing, the suspects had to ignite the condemned items in festive bonfires that rallied public support for the new committees and intimidated the wavering.”

The Patriots called those who pleaded for freedom of speech traitors to liberty. The Philadelphia committee proclaimed that “no person has the right to the protection of a community or society he wishes to destroy” by writing or speaking in ways that “aid and assist our enemies.” A Maryland conservative plaintively asked a friend, “What think you of this land of liberty, where a man’s property is at the mercy of anyone that will lead the mob!”

Though, to be clear, it was not just anyone who could lead the mob now. “Liberty,” as a concept, had gone from a vague good shared by the subjects of a modestly enlightened slaveholding Empire to a concrete force that happened to align neatly with the business interests of speculators and merchants, which is to say it had nothing at all to do with free speech, the liberation of the twenty percent of Americans who were then enslaved, or the rights of colonists to be free of the powerful planters whose land-degrading farming practices and corrupt speculations were forcing Americans into landlessness. The amorphous British ideal of liberty was being given a concrete American definition, one that equated freedom with economic rights.

This new and violently enforced consensus had effects that were to prove almost unfathomably disastrous for the lives of untold millions, and for the political future of the new republic: a perverse logic that equated political freedom with property-holding reached its reductio ad absurdum when, almost a century later, rich, Southern men went to war claiming they were fighting for personal liberty by defending a system of human bondage. And in a society where owning land was the ultimate expression of freedom, and where rich landholders had seized most of the good land east of the Appalachian Mountains, it was inevitable that the poor and landless would push across the Boundary Line and enter into generations of genocidal war in the West. The land had to be taken from someone, the thinking went, and the colonial baronets much preferred that it be taken from Natives than from the rich, lest the rapacious economic and population growth of the new nation be throttled. The histories of this period are curiously bereft of any discussion of broader egalitarian potential amid all this shallow rhetoric and coopted violence. It makes sense, given that anyone who spoke against the Patriotic vanguard could find themselves on a scaffold beneath the Liberty Tree. A rebellion had formed, and then it had been contained. Now a Revolution needed to be finished.

The Revolution took shape more quickly than its authors could have expected. A large part of all societies on the brink of political upheaval believes that such insurgencies are too radical to effect. It’s a basic mistake of any historical analysis to see events unfolding as part of an inevitable plan or process, but after a decade of charged political divisions and deranged hyperbole on the part of Patriot activists, it is difficult to see what else could have come of it all. In 1765, writers were already describing the Stamp Tax in language that could not be answered by reasoned politics, declaring that it would “occasion an entire stagnation of trade, discourage every kind of industry, and involve us in the most abject slavery.” “Slavery,” in a hemisphere with an economy that was deeply involved in the most literal form of abject slavery, was a watchword for Patriot activists during a decade in which they enjoyed many of the choicest liberties anywhere in the world. But the self-pitying paranoia trafficked by white colonists didn’t conform to any real-world threat, and therefore couldn’t be assuaged by any real-world compromise. It was only natural for the Patriot gentlemen to finally forget, in 1776, the kindly affection that only months early they’d expressed for King George. “As the symbol of British sovereignty the king had to become the great villain,” Alan Taylor wrote. “In a pivotal transmutation, the formerly beloved king became a despised tyrant.”

The amorphous British ideal of liberty was being given a concrete American definition, one that equated freedom with economic rights.

And “revolution” is the proper word for what the war unleashed in the colonies. Conservatives and Loyalists had long observed the new Patriot consensus with an uneasy mix of sputtering confusion and acute understanding—a rising generation of Patriot gentlemen, brought up reading Locke and Cato’s Letters and other new radical theory, wanted to sweep away the old British aristocratic order and replace it with a new one that happened to be led by them, one where their interests on the frontier and at the customs house would be well-served. They didn’t care what values they swept aside. The Tories charged with putting the “community at variance, father against son”—leaving “no law, no friendship, no alliance, no ties of blood” left in the face of their “specious show of an exalted kind of virtue.” They were “indeed trying to destroy the ligaments of the older society,” Wood wrote, “and to reknit people together in a new way.”

The Patriots upended timeworn social hierarchies without making an egalitarian revolution, and that was the point. Later republican leaders, like Thomas Jefferson, did write with some passion about how democracy could not exist in the face of deep wealth inequality, but they merely wrung their hands over the “question” of slavery. Federalists like Alexander Hamilton won ratification for an unpopular constitution by using the press, which they largely controlled, to create what Taylor called a “useful fiction” that We the People, and not a set of new aristocrats, had authored it. To this day, many Americans believe the Federalists saw that our system of checks and balances was designed to protect the people against the abuses of government, and not that the system was designed to prevent mob rule by an overly democratic legislature. The revolution had been made manifest—a social and political order had been overthrown, and the people who had made bitter noise about the values of social decency and reasoned debate had been forced to flee to Halifax and London, if they’d been lucky enough to survive the war. But the mob had been carefully controlled, and our long national story—the story of a nation where the rote language of popular liberty has almost always served to protect the interests of oligarchs and businessmen—had begun in earnest.

“The restriction of debate, whether by a repressive government or an intolerant society, invariably hurts those who lack power and makes everyone less capable of democratic participation,” wrote the signatories to the Harper’s open letter against cancel culture. “The way to defeat bad ideas is by exposure, argument, and persuasion, not by trying to silence or wish them away.” This is a nice sentiment. But in sum it’s a radical misunderstanding of our moment—revolutions, whether peaceful or otherwise, create their own logic. They do not conform to societal values, they remake them. Statues of the leaders of our founding Revolution are falling by the dozens. The popular myths inaugurated by our originary acts of mob rule have fallen out of currency, and millions upon millions of Americans no longer believe that this was ever truly a land of liberty. They are right. And now a new coterie of corporate gentlemen and aristocrats are circling, aiming to gain from a moment of popular revolt that began with demands for equality and challenges to the very system that enriched them in the first place. If we’re going to have another revolution, we should be careful to watch who is leading it.
