Montana Free Press

Montana's independent nonprofit news source.

Tim Brunner, a rancher near Great Falls who serves as president of the Montana Cattlemen’s Association, said he doesn’t expect recent efforts by President Donald Trump and Gov. Greg Gianforte to mitigate the high cost of diesel to result in much financial relief for his ranch.

Lt. Gov. Kristen Juras issued an executive order on Friday that allows commercial vehicles engaged “directly in agricultural or timber industry operations” to use red-dyed diesel on public roads until Nov. 23. The order comes about a week after President Donald Trump signed an executive order suspending a federal law that bans the use of red-dyed diesel in vehicles on public roads.

Red-dyed diesel is the same as diesel — a fuel commonly used in heavy machinery, semi trucks and many pickups — except for its color and substantially lower tax rate. The dyed fuel is reserved mostly for agricultural use in Montana. That’s why it’s exempt from taxes that pay for highways, and why it’s usually illegal to drive with red-dyed diesel on public roads.

On Friday, Trump announced on Truth Social a plan to import about 800,000 tons of diesel fuel — about a day and a half’s worth of U.S. demand — from Russia before the end of November. The post also indicated that another 4 million tons will arrive from Russia sometime later.

The price of diesel has spiked this year as a result of the U.S. conflict with Iran and Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, prompting federal and state government efforts to mitigate the price spikes ahead of November’s midterm elections.

Near-record diesel prices are putting pressure on Montana farmers who depend on fuel to run combines, tractors and other equipment, and also increasing the cost of transporting goods once they leave the farm.

Jeffrey Michael, director of the University of Montana’s Bureau of Business and Economic Research, is also skeptical that the Trump-announced diesel imports will ease prices. Diesel fuel is priced similarly — currently at a historic high because of the foreign conflicts — worldwide. Newly available domestic supplies in the U.S. probably won’t bring down the global price.

Montana ranks No. 4 among American states for diesel vehicles per capita, according to Michael. And it’s No. 8 in the amount spent on diesel per dollar of gross domestic product, an economic measure that totals the state’s output of goods and services.

Walt Schweitzer, president of the Montana Farmers Union and a frequent critic of Trump’s trade policies, also expressed doubt that new diesel imports will help agricultural producers.

“If he really wanted to have a positive impact on our diesel price, he would quit exporting our diesel and keep it here,” Schweitzer said.

Schweitzer also highlighted logistical obstacles that might undermine Gianforte’s efforts to provide financial relief to truckers. For instance, gas station aisles with dyed-diesel pumps — there is often one per station — may not physically accommodate semi trucks. Plus, increased demand for dyed diesel may also increase the chances of exhausting rural supply chains. And because the legality of driving on public roads with dyed diesel varies by state, Schweitzer said, the new policy may be “confusing and difficult to manage” for interstate truckers.

And for Montana farmers, he said the policy comes “too late.”

“Most of the farmers that are hauling grain to the elevators have done that already,” Schweitzer said.

Brunner, the Great Falls rancher, is also skeptical that the state’s temporary allowance for dyed diesel will provide much relief. He pointed out that the dye stays in vehicle tanks even after the fuel is spent, so if a driver gets pulled over after the exemption expires in late November, a test could show a false positive and lead to fines.

“In another year, get your tank dipped. It shows red. There’s $1,000 right there,” Brunner said.

Brunner is trying to keep his ranch’s books balanced. Over the weekend, he hired a few semi trucks and drivers to bring his herd, which summers 125 miles to the north, back home. He got his bill on Monday. Unlike the one in spring, it included an 8.5% diesel surcharge.

“It’s ridiculous,” Brunner said.

And he has even more diesel-related costs on the horizon. When he ships cattle to feedlots in the Midwest in the coming months, he’ll pay for the fuel premium. It will also show up when he sells and ships his hay.

“What doesn’t diesel affect?” Brunner asked. “Every single thing we do, everything we eat and use, everything depends on diesel.”

baku-school-hijab-protests:
Azerbaijani authorities arrested 37 people in Baku over protests against new school uniform rules, Minval reported, citing Azerbaijan’s Interior Ministry. According to Minval, protesters clashed with school staff and tried to disrupt school operations and traffic.

Protesters also tried to set fires, Minval reported. In Baku’s Garadagh district, they set fire to a school director’s car, and in the Yasamal district, they tried to set fire to a school. No one was injured in either incident.

A criminal case has been opened on charges of “organizing actions that disrupt public order, or actively participating in such actions.” The maximum penalty under that charge is up to three years in prison.

Azerbaijan’s government approved new rules on school uniforms on September 21, barring students from attending classes in clothing that contradicts the secular nature of education and undermines the uniformity of the school dress code. Starting October 6, similar requirements have extended to teachers’ clothing as well.

On October 12, schools began checking compliance with the new requirements, the APA news agency reported. Students who came to school improperly dressed were given talks involving school doctors and psychologists, and their parents were invited to the school for an explanation.

Azerbaijani authorities say the ban on religious clothing in schools is necessary to ensure equality among students. A uniform dress code is meant to smooth over social and religious differences among children, Azerbaijani lawmaker Sevinj Fataliyeva explained:

The requirements for school uniforms should not be seen as a fight against anyone’s religious faith, but as protection of a neutral educational space: a space where a child is not divided into “religious” and “non-religious,” rich and poor, or belonging to one group or another. Before the teacher sits a student.

great_falls_catholic_schools_closures_20:
Montana Free Press

Montana's independent nonprofit news source.

Aug. 20 was back-to-school night at St. Patrick’s Academy High School in Great Falls. Parents arrived with their kids, who were assigned their lockers, some even stowing away a few personal items for the start of school. The annual event is a tradition that welcomes the Catholic school community to a new school year.

It was a Thursday, and school was to start the following Wednesday. Despite many changes at the high school over the past year, the mood was cautious but positive, parents told Montana Free Press. Students expected to get their class schedules.

The festivities shifted, though, when Bishop Jeff Fleming, who leads the Roman Catholic Diocese of Great Falls-Billings, addressed the crowd.

“And I’ve got to say this was weird, because he always starts every meeting I’ve had with him with prayer,” Aaron Thomasson, whose son was going to be a sophomore at St. Patrick’s, told MTFP recently. “But this one didn’t.”

Fleming announced that the high school would be closed for the year. Thomasson told MTFP that the immediate explanation was that an on-site school administrator had suddenly quit.

School was supposed to start in less than a week.

Parents in the crowd sought solutions. Some stood and volunteered to fill roles at the school — anything to keep the school year on track. They asked what qualifications were necessary and what parents might have applicable experience. Then the bishop and a few other top church administrators hurried out for a private meeting in an adjoining chapel.

“They came out after about 20 minutes and said they were going to make a final decision Monday,” Thomasson said. “And that was when it got heated. Because obviously that gives, at best, for all the parents in Great Falls, two days to get into the local school system.”

After parents voiced concerns about waiting for a final decision, church leaders agreed to make an announcement the next day. That Friday, in a letter to the Great Falls’ Catholic community, the bishop confirmed that the high school would not open.

“I had believed that the school would open this year,” Fleming wrote in the letter, “but the realities that we are facing in the final stages of preparation left us with no workable path forward for the start of the school year.”

Behind the scenes, the path had looked difficult for months. Over the past year, enrollment plummeted as dozens of parents pulled their kids from the three Catholic schools in Great Falls, frustrated by the rollout of several major changes implemented by church leadership.

In April, the Catholic diocese, which oversees church operations for nearly all of eastern Montana, announced the closure of a Great Falls K-8 school after enrollment drops contributed to an unsustainable financial outlook. At St. Patrick’s Academy High, 70 students were enrolled for the fall 2025 semester. By August 2026, only 18 were expected to return.

On top of that, more than half of the high school’s 11 faculty members announced their resignations in May 2026. More staff and faculty left at the end of the school year. The principal and the administrative dean both resigned.

In interviews with more than a dozen former faculty, staff and parents of the Great Falls Catholic school system, stakeholders described longstanding frustration about operations and a lack of communication from the diocese about sudden changes, including a major “rebrand” of three well-known Catholic schools under the St. Patrick’s name. Some described shifting and overbearing policy changes — micromanagement by church administrators that disrupted the educational atmosphere that, by all accounts, had been a small but close and loving Catholic school community.

“I will say that when the school closed and then the other school closed, it really felt like the diocese didn’t have our kids’ hearts,” said Kathi Odenbriet, whose son had been a junior-high student at St. Patrick’s Academy East, which closed last spring. “The teachers, they’ve been great. But the way it went down, it didn’t feel like the diocese cared about the children. And that was hard to take.”

Aubrey Hiller-Rearden, the chief operating officer of the Catholic Diocese of Great Falls-Billings, acknowledged in an interview last week that stakeholders in the school felt unheard and were frustrated with the changes that took place. But she was firm that the “vision” the diocese has for the schools is the right path — and one that the church continues to pursue.

“I think the faculty, staff, students, families and alumni felt that they were left out of the process of how a vision of a K-12 system was going to be executed,” Hiller-Rearden said. “And I think it led to feelings of uncertainty and frustration, and I think they felt like there was the lack of input from them. And I think parents, at that point, started to explore other opportunities for their children. But it’s important to note that the conversation about a K-12 system in Great Falls has been an ongoing conversation for 50 years.”

For decades, there were three established Catholic schools in Great Falls before they were consolidated as St. Patrick’s Academy. Two schools, Our Lady of Lourdes and Holy Spirit, both served students in grades K-8. Great Falls Central High School opened in 2000 after the previous Catholic high school closed in 1973.

While Lourdes and Holy Spirit were run by individual Catholic parishes, the high school had direct oversight from the diocese. In the church hierarchy, a Catholic diocese manages multiple parishes.

Parents and teachers described a devout community. At the high school, some students thrived in the smaller class environment and participated in a range of sports and extracurricular activities. Parents often donated their time and money to maintain those activities in a small school system.

Several parents who spoke with MTFP emphasized that their Catholic faith enriched the culture at the schools. But it was also a welcoming environment for as many as half of the high school students who weren’t practicing Catholics.

Cristen Cochran and her family aren’t Catholic, but her daughter transferred to Central Catholic High School as a freshman three years ago after a poor experience at Great Falls High. Cochran said her daughter made incredible improvements.

“The teachers cared,” Cochran told MTFP. “She was a handful her freshman year there. Sophomore year, she just plugged in, and the love the staff had for the kids was amazing. They cared for her, not as a student, but as a person.”

But big changes came in the summer of 2025. The three schools united under a rebranding effort led by the diocese. The new, unified identity for the three schools was St. Patrick’s Academy, which included St. Patrick’s Academy West (Our Lady of Lourdes), St. Patrick’s Academy East (Holy Spirit) and St. Patrick’s Academy High School (Great Falls Central Catholic High). The schools chose a new mascot, the Wolfhounds.

Although past unification attempts had failed, church leaders pitched this latest effort as Bishop Fleming’s vision. Parents, faculty and staff quickly saw gaps in the rollout.

“The rebranding, to really do it right, all of the things that need to be repainted, redesigned and all that, it’s going to be expensive,” said Sean Donnelly, the high school principal and dean from 2023 to June 2026. “Almost immediately, when the rebrand was underway, we were told we were under austerity measures and you [could] buy only essential purchases.”

The transition was uneven. Fresh floor mats showed up with the new Wolfhounds mascot, but other items remained unchanged. At the high school, for example, the old Great Falls Central High colors and mascot, the Mustangs, remained on the gym floor. The sign on the building still bears the name Central Catholic High School, while a newer sign near the street reads “St. Patrick’s Academy High School.”

Parents said the rebrand was sudden and heavy-handed. Multiple people described efforts to remove references to the old Central Mustangs that led to frustration, particularly among students and alumni.

“There were a couple times when my youngest said, ‘I can’t do that. We can’t wear that anymore,'” said Brooke Corry, who had two kids in the Catholic schools. “It can’t have Central on it.”

There were other big changes. Mass services, which were previously once weekly, became required for every school day. The schools also switched to a four-day week with Friday as an additional, optional day for “enrichment experiences” like field trips. It was met with mixed reviews, but some parents told MTFP it felt like a 20% reduction in their kids’ weekly education for the same tuition. Emily Drazich, who had three kids in the Catholic schools, said the four-day school week pushed her family to enroll them elsewhere.

For Drazich and others who spoke with MTFP, it was a case in which multiple frustrations snowballed. She also felt that, despite the increase in Mass services, the Catholic identity underpinning the school system was eroding amid all the upheaval.

“It was supposed to be about the actual foundation of our faith and forming our children in that environment every single day,” Drazich said in written comments to MTFP. “We felt like, at times, there was more emphasis on the image of Catholic education than the actual foundation underneath it.”

Hiller-Rearden told MTFP that the Catholic faith teaches one to look forward rather than dwell on the past. While she said some parts of the transition could have been handled differently, she repeated that the diocese was carrying out a plan half a century in the making.

“Building on 50 years of dialogue, listening sessions, two previous bishops, feasibility studies, all of that,” she said. “I think we could have done it differently. I’m not sure we would have ended up in a different spot at this point.”

Within a year and a half of the rebranding meant to unify three schools, two of them closed.

Through the 2025-2026 school year, enrollment steadily fell as frustrated parents pulled their kids out of the new St. Patrick’s Academy. It was a huge blow to a private school system that relied heavily on tuition.

In April 2026, there was another sudden announcement: St. Patrick’s East, formerly Holy Spirit, would close at the end of the school year. Leaders connected the decision to a turning point in the school’s enrollment trajectory.

“It was financial, according to our councils,” Laura O’Neill, the former principal at St. Patrick’s East, told MTFP in an April interview. “We were operating in the black until this rebranding came about. We lost 67 students.”

The news was presented as a decision not of the diocese but of the parish and its priest, who had direct administrative control over the school. Responding to swarms of angry Facebook comments, the diocese commented April 24 that “the parishes and the diocese remain responsible for their own schools under canon law both financially and administratively.”

But it was the diocese that instituted the rebranding effort and the four-day school week, parents and faculty told MTFP. People involved with the school repeatedly referred to the diocese’s influence and the impact of that influence on enrollment, even at the parochial schools.

“They changed everything,” O’Neill said in April. “They changed the name. They changed the logo. They changed the colors.”

Online commenters speculated that the diocese was still in a position to assist the school rather than let it close.

Asked what influence the diocese had over the closure of St. Patrick’s East, Hiller-Rearden told MTFP that the ultimate decision was with the leadership at Holy Spirit Parish.

“To answer the question of what impact did the diocese, or influence, did the diocese have — Bishop Jeff confirmed the decision of the pastor to close the school,” she said. “That’s it.”

Odenbriet, whose son was a junior high student at St. Patrick’s East, said that the news hit hard. But she recalled how much the school staff maintained a positive environment for students.

“The teachers found out not very long before the families found out,” Odenbriet said. “And there was school the next day. And those teachers all committed to making sure no matter what was going on with their jobs, at the diocese, whatever, that the kids were taken care of.”

The students at St. Patrick’s East had the option to transfer to the remaining Catholic K-8 school, St. Patrick’s West. Odenbriet instead enrolled her son at a local public junior high school.

“Getting the news, processing it, and then having to make decisions. That was hard for us at that spot,” she told MTFP. “And then when it happened at the high school, and they had two days to figure it out, my heart broke all over again.”

The rebranding, the four-day school week and other policy changes were taking a toll at the high school as well. The small school made enrollment gains in prior years and had 70 students, according to the Montana High School Association. But parents started enrolling their kids elsewhere.

At the same time, the diocese continued to exercise stricter control over the school.

“Throughout the fall, it seemed like every couple weeks, every couple months, there would be a new policy, some rule or process that would have to be filled and come down from the diocesan level,” said Donnelly, the high school principal and later its dean.

Donnelly was a longtime public school teacher and has a doctorate in educational leadership. He started as principal at Central Catholic High in 2023. During that fall of 2025, he said that diocesan administrators approached him and said they wanted to bring on a new principal. Donnelly, meanwhile, was asked to sign a new contract to become administrative dean, a new position at the school.

In January 2026, the diocese announced Brian Held as the new high school principal. The reason given publicly for Donnelly’s reassignment was to “make fuller use of his gifts.”

Suddenly, the high school was supporting two administrative salaries.

“They pretty much split the duties in half,” Donnelly said. “So when Brian was principal, he was doing about 50% of what I was doing as principal. And I was doing the other roughly 50%, just as the title of ‘dean.’”

Hiller-Rearden declined to discuss school leadership changes, saying those are private personnel matters.

Held had served as interim principal at the high school before Donnelly’s hiring and was well-liked by parents and faculty. But the abrupt change alarmed parents, who were already sensitive from the rebranding and witnessing several families in the tight-knit community leave the school. Frustration among students took root as well.

“When Sean was pushed aside and Brian [was] brought in with no communication, they just informed the parents of it. We came back in January to a very different campus,” said Nellie Sholey, who was a part-time assistant to the school counselor through most of the 2025-2026 year.

Donnelly said that throughout the spring, more and more students announced they were leaving. Enrollment dropped to 56.

“Out of those 56 that we still had, of course, seven who were seniors,” Donnelly said. “But then also we had, by probably May, about 20 to 30 of the students who could have come back who said, ‘No, I’m not going to come back.'”

Simultaneously, school staff and faculty had been concerned by the change in school administration and faced frustrations of their own. They described a consistent drumbeat of mismanagement, including shifting pay periods, an inability to fund school programs and being stuck in the middle of frustrated parents and demanding church administrators.

Much of the frustration was directed at Hiller-Rearden, who was described as a close confidant to the bishop and someone who carried out much of the administrative direction, and Kody Diekhans, who was a “unification agent” during the rebranding and is now principal at the remaining Catholic school, St. Patrick’s Academy West.

Kris Warren, who was a science teacher and coach at the high school from 2012 to June 2026, said the diocese restricted access to funds previously available to run long-running club events, such as a Christmas meal donation program that benefits community members in need.

Warren said she could see student morale dropping. She reached a breaking point.

“I just finally got to the point where it was my health or my job,” Warren told MTFP. “Something’s got to give. So I chose my health.”

Warren submitted her resignation in May. She wasn’t alone. That month, when teachers received their contract options for the next school year, more than half of the small faculty — six out of 11 — decided to leave. In addition, the school librarian resigned, as did the school counselor and Sholey, the assistant counselor.

And the school’s two administrators, Dean Donnelly and Principal Held, resigned in June at the end of the school year.

Reached in September, Held declined an interview request from MTFP.

Donnelly, who had kids in the Catholic schools and stuck it out through the job reassignment, said he came to a difficult realization in June when his wife told him he seemed miserable in the job he had loved.

“As an educator, my professional judgment is that trying to run the school in the way that they’re proposing here just wasn’t going to work,” Donnelly said. “It won’t succeed. And it felt like, for me, committing educational malpractice to try and go through the motions and collect a paycheck for something I just didn’t believe could work.”

Like other parents, Donnelly enrolled his kids in a small public school district outside of Great Falls.

Amber Pichler started in a marketing position with the school in 2023 but became the administrative assistant at the high school last year. The role was like an office manager, handling the many logistical tasks necessary to run a school. Pichler was also frustrated and submitted her resignation in March 2026. But she also had kids attending the Catholic schools and agreed to stay on through the summer to help keep the high school afloat.

Like others, Pichler went into the summer of 2026 expecting that the high school would resume in the fall, if perhaps in a diminished form. She had worked through two previous summers at Central High School and knew the work that needed to be done.

But this summer was different.

“Throughout that time, I would constantly ask, ‘OK, do you want me to start tuition letters? Do you want me to start setting up for the school year? Do you want me to start ordering supplies like I would normally be ordering?'” Pichler said.

The response from the diocese was, “Nope, nope, nope. Just hold off,” she said.

In the spring of 2026, Bishop Fleming held one-on-one meetings with high school faculty amid a rush of resignations.

Faculty told MTFP that Fleming listened to their concerns and affirmed a commitment to open in the fall. Parents and faculty said it wasn’t entirely fair for Fleming to act surprised in August.

“And the fact that he didn’t know two days before school started that nothing’s going on — as an administrator, what’s he doing?” said Warren, the longtime teacher who resigned in the spring. “He knows his staff is gone. What’s he been doing all summer?”

While working in the high school office over the summer, Pichler said she fielded calls from job applicants who couldn’t reach the diocese to schedule interviews. Her last day working for the school was Aug. 13.

Hiller-Rearden said that the diocese received several applications through the spring and summer and conducted four job interviews.

“We beat the bushes and had a lot of conversations and worked really, really hard to make sure that we had at least the minimum to be able to operate the school and open in the fall,” she said.

The most important piece was a licensed school administrator. Hiller-Rearden said that Diekhans, principal at the remaining K-8 Catholic school, was named interim principal at the high school for the 2026-2027 year. She said that on Aug. 20, Diekhans decided he couldn’t manage both the high school and his K-8 school and withdrew from the high school obligation.

In addition, Hiller-Rearden said the high school hired an “on-site manager” who also backed out of the job on Aug. 19. She declined to name that person. Even as students were invited to back-to-school night on Aug. 20 to receive their locker assignments, Hiller-Rearden said Bishop Fleming held out hope that some new development would allow the school to stay open.

“I do believe, even up until Friday [Aug. 21] afternoon, we were hopeful that we were going to be able to open the high school,” Hiller-Rearden said. “And it became very apparent that we didn’t have what we needed in place to be able to do that responsibly.”

Through all of the turmoil, many families remained committed to the Catholic system. Because they believed the schools had been the best place for their children, many held out hope that their continued support would keep the institutions going.

Tom Cook, a parent who pulled two kids from the high school just weeks before the start of the school year, said his family had been dedicated to the success of the Catholic school system. Three of his other children had already graduated from Great Falls Central Catholic High. He told MTFP that the Catholic model and the small-school atmosphere were important to his family.

While Cook said there wasn’t much communication from the diocese over the summer, the message they did receive was a message of commitment — including from the bishop himself.

“We were entirely expecting the school to be open,” he said. “We were promised that was their plan. They said no matter what, they were going to keep the school open.”

With two of the three schools not operating this year, some parents wonder what the continued financial fallout will be for the small Catholic school system that’s so dependent on donor support from alumni and community members.

“I just really feel for everyone who has been affected by that loss of something that was a really special place and headed in the right direction,” said Donnelly, the former principal and dean. “And to have it just kind of taken away, and affected by these things that came from outside and had such a terrible impact on it, that was just really hard.”

While the diocese hasn’t announced plans for the high school’s future, representatives have emphasized that the decision to close is, for now, limited to the 2026-2027 school year. Hiller-Rearden said the diocese hired a director for Catholic education who will spearhead plans to reopen at some point.

“I know that we have the best interest of the school and our community at the forefront, and the vision hasn’t changed, even with all of this disruption,” Hiller-Rearden said. “The vision is one K-12 system campus for Catholic education in Great Falls.”

Across multiple interviews, parents raised a common theme: Their voices weren’t being heard by church leadership. Changes came on abruptly, the reasons weren’t clearly communicated, and those decisions set in motion a series of events that compelled families to change schools and disrupt the social ties that existed there. Even the high school’s Facebook page was deleted.

“Honestly, it felt like they didn’t really care that people were leaving,” said Drazich, a parent, in written comments to MTFP. “There wasn’t much effort to keep families. It felt like this is what we’re doing, and that was that. It became very much an ‘either you’re with us or you’re against us’ feeling. That was incredibly painful.”

Reporter Zeke Lloyd contributed to this story.

Catholic school stakeholders described longstanding frustration about operations and a lack of communication from the diocese about sudden changes, including a major “rebrand” of three well-known Catholic schools under the St. Patrick’s name.

Four U.S. Senate candidates — Republican Kurt Alme, Democrat Alani Bankhead, independent Seth Bodnar and Libertarian Kyle Austin — debated in Bozeman on Oct. 11, marking Alme’s first debate appearance. Alme, the frontrunner, was the target of the lion’s share of the debate’s attack lines, mostly for backing congressional Republican stances on tariffs, immigration and the war in Iran. Bankhead and Austin each took notable swings at Bodnar, primarily arguing that he is not as “independent” a candidate as he claims.

On Oct. 9, local election offices mailed out absentee ballots, which account for the majority of ballots cast in Montana. Many Montanans will have their ballots in hand early next week. Many more are preparing to vote at their local polling place on Election Day, Nov. 3. However you choose to vote, you may have questions. And we have answers.

tropical-storm-rachel-downgraded:
Adrian Florido

Long Beach Public Works workers clean up along Alamitos Peninsula in Long Beach, Calif. that was affected by Tropical Storm Rachel, Sunday, Oct. 11, 2026.
                
                    
                    Jill Connelly/AP Photo
                    
                
                hide caption

The National Weather Service said on Sunday that Rachel has been downgraded to a post-tropical storm after causing flooding and damage in southern California over the weekend before moving inland across the desert southwest.

The region is still at risk of flash floods as the storm's remnants were expected to continue dumping rain and bringing wind gusts through the weekend, the weather service said, adding that high surf would continue battering coastal communities.

Oceanfront homes in coastal California cities, such as Long Beach and Newport Beach, were partially submerged as heavy surf breached sand berms that had been erected to keep the water away.

Flood warnings remained in effect for much of the California coastline through the weekend, from San Diego up to the San Francisco Bay area.

As the storm moved inland and northeast, some areas saw rockslides that temporarily blocked roads. Rain pounded Las Vegas, which broke a daily rainfall record Sunday. And the National Weather Service issued a flood watch for much of Utah, including Salt Lake City, which it said would get heavy rain beginning Sunday evening.

Waves batter homes and a boardwalk damaged by Tropical Storm Rachel along the Alamitos Peninsula on Sunday, Oct. 11, 2026, in Long Beach, Calif.
                
                    
                    Jill Connelly/AP Photo
                    
                
                hide caption

Forecasters warned that Rachel could be just a preview of what's to come for California over the next several months. They expect this winter to usher in the strongest El Niño weather pattern on record — which brings hotter-than-average ocean temperatures — and with it likely record rainfall, explosive surf and mudslides well into next year.

Last month, California Gov. Gavin Newsom issued an emergency proclamation, releasing money and other resources so the state could start preparing to protect critical infrastructure and educate the state's residents on how to prepare for severe weather.

"That means getting flood-fighting supplies into position, bolstering our water infrastructure, and helping communities across the Golden State prepare," Newsom said in a statement following the proclamation.

The state is pre-positioning more than 4 million sandbags, more than 50,000 feet of portable flood barriers and 400,000 tons of rock to repair levees. It's also inspecting dams across the state and taking other precautions, such as strengthening the pillars that hold up beach piers.

The strong El Niño is also expected to bring severe weather to Mexico. Over the weekend, Hurricane Simon lashed at the country's Pacific Coast as a Category 4 hurricane. The eye of the storm was moving parallel to the coastline about 60 miles offshore, near the city of Manzanillo. It's unclear if the storm will make landfall, but Mexican officials said they expected heavy damage from its pounding rains and winds nonetheless.

Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum urged residents to stay indoors.

"Precautionary evacuations to safe zones are ongoing," she wrote on social media. "The priority is to protect ourselves."

us-china-drones-police-lurch:
Jaclyn Diaz

Loading...

For hours, bullets tore through the home, hitting neighboring houses and cars.

Inside, a man wanted by police for allegedly killing his ex-girlfriend was holed up with his new girlfriend.

As the SWAT team prepared to enter, Kevin Fennessy with the Ocean County Sheriff's Office tried something new first. He sent in a tiny assistant: a small drone equipped with a camera.

From a safe position outside, Fennessy slowly piloted the device through a blasted-in window, while he and other officers watched on a monitor. The video, viewed by NPR, showed hallway walls and furniture riddled with bullet holes.

As it entered a back bedroom where the couple had holed up, footage showed the man's body on the floor. He had killed himself. With the drone still hovering above the macabre scene, police deployed two flash bangs into the room. The woman rushed out and surrendered.

The incident, which happened about three years ago, sticks in Fennessy's mind when he considers the value of his department's drone program, which he heads.

"No one's hurt. Everyone's safe," Fennessy says. "Forty-one times they shot out the house at us. But at the end of the day, we were able to clear the house."

Chief Warrant Officer Kevin Fennessy lifts an Ocean County Sheriff's Office DJI Matrice 300 RTK drone out of the custom-built bed of a department SUV at Robert J. Miller Airpark on Sept. 4.
                
                    
                    Albert Yee for NPR
                    
                
                hide caption

New Jersey's Ocean County Sheriff's Office is one of an estimated 6,000 law enforcement agencies across the country that now have drones, used for search and rescue, fire and traffic crash investigations, and tactical response, according to the Law Enforcement Drone Association. It's an organization that advises, trains and certifies police across the country on their drone programs.

Ocean County's entire fleet is from DJI, a Chinese manufacturer of drones. LEDA estimates that about 80% to 90% of law enforcement agencies flying drones use DJI devices. China controls a vast majority of the global drone market, and it's the dominant source for the minerals and raw materials needed to build them, researchers say.

The Trump administration wants that to end. It's made several moves to bolster U.S. drone makers, including by banning many new foreign-made drones from entering the American market. Most recently, his administration announced tariffs of 15% to 100% on some foreign-made drones, making it much more expensive for agencies to buy these devices.

Critics of these moves say the American drone industry is not yet able to keep up with demand, nor can it match the high-quality and low-cost drones made in China. Law enforcement agencies that rely on these drones are getting caught up in the fight as the federal government pushes back on the dominance of Chinese technology.

"We're seeing lives being saved with the use of this technology," says Jon Beal, head of LEDA. He says the organization supports efforts to boost the American drone industry, but that reducing access to Chinese drones is not a good solution.

"What that's going to do is cancel out perfectly viable drone programs that are doing great work out there," he says. "We don't want to cut off our nose to spite our face."

Agencies pay for drone programs in various ways, including with grants and fundraising. The Ocean County Sheriff's Office uses profits from asset forfeiture and through their municipal operating budget to cover their fleet of 25 drones.

"We have to be cost-effective. And to do that, get the best product that's available to us," Ocean County Sheriff Michael Mastronardy says.

Loading...

A Seabob rescue vehicle inside the garage of the Seaside Heights Volunteer Fire Department Ocean Rescue office in Seaside Heights, N.J. This vehicle propels rescue swimmers during water rescues. The department is looking into aerial drones equipped with flotation devices and unmanned water drones like the ones the Ocean County Sheriff's Office uses to aid in water rescue.
                
                    
                    Albert Yee for NPR
                    
                
                hide caption

For them, that meant turning to DJI drones.

In the parking lot of the Ocean County Sheriff's Office in early August, Fennessy breaks down the costs of the equipment one of his deputies carries in his vehicle.

A DJI Matrice 300 RTK: $13,699

A set of two batteries: $1,400

A camera with infrared thermal imaging: $11,499

A (very fancy) remote controller: $1,600

A RESTUBE Automatic, a flotation device that can be dropped into water for rescues by the drone: $130.99

A payload release system: $1,099

That comes to a total of $29,427.99

Fennessy acknowledges this is a huge investment, but says the devices are well-used and well worth it — especially in the summertime, when Ocean County's population nearly doubles. Major events constantly pose a policing challenge for the department, and they've found that drones have helped keep an eye on big crowds.

In July, the department used a drone to drop flotation devices to two swimmers in distress, and rescuers were able to bring them to shore.

Fennessy has become passionate about drones professionally and as a hobbyist. He's done a lot of research, including into the American drone market. "All their stuff is good," he says. "I've flown almost all of them. And I like them. I do. They make good products, but probably about three times the cost" of the DJI tools.

Beal, who says his organization is "agnostic" when it comes to what drones departments use, says he thinks Chinese-made drones are "light years ahead of what our American drones are able to do."

For instance, Beal says DJI offers a drone with an impressive, high-resolution thermal camera that costs less than $10,000 right now. He says American-made drones have worse flight-time capabilities, thermal imaging and zoom. And still they usually cost between $20,000 and $50,000, depending on the type and the model.

NPR compared the cost of two drones with similar features. The DJI Matrice 400 drone retails for about $10,500. The American-made Inspired Flight IF800 TOMCAT is going for $21,000.

Ocean County is closely monitoring recent actions by the Trump administration that could limit options for updating its fleet in the future.

Agencies in other states like Florida, Texas, Mississippi and Tennessee have had to terminate their drone programs or plans for one after state lawmakers passed bans on agencies using foreign drones. Beal says some were left scrambling to find ways to pay for more expensive American alternatives when tight department budgets couldn't cover the additional costs.

And there are more federal actions in the works.

The Federal Communications Commission is considering a new rule that would reclassify drones that use tech like thermal imaging as "military grade" — effectively banning many Chinese-made drones that have this integrated technology. Ocean County and other law enforcement use thermal imaging to assist in finding lost people or pets.

An aerial view of an Ocean County Sheriff's Office DJI Matrice 300 RTK drone with a thermal-capable camera payload at the Ocean County Fairgrounds with the New Jersey Pinelands stretching into the distance. A propeller plane can be seen below and right of the drone.
                
                    
                    Albert Yee for NPR
                    
                
                hide caption

The FCC already bans the sale of some new models of foreign-made drones without the agency's approval. Federal agencies and contractors cannot use certain foreign-made drones.

The FCC said in response to NPR's questions, "Thanks to President Trump's leadership, America's drone industry is booming with new investment, manufacturing, and jobs. At the FCC, we're doing our part — working hand-in-glove across government and the private sector to make sure that U.S. drone and counter-drone supply chains are safe, secure, and reliable for all."

The administration says that Chinese-made drones, and DJI drones specifically, pose a threat to national security — with, for instance, their potential for major attacks during large public gatherings, like the recent World Cup games, among other concerns.

DJI has pushed back against claims that its tech is shared with the Chinese government or that it accesses cameras and other footage collected by users, even hiring a U.S.-based cybersecurity firm to test the company's products for vulnerabilities.

Adam Welsh, head of global policy at DJI said in a statement published in May, "These findings confirm what DJI has consistently maintained: our products are secure, our data practices are transparent" and the concerns that led to the company being banned "are not supported by technical evidence."

There's also the allegation that DJI uses forced labor from Uyghurs, a primarily Muslim ethnic group facing human rights abuses under the Chinese government, to build its products. In 2024, the Customs and Border Protection blocked certain DJI drone imports under the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act. DJI has strongly denied these allegations, too.

Fennessy says he understands these concerns. "But to be honest, right now," he says, "I want something that's capable to go out there and do the job. And I have it."

Beal says he's seen no hard evidence that China is using these drones or its technology to spy on communities that are using them. He says he can understand the argument to bring more of the drone supply chain stateside.

But that's a problem too, right now.

"We don't have a lot of the minerals. We can't produce the battery now. Even the American companies are using Chinese batteries," he says. "We're kind of limited to the resources that we have in-country or in an allied country, and sometimes that's just not there."

The National Sheriffs' Association, which represents more than 3,000 sheriffs, has called for the FCC to reconsider the proposed reclassification of certain drones as military grade. In a recent letter, the association wrote that it "recommends that the FCC confirm the adequacy of the domestic market for [Unmanned Aircraft Systems] and [Unmanned Aircraft Systems]-critical components for sheriffs and their colleagues in public safety to acquire drones to fulfill their various mission types, including drones that meet the definition of military grade." In addition to thermal imaging, that classification includes capabilities such as the ability to spray aerosols and lidar, or laser-based sensors.

The NSA recommends that otherwise the FCC add an exemption for state, local, tribal and territorial law enforcement agencies to continue to purchase and operate this equipment until the domestic market is built up.

An Ocean County Sheriff's Office drone lifts off at the Ocean County Fairgrounds on Sept. 4 as Chief Warrant Officer Kevin Fennessy (left) and Officer Adam Wright (at right, with the controller) stand near a department SUV.
                
                    
                    Albert Yee for NPR
                    
                
                hide caption

Keith Miao, the CEO and founder of Birdstop, a Detroit-based manufacturer of autonomous drone technology, says China "hands down" dominated what he calls "the first era" of drone technology. He says American manufacturers have the potential to "define the next era of enterprise and government use of drone technology."

To Miao, the federal government's latest moves are an acknowledgment that this is a critical technology that, if not manufactured at home, could be a serious problem down the road.

"I think this is going to give American manufacturers an opportunity to rethink … and build out drone manufacturing," Miao says. "We are going all in on manufacturing drones in America and building up the supply chains to do that long term. And so we obviously believe it can be done."

There are several federal and state grants that law enforcement can use to buy American-made drones. But they are competitive.

Fennessy hopes more federal funding comes through, especially if the government eventually wants them to park their DJI drones for good.

"If the federal government wants to say, hey, listen, you can't fly your DJI drone anymore, well, that's cool. Um, how am I going to afford to buy the drones that you want me to fly? The taxpayers of Ocean County are going to absorb that," he says. "The funding's got to be there."

BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

On Saturday, September 22, solar and wind met 80.4 percent of demand on Australia’s national electricity market, with the grid covering the eastern states, South Australia, and the Australian Capital Territory. For about 30 minutes around lunchtime, rooftop panels on homes and businesses across the country carried more than half of the total load by themselves. Large-scale solar and wind farms covered most of the rest, with hydro adding around one percent. Fossil fuels accounted for 20 percent.

More than 4.3 million Australian households now have rooftop solar installed. Saturday’s record showed what those installations add up to in practice: enough distributed generation to carry the country through the middle of the day without needing much from the main grid at all. Energy Minister Chris Bowen called it “more clean, cheap, sovereign energy powering our homes and businesses than ever before,” and said more records should be expected as the transition continues.

Dr. Dylan McConnell, an energy systems researcher at the University of New South Wales, called it “record season” for renewables. The conditions helped: clear sunny days, low demand from heating and cooling, and timing that landed right as a full year of new generation capacity came online all at once. “These records are probably not going to last very long,” McConnell said. “They’re probably going to be broken in the next couple of weeks.”

Some of the surplus went into pumped hydro storage and batteries. A fair amount was curtailed: system security rules, network constraints, and the low wholesale prices that come with too much supply at once all played a role. Coal generation in Queensland hit a record low over the same weekend.

The record is a signal, but McConnell was direct about where real emissions progress gets measured. “From an emissions perspective, what matters is the annual contributions and how much coal we are burning.” The average renewable share for the 12 months ending in June was 44 percent, according to the Australian Energy Market Operator. The gap between 44 and 80 tells two things at once: how much a good sunny Saturday can flatter the numbers, and how much infrastructure still needs to go in the ground before those numbers look like that on a typical Tuesday. Australia’s target is 82 percent renewables by 2030, and recent analysis suggests new capacity investment needs to pick up considerably to get there.

The Daughters of the American Revolution (DAR) voted Saturday to disband its Martha Laird Chapter in Texas that fought to bar transgender women from joining the historic organization, citing violations of its national bylaws.

In a letter to chapter members, DAR Organizing Secretary General Marguerite Hogan Fritsch announced that the National Board of Management had approved the chapter’s dissolution by a two-thirds majority vote.

“On October 10, 2026, at the meeting of the National Board of Management of the National Society, Daughters of the American Revolution a resolution passed by two-thirds majority vote to disband the Martha Laird Chapter, NSDAR,” Fritsch said in the letter. “The actions of the chapter have been found in violation of Article XIX, Section 4 of the Bylaws of the National Society Daughters of the American Revolution,” the letter continued.

The letter did not identify the specific conduct that constituted a violation or state whether the chapter’s opposition to transgender membership contributed to the decision.

The National Society Daughters of the American Revolution confirmed to Fox News Digital that the organization had voted to disband the local Texas chapter but denied it was due to its views on membership.  “The National Board of Management voted on October 10 to disband the Martha Laird Chapter in Texas after finding that chapter officers had used the chapter’s name, leadership positions, communications, and governance processes to further the goals of a separate advocacy organization,” the group told Fox News Digital. “The Board determined that it was this use of chapter authority and resources – not the views being advocated – that constituted conduct discrediting the National Society under Article XIX, Section 4 of the National Bylaws.” “The Board’s decision was not based on the chapter’s or its members’ views concerning membership eligibility, their efforts to propose changes to the National Bylaws, or their right to advocate for changes in National Society governance,” the statement continued.

The group noted that at their June 2026 meeting, national members had rejected a resolution to add further membership restrictions. Individual members of the Texas chapter retain their DAR membership and are free to advocate for changes to the National Bylaws through the Society’s established governance processes, the organization said.

The chapter previously challenged DAR leadership’s position on transgender membership, with member Laura McDonald telling Fox News Digital last year that the organization was contradicting its founding mission by recognizing transgender women as eligible members.

“But, then they go on to say that a man who claims he’s a woman is a woman, and therefore he’s eligible for membership. But if you are a man that doesn’t claim to be a woman, you’re not eligible for membership,” McDonald said.

Conservative California superintendent candidate Sonja Shaw told Fox News Digital that women and girls are being told that spaces created to protect their privacy, dignity, and opportunities “no longer belong to them,” including sports, restrooms, locker rooms, and now, according to her, the Daughters of the American Revolution.“The women of the Martha Laird Chapter in Texas stood their ground. They sought to preserve a definition of “Daughters” based on biological sex and asked for a clear vote. On October 10, national leadership dissolved their chapter,” Shaw said.

“Think about that. Women who stood up for their convictions saw their chapter, with a history dating back to 1942, dissolved. Here is the damning question national leadership needs to answer: Why should women be punished for standing up for the very definition of the organization they belong to?” she added.

Shaw also pointed to similar debates across the country concerning sports and privacy in women’s spaces, and said “this is about more than one chapter.”“Our daughters deserve a future where they never have to ask permission to stand up for the truth, and where no woman is punished for having the courage to speak it,” Shaw said.

Under DAR’s national bylaws, Article XIX, Section 4 authorizes the National Board of Management to discipline or disband chapters that violate organizational rules or engage in conduct that discredits the DAR.

The dissolution comes nearly three months after Rep. Ben Cline, R-Va., introduced the Daughters of the American Revolution Membership Integrity Act, which would amend DAR’s congressional charter to restrict membership to biological women.

Sen. Marsha Blackburn, R-Tenn., subsequently introduced companion legislation in the Senate.

“Rather than honoring and preserving a lineage-based organization for women, it has embraced radical gender ideology at the expense of the women it was created to serve,” Cline said.

In September 2024, the Martha Laird Chapter, supported by 11 other chapters, submitted a proposed bylaw amendment defining membership eligibility based on biological sex.

The Center for American Liberty also provided legal assistance to the chapter, challenging DAR leadership’s contention that excluding transgender applicants could jeopardize the organization’s tax-exempt status.

The proposed amendment was rejected by DAR’s National Board of Management in February 2025. McDonald criticized the decision at the time.

“The rejection by the National Board of Management of our proposal to define a woman in our bylaws sadly confirms what we knew all along – that leadership is taking a political stance which is not based on fears of the loss of 501(c)(3) nonprofit status,” McDonald said in a statement to Fox News Digital.

DAR, founded in 1890, previously maintained that its longstanding membership policies allowed women with legally amended birth certificates to join, provided they otherwise met the organization’s genealogical requirements.

Emmanuel "Mike" Mathews, 81, and David Mattai, 55, got into a shootout at an Ohio dog park on April 21 after arguing about President Donald Trump, according to authorities.

A shootout sparked by an argument over President Donald Trump at an Ohio dog park could end with a jury finding that both men acted in self-defense, or that neither did, a legal expert told Fox News Digital.

Emmanuel "Mike" Mathews, 81, is charged with felonious assault for shooting David Mattai, 55, on April 21 at Centerville Mills Park in Bainbridge Township, according to authorities.

Mathews has pleaded not guilty.

Case Western Reserve University law professor Michael Benza said that under Ohio law, defendants lose the right to claim self-defense if they helped ignite the confrontation that led to the shooting.

Emmanuel Mathews faces charges in connection with a shooting at an Ohio dog park. (Geauga County Sheriff's Office)

VIDEO SHOWS MOMENTS BEFORE ARMY VETERAN WAS FATALLY SHOT IN WALMART PARKING LOT DISPUTE

Since both men allegedly took part in the escalation, he said, the case presents a unique legal puzzle.

"They could both be found at fault, which means neither of them would get self-defense," Benza told Fox News Digital.

Since self-defense relies heavily on subjective fear and perceived danger, Benza said, "It's also possible both get self-defense."

Mathews' attorney, Ian Friedman, said the encounter began as a verbal argument, which turned physical in the park before ending in gunfire in the park’s parking lot.

"Mr. Mathews was attempting to leave," Friedman told Fox News Digital. "He was attempting to keep himself safe."

Friedman said it started when Mattai, who overheard Mathews talking to an eyewitness about Trump, disagreed with Mathews' view that Trump is one of the country's greatest presidents.

Bainbridge Township Patrolman Friedrich Kaufmann testified at Mathews’ May 5 preliminary hearing at Chardon Municipal Court that following that initial verbal altercation, Mattai drove away, then returned to the park about five minutes later.

David Mattai faces charges in connection with a shooting at an Ohio dog park. (Geauga County Sheriff's Office)

FLORIDA MEN WIELDING HATCHET AND MACHETE CLASH IN PUBLIX PARKING LOT, POLICE SAY

Mathews was still sitting at a picnic table with his dog when Mattai returned.

Mathews gathered his belongings and began walking toward his vehicle, but after crossing to the other side of a park fence, an exchange of insults between the pair caused a physical confrontation.

GUN-WIELDING COUPLE IN VIRAL BLM STANDOFF GOT FIREPOWER — AND 'A VOICE' — BACK AFTER LEGAL SAGA

Friedman said that Mattai grabbed Mathews by the hair and pulled him into the fence. Mathews also reported being headbutted. Mattai denied the headbutt allegation, but Friedman said an injury below Mathews' eye supports that account.

Following the physical altercation, both men retreated toward their vehicles after witness Jamie Jedlinsky, 70, reportedly stepped in to diffuse the situation.

The dog park at Centerville Mills Park in Bainbridge Township, Ohio. (Google Maps)

OHIO MAN CONVICTED AFTER TRYING TO SHOOT EX-WIFE AT POINT-BLANK RANGE INSIDE RESTAURANT IN CHILLING VIDEO

Mathews got into his vehicle and allegedly placed a .45-caliber gun on his dashboard, when Mattai, who stood in the parking area after loading his dog in his vehicle, saw the weapon.

The men allegedly exchanged words before Mathews fired once. Mattai retrieved a 9mm Taurus handgun from inside his Hyundai, then fired six shots "almost contemporaneously" near Mathews' head and body, according to Friedman.

"We believe that Mattai was turning to retrieve his gun and coming back to aim at Mathews when the bullet struck the lower right portion of his back," Friedman added.

Mathews was not injured in the gunfire exchange, but Mattai's return fire hit Mathews' vehicle at least four times.

Mattai previously told The New York Times that he did not physically touch Mathews after seeing Mathews’ weapon, and fired back in fear of his own safety.

Mattai’s wife, Sally Mattai, told the Times that her husband almost died after suffering a severe gunshot wound to his lower back that damaged his spine and required two separate emergency surgeries.

Mattai's attorney, Ryan Fisher, said he believes public opinions have convoluted the case and created confusion.

"There are a great deal of differing opinions of what went on in the dog park that day," Fisher told Fox News Digital.

Fisher's response did not address the defense's claims about the gun or the timing of the shots.

Geauga County Sheriff's Office deputies arrested Mattai Aug. 5. He’s currently facing misdemeanor charges of assault and disorderly conduct.

Benza said introducing a firearm changes the legal footing of a physical scuffle, but he emphasized that the order of events greatly matter.

"You go from OK, we're hitting each other... physically, punches are being thrown. Now you've pulled a weapon. You have now escalated this fight, which then justifies me escalating my response by then pulling my own gun and defending myself," he said.

"But you can't be the first one to draw the gun."

Ohio law removes the duty to retreat when someone is lawfully in a location. Friedman said that since Mathews was legally allowed to be at the park, he had no obligation to flee.

"He certainly had no duty to retreat," Friedman said. "Had he done anything different from what he did do in those seconds, he may not be here to talk about it today."

Friedman said although the verbal argument began over politics, his client acted out of fear for his safety, not political retaliation.

"This was never about a political dispute for Mr. Mathews," he said.

Benza, however, said the county’s politics could potentially complicate seating a jury, regardless of why the incident happened.

"In Geauga County, where this happened, it is a very Republican-dominated county," Benza said.

"The one defendant may be concerned that he will end up with jurors who are very pro-Republican or pro-Trump, which would create his concerns about a fair jury."

"The other defendant may want a pro-Trump jury because they would be so, well, he got what he deserved or something to that effect."

President Donald Trump listens as a reporter asks a question in the Oval Office of the White House, on Thursday, Aug. 27, 2026, in Washington. (Manuel Balce Ceneta/AP)

Now, the case may come down to a jury deciding whether Mathews had a genuine, reasonable fear for his life when he is accused of shooting Mattai.

GOT A TIP?

Friedman predicted the evidence would show Mathews should never have been arrested, while Fisher said the case is "going to have to be flushed out by the jury in the upcoming trial."

Mathews’ trial is scheduled to begin Feb. 16, at the Geauga County Court of Common Pleas.

Have you ever recorded a great video and then realized the moment you really wanted was buried somewhere in the middle? Maybe your grandchild flashed the perfect smile for half a second. Perhaps your dog made an expression you could never get again. You might even have caught the exact moment someone crossed a finish line or blew out birthday candles.

A lot of us would pause the video and take a screenshot. That can work, but your phone may already have a better way to pull a frame directly from the video and save it as its own photo.

Apple now makes this especially easy in iOS 27. Google Pixel and Samsung Galaxy owners can do it too, although the buttons are in different places. Here's how to find them.

Join us for a free CyberGuy LIVE class.

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson shares practical ways to stay safer, smarter and more confident with technology. Explore classes on stopping spam, phone security, financial protection and using AI to get better health care. Each class is free, easy to follow and comes with a free printable checklist.

See the classes and register at CyberGuyLive.com.

HOW TO SEARCH ANYTHING ON IPHONE, GALAXY AND PIXEL

A video on your iPhone can hold a still photo you may have missed while recording. (Stanislav Kogiku/SOPA Images/LightRocket)

Apple added a dedicated Save Video Frame as Photo option to the Photos app in iOS 27. It lets you find a specific moment in a video and save that frame as a separate image in your photo library.

Steps to save a video frame on iPhone

Your iPhone saves the frame as a separate photo in the Photos app. To find the photo you just saved, open Photos, tap Collections at the bottom, scroll to Recent Days, then tap Saved Today and look for the new frame.

Samsung Galaxy phones have a similar tool built into the Gallery app. Once you find the moment you want, you can use the capture button to turn that video frame into a photo.

Samsung notes that menus and settings can vary by Galaxy model, software version and region.

To find the photo you just captured, open Gallery, tap Albums, tap View all if needed, then open the Video captures album.

12 BIGGEST APPLE WWDC 2026 TAKEAWAYS YOU NEED TO KNOW

In iOS 27, tap the three-dot menu while viewing a video and choose Save Video Frame as Photo. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)

Pixel owners can use Google Photos to pull a still image from a video. Google calls the feature Export frame. Google has changed where this control appears in newer versions of Photos, so you may need an extra tap before you see it.

Settings and wording may vary slightly depending on your version of Google Photos.

If Export frame does not immediately appear, do not assume the feature disappeared. In newer versions of Google Photos, selecting the frame or tapping the camera icon can reveal the export control.

Google Photos saves that moment as a separate still image. To find the photo you just created, return to the main Google Photos screen and look in your recent photos. You can also tap Collections and check the relevant album if needed.

Taking a screenshot can still get the job done, especially when you are in a hurry. However, using the built-in frame tool gives you a dedicated photo created from the moment you selected in the video. It also makes the process easier because you do not have to worry about hiding video controls before taking the screenshot. Once the frame is saved, you can treat it like another photo in your library. The finished image can only be as good as the frame inside the original video. A sharp frame from a high-resolution video may look great. On the other hand, fast movement, low light or heavy compression can leave an individual frame blurry.

ANDROID MALWARE CAN STEAL YOUR PIN AND BANK LOGINS

Phone settings allow users to select a moment in a video and turn it into a separate photo. (iStock)

Here is one tip that can make a big difference. Slowly move through the video around the moment you want instead of stopping at the first frame that looks good. Just a fraction of a second can change someone's expression or give you a sharper image. You may also find a frame with less motion blur than the one you originally noticed. This is especially handy with family videos, pets and sporting events where the best moment can disappear almost instantly.

There is another phone trick that sounds similar but works differently. An iPhone Live Photo captures a brief period of movement around a still photo. Many Android phones offer a similar feature called Motion Photo. With those, you can often go back and choose a better frame from the short clip surrounding the original picture. Here, we are starting with an actual video and pulling one frame from that recording to create a separate still image. If you are trying to rescue a group photo because somebody blinked, Live Photos and Motion Photos may be the better place to start.

Start with the same photo app you used to create the frame. On iPhone, the saved frame goes into your Photos library. On a Galaxy phone, Samsung saves it in Gallery and may also place it inside the Video captures album. Pixel owners will find the exported image in Google Photos. If you have thousands of photos on your phone, search can save you from endless scrolling. Names, locations and objects can often help narrow down the image much faster.

I like this trick because so many of the moments we want to keep happen while we're recording video. You may think you missed the photo, only to discover that the exact expression or moment you wanted was sitting inside the recording all along. Apple, Google and Samsung each approach the feature a little differently, but you can get to the same result without downloading another app. Before deleting a video or giving up on a shot you thought you missed, take a closer look at the frames inside it. You may find a keeper.

Have you ever pulled a great photo out of a video, and what other camera feature do you wish Apple, Google or Samsung would make easier to find? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com.
