A media outlet tied to Everytown for Gun Safety sued the Justice Department, demanding information regarding an allegedly secret “plan of action” to comply with President Donald Trump’s executive order regarding the Second Amendment.

Trump issued the executive order regarding the right to keep and bear arms directing then-Attorney General Pam Bondi to “assess any ongoing infringements of the Second Amendment rights of our citizens” and develop a plan to address them in February 2025. In the complaint filed Sept. 4 in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of New York, The Trace claimed the DOJ was keeping the “plan of action” out of the public view, citing the establishment of the Second Amendment Section of the DOJ’s Civil Rights Division announced by Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights Harmeet Dhillon. (RELATED: Trump DOJ Seeking Major Role In Landmark Supreme Court Second Amendment Hearing)

I’ve directed the @CivilRights Division, through our new Second Amendment Section, to defend law-abiding Americans from unconstitutional restrictions. No one should face criminal penalties simply for exercising a right shared by tens of millions—regardless of where they live.…

“[I]llustrative of the existence of a DOJ plan of action is a December 8, 2025, announcement by Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon on social media, highlighting that DOJ had just created a new Second Amendment Section within its Civil Rights Division, and that DOJ ‘has a lot of 2A work planned, in addition to what we’ve already done!’” the outlet claimed. “The new Second Amendment Section of the Civil Rights Division also has a clear published mission statement on its website that tracks the language of the Executive Order.”

The Trace, founded by former New York City Mayor Michael Bloomberg, lists the Everytown for Gun Safety Support Fund, a 501(c)3, as an “institutional funder” and has Everytown for Gun Safety President John Feinblatt on its board of directors. Everytown and its predecessor groups, Mayors Against Illegal Guns and Moms Demand Action, have been the recipient of over $270 million from Bloomberg since 2007, according to the New York Times.

The Department of Justice did not immediately respond to requests for comment from the Daily Caller News Foundation.

“This is a FOIA lawsuit seeking public records from the Department of Justice,” staff writer Chip Brownlee told the DCNF when asked for comment. “President Trump’s executive order on the Second Amendment directed the DOJ to conduct reviews and create a plan of action. Those records, along with other documentation from the process, should be public. We sued only after the department didn’t fulfill routine FOIA requests.”

The Trace asserted that recent enforcement efforts by the Civil Rights Division’s Second Amendment Section also pointed to a “plan of action” that the Trump administration was keeping secret.

Since the section’s establishment in December, it filed suit against Denver, Virginia, the Virgin Islands, the District of Columbia and Colorado over bans on modern semiautomatic firearms and standard-capacity magazines. The section also investigated Philadelphia over its handling of concealed carry permits and sued California over legislation banning Glock pistols.

“The Second Amendment Section of the Civil Rights Division has published myriad press releases highlighting numerous court actions that have been brought by the new Section against states and municipalities for alleged unconstitutional patterns and practices with respect to the Second Amendment,” The Trace asserted in its complaint.

“The combination of a formal new Section within DOJ, along with its active litigation docket, is suggestive of a guiding agenda, and one that is substantively similar to the themes and commands of the Executive Order,” the complaint adds.

Article text size: This control adjusts article text size. For broader accessibility options, please use your browser or device text scaling settings.

The teal independents are in a similar place on the political spectrum to the United Kingdom’s Liberal Democrats, who hold 72 seats in the House of Commons. In Australia’s changing scene, they have similarities to a reinvigorated Australian Democrats, founded by former Liberal minister Don Chipp.

A looming challenge for the teal independents is what to do when, inevitably, they win the balance of power. There is a high chance that the 2028 federal election will see Albanese Labor lose seats and One Nation, the Greens and teal independents gain seats. Labor may keep its majority, but at some point that balance of power outcome is inevitable. What then?

Independents without some form of cohesion are easy pickings. The first threat by Labor will be to ask the governor-general to have it seek a vote of confidence in the House of Representatives. Without others to give Labor a majority, this would effectively force the independent teals to back Labor – or Coalition/One Nation – or face another election. In the case of another election, Australia’s right-wing media would be in full-throttle condemnation of the independents and anyone else on the crossbench for not supporting a new government.

More likely, the independents would be picked off by inducements from Labor or the conservative blocs. Offers might include the speakership or ministries, or hospitals, school halls, convention centres, sports grounds and better roads in home electorates. Perhaps there would be an underwhelming promise of a “reduction” – not a total ending – of approvals for new or expanded coalmines, gas fracking or forest logging. Without cohesion, the teal independents may end up losers, not the powerhouse they could be.

There is rumour and speculation about whether they will form a party. Don’t expect the press gallery in Canberra to think much outside the conventional bubble of two-party politics. It will tend to vilify rather than simply cover such a transformation to consolidate the teal independents’ power.

A teals party could allow freedom of conscience for its members on all matters. It would not be burdened by the forced solidarity of a party such as Labor. Similar freedom was allowed within the Democrats, and the Australian Greens’ party constitution allows for freedom of conscience for its representatives, except those from New South Wales, which required an exclusion clause when the constitution was adopted.

A teals party, under a suitable new name, would set out its basic objectives, including more action to tackle climate change. Party status would avoid the restrictive clauses for independents in the recent Labor–Coalition legislation giving parties privileged fundraising and election spending options.

The teal independents will need to be united in intent. The opportunity to form a government, ready to confront corporate intransigence in the face of global inequity and breakdown, should not be lost. Simple as that.

There are, however, other good alternatives to becoming a traditional party.

One fine option would be for the teal independents to agree to a set of guidelines for negotiating as a group, to use the best possible leverage when minority government comes. For example, they could adopt baseline requirements for tackling the climate emergency or corruption. They could have an established mandate for post-election negotiations.

This would not be new. Five independents, called “The Independents”, including myself, were elected to the balance of power in the Tasmanian House of Assembly in 1989. We had a set of agreed requirements to put to Labor and the Liberals in order for them to form government. We negotiated with both parties and, when the Liberals dropped out, signed a Labor–Green accord that achieved many of the requirements we had set out, including prohibiting the proposed Wesley Vale pulp mill, enlarging the Tasmanian Wilderness World Heritage Area, the introduction of freedom of information legislation and an end to public funding for ministerial liquor cabinets.

After the accord was signed, the independents and our supporters set up the Tasmanian Greens and helped, in 1992, to formulate the Australian Greens. At the next election Labor lost office but all five independents were re-elected as Greens. That’s a direction in which the teal independents are not likely to go.

A third alternative would be for the teal independents to simply agree to negotiate en bloc in any future post-election scenario. This minimalist position would obviate the risk of them being played off against each other or picked off one by one. They would be committed to working together and equally negotiating an outcome.

In democracies in recent centuries, parties began forming to pursue the special interests of various sections of society, especially financial self-interests. More recently still, green parties arose around the world, as if by spontaneous combustion, to tackle the looming ecological crises, including climate change, forest destruction and species extinctions. That inevitably led them to also promote social justice, peace and democracy.

Money rules, however. Democracies – just like autocracies – are overridden by the corporate rich who wield the financial power of advertising, media ownership, lobbying and political donations. You only have to look as far as the recent gift of a plane from Gina Rinehart to Pauline Hanson, or see the weapons manufacturers’ billboards around Canberra Airport, or count up the 800 lobbyists who work in our capital.

Two factors are leading to a national and global showdown in human affairs: the environmental crisis, including global heating threatening prosperity, and the growing gap between rich and poor, which is a potent flux for civil disruption.

In Australia – one of the richest per capita countries on Earth if its resource base is considered – these factors are stalking politics and are destroying the time-honoured two-party political system. They shaped the emergence of the Greens and the teal independents and the fierce big-end-of-town opposition to both, although a portion of those rich voters, alarmed by the global crises, is shearing off.

Recent elections have shown voter support for the old parties dropping consistently. The 2028 election will likely see the lowest vote for the Coalition and Labor in history. Labor, duchessed by corporate interests, has replaced the Coalition as Australia’s right of centre party, leaving the Coalition splintering even further right, to territory it’s now unsuccessfully fighting over with One Nation.

The teal independents have occupied the middle ground abandoned by both the Liberals and Labor. The Greens have taken over much of the Labor left’s traditional concern for the environment; the least well-off citizens; human rights, including First Nations’ rights; and opposition to overseas military involvement.

The above analysis is contestable but gives an insight into what is not contestable – the collapse of the once-entrenched two-party system.

Here’s the crunch question emerging from that collapse: given that a new polyglot right could form a future government, can a new polyglot left? That is, if or when the teals and Greens win more seats than Labor, how do the teal independents take due control of their situation? A question that precedes that question is whether the teal independents and Greens should swap preferences before directing votes to Labor or the Coalition.

The appearance of teal independents as a grouping is already there. Their coherence should not be missing when the crunch comes. Some form of publicly understood agreement needs to be embraced.

The global economy could face a 50 per cent loss in GDP between 2070 and 2090 unless immediate policy action is taken on risks posed by the climate crisis, warns a new report by the Institute and Faculty of Actuaries in the UK. Billions of people will die in this scenario.

As the Albanese government fails to measure up, and the Coalition and One Nation offer denial and inaction, here’s a possible outcome of an election down the line as the climate crisis worsens:

The House of Representatives has 150 seats, so a majority is 76. In the climate crisis with the economy collapsing, Labor wins 40. The Coalition/One Nation/right independents win 34. The Greens and teal independents each win 38, totalling 76.

It will require the independents as well as the Greens being prepared to act together to form a crisis-management government. Assuming the age-old enmity between Labor and the Coalition and other right parties, the teal independents will need to be united in intent. The opportunity to form a government, ready to confront corporate intransigence in the face of global inequity and breakdown, should not be lost. Simple as that.

Regardless of prognostications about Australia’s political future, it is healthy to talk about the alternatives that may be coming for voters. The teals will, of course, choose for themselves between remaining isolated independents or achieving some form of togetherness in the face of the unprecedented forces and fortunes challenging national politics.

It is a classic case of doing nothing being a decision of very great consequence.

Officers uncovered two buried chest freezers, with one containing Mr Thornton's heavily decomposed and dismembered remains.

Weaver was arrested days later in Byron Bay and extradited to Queensland.

On Monday, more than seven years after Mr Thornton's death, Weaver was handed the mandatory life sentence for murder in Queensland.

During a sentencing hearing, the Supreme Court in Brisbane heard Weaver, who was 24 at the time, shot the victim twice in the head and severed his legs below the knees with a saw so his body could fit in the freezer.

David Thornton's body was found in a freezer buried in his Ipswich backyard. (Supplied: Queensland Police Service)

The court heard Weaver then stole Mr Thornton's phone and repeatedly messaged his family and friends, telling them he had gone "off grid" on holiday in Western Australia.

Weaver also stole $30,000 from Mr Thornton, which he used to buy a motorcycle, the court heard.

The prosecution told the hearing that while on remand, Weaver confessed to a fellow inmate and tried to coax him to execute one of Mr Thornton's daughters and stage it as a suicide.

Justice Paul Smith said Weaver "murdered a friend in cold blood" because of greed.

"It was premeditated, he was shot in the head twice, there was no indication of a struggle, he was seated at the time and the treatment of the body is disgraceful.

"There was a protracted and highly manipulative campaign to deceive family, friends and neighbours.

Justice Smith told the court the killing had a "profound effect" on Mr Thornton's family and friends.

In a victim impact statement read aloud by the prosecution, Mr Thornton's daughter said it had been "seven years of waiting".

"We didn't just lose him; we lost a part of ourselves … and we still bear the consequence of other people's actions each and every day."

Justice Smith acknowledged Weaver's guilty plea and lack of criminal history, but said it was "difficult to accept" he was remorseful, given the "prolonged campaign of deception" after the murder.

With time already served, Weaver will be eligible to apply for parole in 2039.

Editor's Note: This is an excerpt from WBUR's Saturday morning newsletter, The Weekender. If you like what you read and want it in your inbox, sign up here.

The water surrounding Boston is dotted with sailboats year-round, and now that summer’s nearly begun, you’re sure to see plenty of them cruising through the Charles River and Boston Harbor on pleasant, breezy days.

The question is: How can you get on one?

As a matter of fact, you don’t need to know a sailor or own a sailboat to go sailing in Boston. (You will have to take a few classes, though.) Once you’ve gotten started, it’s a skill you can hone over time and enjoy for summers to come, according to local sailing instructors.

"We have people who in one season go from complete beginners to sailing in high wind conditions, sailing on more advanced boats,” said Anna Braun, education and volunteer manager at the Boston nonprofit Community Boating Incorporated. “So, if you're really dedicated to it and you come a decent amount, I would say you can become a good sailor in a season.”

Think this might be the season you set sail? First, check out the tips below from Braun, Boston Sailing Center general manager David Bryan and Community Boating member and volunteer Thea Berthoff so you don’t get stuck “in irons” as you get started.

How hard is sailing, really?

Operating a sailboat isn’t like renting a kayak. The watersport has enough jargon to warrant its own glossary, and you’ll need to complete a training course before you can take the helm. But all in all, “it’s not that hard,” Bryan said. “It just takes a lot of patience and understanding that there’s a lot of variables.”

The biggest variable, of course, is the wind. A sailboat needs wind pressure to move, but the gusts can be tricky to harness.

“If the wind always blew from the same direction, you could learn how to sail in an afternoon,” Bryan said. “But the wind's always changing direction, increasing or decreasing in velocity, so it can be a little frustrating when you're a beginner.”

It takes practice to learn how to detect where the wind's coming from, he added. But once you finally do, “then you can learn how to trim your sails and get to where you're headed.” (See? Sailing really does have its own lingo — but more on that in a moment.)

First, let’s talk about lessons. A monthly membership at a sailing school can run you anywhere from $99 to over $1,000. So before you get on a boat, you’ll want to ask yourself: do you want to do this for a summer, or for your life? How you answer will help you choose a local program that fits your goals.

Community Boating, which launches out onto the Charles River, has a basic, 30-day trial membership that comes with introductory sailing lessons and an opportunity to take the boat out on your own for $99. You’ll have to take two courses — rigging and shore school — totaling four hours of instruction. You’ve also got the option to go on a guided sail with an instructor after that. Once the first month is through, the membership renews at $175 a month, which grants you unlimited boat sign outs and free beginner and intermediate classes so you can keep learning.

Boston Sailing Center, which launches onto the harbor out of Lewis Wharf, also offers an introductory sailing program that comes with a monthlong student membership for a one-time fee of $1,200. Their program totals 22 hours of instruction, which you can either take over a weekend, over four weeks or over a singular vacation week. Bryan says the center’s courses are well suited for complete beginners or people who might have sailed as kids and need a refresher.

“And when you complete the course … you have access to the boats you learned on for 30 days afterwards, which is a great way to kind of practice and internalize what you just learned,” Bryan said. Once that trial is through, however, you’ll need to sign up for a daysailing membership, which can range from $765 (for a monthly membership) to $1,930 (for a yearly membership). But that’s still a lot cheaper than buying and maintaining your own boat.

At a glance, you can tell Community Boating and Boston Sailing Center offer programs with two different levels of time commitment. There are even more sailing schools in Boston, like Courageous Sailing, First Reef Sailing and the Piers Park Sailing Center that offer a range of memberships and lessons for you to choose from.

Not interested in joining a boating club? If you or a friend already have sailing experience, you can also rent a four-person sailboat for two hours for $99 from Community Boating from now through Oct. 31. (But before you can head out, the skipper will need to answer some questions from the dockmaster on duty, so make sure to brush up on your sailing knowledge.)

The learning curve

As you’re learning, both Bryan and Braun agreed sailing regularly is key to picking up the sport quickly and safely.

“It's good to get out at least once a week on your own,” Bryan said. Like any skill, getting better at sailing “depends on how much time you want to put in,” Braun added.

Learning the basics of handling your boat includes knowing how to “trim your sails” — that is, adjust your sails to the wind — as you venture out on the water. Here are a few important terms to get you started on that:

Bryan reiterated that navigation errors like sailing into the wind and sailing into shallow water are common when first learning to sail.

But “the most common mistake is when people get into a kind of a tight situation, sometimes trying to force the boat into that area that it doesn't really sail,” Bryan said.

Braun, who has taught more than 200 people to sail during her time at Community Boating, said she thinks the biggest thing people struggle with is confidence. “ People get super intimidated by seeing people run into the bridge or capsize,” she said.

But the instructors noted such errors are inevitable when you’re first starting out.

“We're dealing with mishaps pretty much every day with every beginner. No matter what, whenever you start, you're gonna flip your boat, you're gonna run into the bridge, you're gonna hit the island,” Braun added. “But everything always works out, and people's reaction afterwards is always, ‘that wasn't so bad.’”

Field Guide to Boston: Discover — and rediscover — your Boston.

And you’re not alone out on the water. Both Boston Sailing Center and Community Boating have safety teams you can contact via VHF radio for help during any sail — though it’ll cost you $115 per man hour for a rescue at Boston Sailing Center.

New hobbies, new friends

Berthoff, a member of Community Boating, began sailing four years ago. “I kept walking by and biking by on the Charles River Esplanade, and seeing how beautiful and fun it looked out there, and I was like, ‘What better thing to do in the Boston area?’” she told me.

“ The culture has been incredibly supportive, especially whenever you have a question or you're wondering about something, or you wanna just practice out on the river a little bit,” Berthoff said. “There is somebody who's gonna be in your corner, who's gonna be willing to help you out and to just give you an extra push.”

Boston Sailing Center also boasts a tight-knit community. Bryan says many of the students in the introductory program will pair up for sailing practice; eventually becoming members of the club.

“We do see a lot of the same folks coming back year after year,” Bryan said. “Some of our best members are those who have purchased a boat, realize how expensive it is, and then come back and join our program so they don't have to do the maintenance.”

Where to set sail

Once you’ve built up your confidence at the helm, Braun, Bryan and Berthoff suggest trying these routes as you traverse through Boston Harbor or the Charles:

“There are so many beautiful spots on the river,” said Braun. “There’s the MIT Boathouse; there are different public docks on the Esplanade. So bouncing back and forth between them and just seeing what else is going [on] around Boston is my favorite.”

Berthoff prefers sailing bridge to bridge on the Charles.

“I love going from the Longfellow all the way to the Mass Ave. Bridge, especially because it encourages me to practice,” she said. “Being able to be fast or slow, to take in everything that's on the water and enjoy all of the different views that are along the way.”

Launching out of Boston Harbor for a quick sail, Bryan said the first island you’ll hit is Spectacle Island and a round trip takes less than three hours.

“If you have some time, one of my favorite routes is to go out around the Graves Lighthouse, and then continue out in Broad Sound there, and go around Boston Light and come back in past Hull. You're rounding more islands and it's just a beautiful sail,” he said.

P.S. — It’s not just locals setting sail this summer. The Tall Ships will be returning to Boston for the first time in nearly a decade this July. Click here to learn more about those gigantic multi-sail ships and their role in MA250 celebrations.

Hanna Ali is an associate producer for newsletters at WBUR.

boston_scotland_world_cup:
With just hours to go until Scotland's opening World Cup match, anticipation is building across the city that has become a temporary home for the Tartan Army.

Scotland will play Haiti in their first World Cup encounter in 28 years. The long-anticipated match will kick-off at the Boston Stadium in Foxborough at 21:00 local time, 02:00 in Scotland.

It is estimated that between 20,000 to 30,000 thousands fans have travelled to Boston for the match.

They are now being joined by a last-minute influx of fans staying further afield in areas such as New York and Rhode Island.

"It's a Scotland invasion, absolutely everyone is here. I don't know how there's anyone left at home," said David Martin, 28, from Glasgow.

He added: "I quit my job to be here, I couldn't miss it. I missed out on on the Euros so I wasn't going to let that happen again."

The Tartan Army is certainly making its presence felt in the city.

Flags hung on buildings marking 250 years since US independence have been outnumbered by Saltires.

Fans wearing Boston Red Sox memorabilia have been trumped by Scotland strips, and walking down the street it feels as though every second person you see is wearing a kilt.

Even the local statues are now wearing traffic cones - just like the Duke of Wellington in Glasgow.

"It's like a little Scotland in one city, it's a festival atmosphere," said Adam Gray, 39, from Haddington.

He travelled to the US with his dad, Adam Snr, and son Callen. But along the way they bumped into a familiar face.

While in a queue to buy a beer, he was approached by school friend Niall Stone, who is originally from the same town but has been living in Australia for a number of years.

"It's mad when you've not seen someone in years, football really brings everyone together," Niall said.

They are now going to attend a baseball game together.

Almost 1,000 fans have made their way to the match on traditional American school buses, in a bid to save money.

Buses have left from Boston city centre and Providence in neighbouring Rhode Island, which is close to the match venue.

Some fans will get there early to take part in traditional American tailgate parties in the stadium carparks.

Local politicians have taken notice of the hysteria too.

Massachusetts Governor Maura Healey said: "I was speaking to lawyers and judges earlier today who told me they could not hear anything in the courthouse because of the noise outside from the Tartan Army.

"I think I'm going to have to call Canada and call the governors in Maine and Vermont to put out an SOS for more alcohol."

Boston's mayor admitted the city had been rethinking plans to deal with fans and they are now looking into implementing a consumption zone.

While many fans head out of the city to attend the match at Boston Stadium - which is situated in Foxborough, 22 miles south-west of downtown Boston - thousands more have been left behind scrambling for somewhere to watch the match.

About 5,000 will watch at the official Fifa fan zone in Boston city centre. However, the facility is oversubscribed and has been forced to turn fans away.

A number of local watch parties have been hastily planned.

Temperatures in Boston are expected to reach 32C on Saturday, dipping to a slightly cooler 27C during the match.

Elsewhere in group C, Morocco and Brazil will play each other in their opening matches at the Met Life Stadium in New Jersey.

boston_world_cup_live:
Support WBUR

After months of hype, infighting, sticker shock and genuine cuteness, it's time to play soccer (excuse us, football). Scotland and Haiti will face off in a Group C match at "Boston Stadium," aka Gillette Stadium in Foxborough.

We'll continue to update this post until the match is over. Feel free to check back in throughout the evening.

The match is over but that doesn't necessarily mean it's time for bed. The folks emptying out of the stadium in Foxborough are allowed to tailgate, which sounds like a totally normal thing except — as with so much around this tournament — FIFA made it weird. Local organizers in Boston and several other cities initially said the onsite cookouts were banned. But FIFA swore it said no such thing. Either way, pass the wings.

For everyone else, Massachusetts lawmakers betrayed the state's Puritan roots this one time, and temporarily extended "last call" at bars and restaurants an hour, to 3 a.m. But they didn't completely abandon Bay State tradition: They made the extended booze time a local option, so check with your local bartender if they are working late.

If you're a home body, you can relive the action through photos. We've collected some of our favorite shots from WBUR's Jesse Costa and Robin Lubbock, along with a few game photos from the Associated Press. You can check them out here.

With the game over, Foxborough is about to experience something very familiar: The long, soul-crushing gridlock of thousands of drivers fleeing the area.

If you were wondering about the price for parking outside the stadium, it's exactly what you thought it would be.

WBUR's Meghan Kelly walked the final mile to the stadium earlier this evening, thanks to a cavalcade of travel woes too long to include in tonight's live blog. The prices of the off-site lots rose steadily as she went.

About a mile out, a local business offered drivers a spot for $140, promising easy access out of the area post-game, using the distance from Gillette Stadium as a selling point.

Further along the road, the price jumped to $150 "cash," or $155 if you wanted to use Venmo.

Closest to the stadium, parking would run you an astronomical $200.

While those parking prices feel more like car payments, they aren't that far off from the cost of a spot on site at the stadium: Spots for the upcoming Iraq-Norway match will run you $175.

And just like that, the first of seven World Cup matches in Boston is over, with Scotland besting Haiti 1-0.

The result leaves Scotland atop Group C after the first set of matches. The win means three points, putting them two ahead of Brazil and Morocco, who each earned a point for their tie earlier in the evening.

Haiti dominated late in the second half, really taking the fight to a Scotland team clinging to its lead. As French soccer legend and Fox commentator Thierry Henry said after the game, "Haiti was a joy to watch."

Both teams face tough fights in their next two matches, with both Brazil and Morocco in FIFA's top eight-ranked teams in the world.

Melrose's Frantzdy Pierrot just struck a wicked header that blazed just wide of the net. Haiti was inches from tying the game.

Rob Lane, our reporter at the Boston fan festival just filed a single-line update about the mood at the watch party:

"The Scots are TENSE."

With about 10 minutes left in the match (plus stoppage time), Scotland still leads but Haiti's pounding on the door. The team's are dead even on possession of the ball, but Haiti's taken more shots during the match: 12 to Scotland's nine.

It's time for a hydration break — FIFA has mandated these three-minute stops of play for every half of every match because North America gets stupid hot during the summer.

This break comes during a nervy second half of play, with both teams taking real chances to score.

Scotland goes into the break with a one goal lead. But they haven't dominated the match; Haiti's had 45% of the possession and one massive opportunity to score that took some defensive heroics to foil by the Scots.

And what about the Mass. guy? Frantzdy Pierrot hasn't touched the ball a ton, but he's made it count when he has, with a hand in Haiti's missed scoring chance and four out of four completed passes, according to Fotmob stats.

As the action unfolds in Foxborough's "Boston Stadium," the official fan festival is happening in Boston Boston. Scottish fans overwhelmingly outnumber Haiti's backers, according to WBUR's Rob Lane, but the atmosphere is laid back.

Or it was, until Scotland scored its goal and the crowd erupted into pandemonium, throwing cans in the air and serenading goal scorer John McGinn with a variation of "Acky Breaky Heart." (It's a soccer thing. Really.)

Scotland's John McGinn just scored the nation's first World Cup goal in 28 years. His 29th-minute goal breaks the ice on what has so far been a back-and-forth match.

As packed at the sidewalks were outside of South Station today, things seemed to go smoothly. Here's more on the amiable mob from WBUR's Andrea Perdomo-Hernandez:

MBTA Senior advisor Rod Brooks watched the crowd lining up on Summer Street. He said a lot of the boarding groups were at the station at the same time, “but it’s controlled.”

The line was steadily moving.

“The trains are getting loaded, we’re in good shape,” he said about halfway through the queuing process.

Outside the station, a Scottish fan, Douglas Macleod lamented the long boarding line after standing in it for about an hour.

“I've been in queues, but this is the longest queue I've ever been in in my entire life, like, ever” he said.  “Like, it's the longest queue I've ever seen for anywhere, ever.”

But 14-year-old Yahia Chakar, of Charlestown, shone bright with elation as he took in the action at South Station leading to his first ever in-person soccer match. Clad in a Morocco jersey, he said his father Mustapha Chakar, surprised him and his sister with the tickets the night before.

“ I'm one of, like, 10 of my family members who live in the U.S., so being able to have the opportunity of going to a World Cup match, for the first time and being one of the only people in my family eligible to do this, it feels, like, honorable,” Yahia said.

The Chakars planned to take in some of the Morocco-Brazil match before going to the stadium, “ I wish Morocco’s going to win 3-0,” the elder Chakar said, hours before the two teams fought to a draw. “And after that, we're going to support Haiti.”

Congratulations, you've survived the hype and made it to kickoff. Scotland vs. Haiti is officially underway in Foxborough.

This match has been a long time coming for both countries. Scotland hasn't been to the World Cup in 28 years. According to the Fox broadcast, eight of the team's players weren't born in 1998, when Scotland was last featured in the tournament. Phew.

But that's like yesterday compared to Haiti, which hasn't made it to the World cup in 52 years. As WBUR's Nik DeCosta-Klipa wrote in our teams preview, the accomplishment is all the more remarkable because they never played a match in their home nation during the qualifying games.

Keep an eye out for Melrose's Frantzdy Pierrot, who'll lead Haiti's attack as a starting forward tonight. For the Scots, don't sleep on Scott McTominay, their gifted midfielder who scored a gobsmacking goal against Denmark to help the team make the World Cup.

We're 27 minutes away from kickoff in Foxborough, but folks in Boston and around the state are already out and celebrating. The official Boston Fan Festival opened its gates at 2 p.m. Across the state, cities and towns have set up watch parties with food, drinks, music and monster screens playing the match. Here's a handy map to help you spot some fun close to home:

And if you want to root your team on in a more traditional soccer setting, there are plenty of bars, cafes and restaurants tuning in to the World Cup. Here's a run-down of some of the area's prominent soccer bars.

Tonight's match between Scotland and Haiti is part of the World Cup's group stage. Unlike American playoff tournaments, like March Madness, the World Cup has a first round where a team can lose but still continue competing.

There are 48 national teams playing in the World Cup. A few months ago, FIFA sorted these clubs into four levels of relative talent, called pots. Then they held a big lottery, where a team from each pot was added to one of 12 groups. The idea is each group has an elite team, a really good team, a pretty good team, and a "Look ma, I'm in the World Cup!" team.

Scotland (pot 3) and Haiti (pot 4) are in Group C, along with Brazil (pot 1) and Morocco (pot 2). They'll all play each other in the group round, and the two best teams move on to the knockout rounds. The eight best third-place teams in the group stage also move on.

Brazil and Morocco's match in New Jersey just ended in a 1-1 tie, so if either Scotland or Haiti can pull off a win tonight, they'll lead the group.

If you're wondering, the U.S. men are a "pot 1" team. Not because they're an elite club, alas; they get that honor because they're a host nation, along with Canada and Mexico. That may explain how a team as good as Morocco ended up in pot 2.

Here are all the groups in the World Cup:

There are lots of World Cup fandoms here in Massachusetts, including thousands of Haitians, Brazilians and Moroccans watching Group C matches tonight. But the biggest surprise may be the arrival of the Tartan Army — traveling Scots here to watch their beloved Scotland play its first World Cup match since 1998. To say they're excited about their return to football's biggest stage would be an understatement.

The plaid partisans have descended on the city, bringing a party vibe wherever they go. Like Boston Common, where they greeted a fellow traveler who just walked 3,500 miles from Los Angeles to Boston to raise money for a mental health charity. (If you're interested in the math, that's three-and-a-half times the 500 miles and 500 more The Proclaimers said they'd walk to be your man. Talk about commitment.)

And down in Providence, WBUR's Eve Zuckoff was there as more Scots packed some school buses they chartered to get to tonight's match. Their departure was a bit delayed as late stragglers and cases of Narragansett beer were piled into the convoy. Bus driver Linda Semper told Zuckoff she's “only seen this many Scots on Outlander.”

If you're new to soccer, the vocabulary can feel a little daunting. You'll get it eventually, but it helps to have a crib sheet to explain things as you go. Call it a security blanket.

We wrote a very long, very detailed and (hopefully) very fun glossary to help you with the Britishisms that slip into even the American broadcasts. You can read that here.

If you're the kind of person who needs a rooting interest to watch a game, you may be interested in cheering for the guy from Massachusetts.

Melrose's Frantzdy Pierrot has played 52 games for Haiti since 2019, scoring 34 goals along the way. The 31-year-old striker was feted by Gov. Maura Healey ahead of this year's tournament.

You can read more about Pierrot here.

He's not the only Bay Stater playing in the World Cup. The other is from the other side of the Middlesex Fells: Miles Robinson, of Arlington, is a defender for the U.S. team.

If you're curious about the rest of the U.S. men's national team players, learn more here.

After all the sturm und drang over the MBTA's World Cup rail plans, and the $80 tickets, and the fight over street closures, and and and, we finally got to see whether people would bother with catching a ride.

Boy howdy, did they. The first train from South Station to Foxborough was sold out, ferrying thousands people to the stadium, according to T officials at the scene. The queue of travelers stretched from the platform, through the station and out into the street, with WBUR's Andrea Perdomo-Hernandez describing it like the lines at Disney World.

Kickoff is scheduled for 9 p.m., but WBUR has been busy all day, checking in on travelers grabbing that $80 train to Foxborough, riding the school bus with the Tartan Army, taking in the crowd at the official Fan Festival on Boston's City Hall Plaza and, later tonight, chilling with a Haitian family as they watch the match in their Foxborough living room. We'll be updating here to keep you up to speed as the evening progresses.

If you're staying home, you can catch the match in English on Fox or on the Fox One app. Tune in to Telemundo or log in to Peacock to watch the match in Spanish.

You can also head down to your local sports bar or community watch party to take in the vibe. Even if you're a person who dismisses "sportsball," you’re going to feel the giddiness from the fans. It’s infectious. Let yourself enjoy it!

Digital Replica Edition

Digital Replica Edition

Trending:

When they realized their son was struggling, Jordana Ash and Oliver Lignell dropped everything to fly from Colorado to Seattle, where they helped him connect with a psychiatrist and asked the hard questions.

Everyone had taken the right steps, including their son Maddy Lignell, when he asked for help. After 26 years of observing their son, Ash knew his mannerisms, and is sure he wasn’t lying when he told the psychiatrist he didn’t have a plan to die by suicide.

And yet, less than 24 hours before he was scheduled for an evaluation and six days after a Mother’s Day call where he didn’t seem quite himself, their “goofy,” compassionate, outdoorsy and endlessly curious Maddy was gone.

“Neither he nor we knew he was in a fight for his life,” Oliver Lignell said.

Since Maddy’s death in 2021, his parents have made it their mission to raise awareness of what some in the field are calling “suicide crisis syndrome” — a state characterized by feeling trapped and hopeless, while also withdrawing from people and being jittery or sleepless. The term can apply to people with a long-term mental illness who are at a crisis point, or those like Maddy without an apparent psychiatric history.

“We understood the tragedy of suicide to be the result of a long-term mental illness,” said Ash, a Boulder resident who works in the mental health field.

But Maddy had never shown previous signs of mental health problems, and while he was adjusting to a new job following a mid-pandemic move, he hadn’t gone through an obvious crisis, such as unemployment or a bitter breakup.

In 2024, the couple worked with the nonprofit Healthier Colorado to convene a group of experts to learn about suicidal crises in people without a preexisting mental illness.

Since then, Lignell has given a presentation alongside other bereaved fathers to the American Psychiatric Association, and Ash is collaborating with a researcher to develop additional screening questions to assess suicide risk. The current questions about thoughts of suicide, planning and access to lethal means are important, but may not flag risk in people without long-term ideation, she said.

Suicide deaths in Colorado gradually trended up from 2004 to 2021, rising from 792 to 1,370 deaths a year. Since then, they’ve been relatively stable, fluctuating around 1,300 per year.

The death rate also rose nationwide, and experts have proposed a variety of possible causes, including precarious economic conditions since the Great Recession, increases in depression diagnoses among youth and the rise of social media.

Colorado typically has one of the nation’s highest suicide rates, particularly among young people. From 2021 to 2023, the most recent years with detailed data, Colorado had the seventh-highest suicide rate among people between 15 and 19, according to America’s Health Rankings. The death rate from suicide was more than three times as high in Colorado as the state with the lowest rate, New Jersey.

The most recent data on contributing factors, from 2024, found 66% of people who died by suicide in Colorado had some sort of crisis in the two weeks before killing themselves. More than half had a diagnosed mental health problem, and a similar share had a known history of suicidal thoughts.

Dr. Megan Rogers, an assistant professor of psychology at Texas State University, is testing whether a new screening tool could catch more people at risk. Research has found that people do most of the active planning before a suicide attempt in an average of six hours, creating a tight timeframe to intervene if others haven’t spotted the signs before.

The majority of suicide decedents who sought medical care before their deaths said they weren’t thinking about killing themselves. Conversely, only about 14% of those who said they had serious suicidal thoughts in the past year made an attempt, according to the Colorado Office of Suicide Prevention.

“For some, they may be concealing (suicidal thoughts). For others, they had a more rapid onset,” Rogers said.

A 2016 study found that roughly four out of five people who died by suicide displayed at least one warning sign, though not always to those who were in the best position to intervene, said Mandy Doria, an associate professor of psychiatry at University of Colorado’s Anschutz Medical Campus. And, of course, people may not recognize something like a change in sleeping patterns or an unexplained mood improvement in someone with longstanding depression as red flags, she said.

“It’s more of a rapid change in behavior that you want to look for, rather than just feeling worse,” she said.

The human body is hard-wired to prioritize survival, and a person needs to be in an intense state of despair and agitation to knock that instinct offline, Rogers said. Fortunately, emotions that powerful don’t last long, so if something prevents people from completing an attempt, most ultimately don’t die by suicide, she said.

Dr. Chase Anderson, an assistant professor of child and adolescent psychiatry at University of California San Francisco, said people become suicidal when a situation feels unbearable and they can’t see a way out of it. A mental health provider’s role is to keep the person safe in the moment, then help them get to a place where they see their problems as something they can either fix or cope with, they said.

One of the things Anderson does with youth experiencing suicidal thoughts is to normalize them as a thing some people live with, and not a sign that someone is broken or should die, they said. Then they start working backward to identify what might have triggered the thought, and possible coping skills to use if it happens again.

“There are people living with it, and they can get help,” Anderson said.

Attempting to identify people at risk of suicide and get them into treatment is important, but it can’t be the only form of prevention, because no form of screening will ever be perfect, Rogers said.

“It’s similar to a heart attack. We know risk factors,” she said. “We still can’t predict who (will have one) and when it’s going to happen.”

Colorado is investing in a continuum of suicide prevention, with a focus on groups known to be at higher risk, such as youth and veterans, said Dr. Ned Calonge, the state’s chief medical officer. Some of the efforts include encouraging schools to teach students about resilience; supporting peer networks for groups such as farmers and ranchers; educating the public about how to respond if someone might be in crisis; and working with hospitals on “postvention” programs for people who survived an attempt.

Ideally, the state could do more to ease life’s blows through economic support, but with limited funding for suicide prevention, they have to put more focus on people at increased risk, Calonge said. People in more precarious economic circumstances have a higher risk of suicide, and suicide rates tend to go down following efforts to boost financial wellbeing, such as raising the minimum wage and expanding health insurance coverage.

“One of the problems with upstream prevention efforts is they have to be provided broadly, across the entire population,” he said.

Medical providers and the general public will always have an important role in looking for warning signs, but they can’t be the only line of defense, Rogers said.

“It’s not just, ‘How can we keep people from dying?'” Rogers said. “It’s, ‘How can we work upstream to make life worth living?'”

DALLAS — Rep. Brandon Gill (R-TX) told the Washington Examiner that Vice President JD Vance is the Republican Party‘s “clear front-runner” for president in 2028.

“He is a huge leader of the party right now, and he’s done a phenomenal job supporting the president and making the case to the American people that what the president has been doing both domestically with economic policy, with the border, but also in many instances with foreign policy, makes a lot of sense,” Gill said.

“So I’d love to see Vice President Vance at the top of the ticket,” he added.

Vance has emerged as one of the most prominent potential successors to President Donald Trump, with his Thursday keynote at the GOP midterm convention drawing attention to the party’s post-Trump future. As Trump’s presidency inches closer to the halfway mark, focus has shifted to who will be his successor.

But before a successor can be finalized, Republicans must first face the midterm elections.

“I just want to make sure that we can keep a majority in the House,” Gill said. “I want to make sure that we can make the case to the American people that this election is about mainstream values for the Republican Party and extreme values.”

Gill, speaking with the Washington Examiner at the Republican National Committee’s first-ever midterm convention in Dallas, Texas, his home state, emphasized the energy and excitement from attendees.

“My favorite [thing is] getting on stage and seeing the excitement from Republican voters all over the country, and seeing how engaged they are and how ready they are to fight for our country this election cycle,” Gill said to the Washington Examiner.

The convention has brought together some of Trump’s staunchest supporters, with Trump asking them to “vote like I’m on the ballot” in his Wednesday keynote address.

Gill called on Republicans to take a lesson from Trump’s time in office: follow through on campaign promises.

“I think the No. 1 thing Republicans are taking from the Trump era is that we ought to be doing what we said we’d do,” Gill said.

He argued that Republican and Democratic presidents have spent decades promising to secure the southern border, but that Trump followed through on this promise.

“It was President Trump who actually had the backbone and cared enough, frankly, for the American people and had enough respect for the American people that he was actually going to do what he said he was doing,” Gill said.

‘ELECTRIFYING’: TRUMP SUPPORTERS BRING ENERGY TO GOP MIDTERM CONVENTION

Gill said Republicans should look at Trump’s record as they consider the party’s future beyond the current president.

For Gill, that future currently points toward Vance.

The Justice Department has been eyeing Brennan for months, with lawyers interviewing former intelligence officials and issuing subpoenas as part of a conspiracy investigation, The Washington Post reported.

Brennan's attorneys requested that a judge order the administration to preserve any internal records and communications from the investigation.

For a group of teenagers learning English in Providence, Rhode Island, summer school this year looked a little different.

There were vocabulary games and journal entries, but also trips into the community where students could put their new language skills to work—whether speaking with a cashier at a local market or learning how to describe their experience on a résumé.

Teaching the 4-week class was Brown University student Justin Dunn, who spent the summer leading intermediate English courses for teens at the city’s public library.

“We’re helping these students, but I’m learning and gaining just as much,” said Justin. “I’ve learned so much about Providence and the amazing people here.”

The rising sophomore found the library opportunity through the university’s SPRINT-iProv fellowship, which places undergraduates in full-time summer positions with nonprofit groups throughout this capital city—including helping to create and teach a 4-week English-language curriculum.

Above all, Justin wanted to teach the teens English sentences they could actually use.

“Most of my lessons focus on real-life skills.”

When the class studied food and shopping, for example, Dunn didn’t stop with vocabulary exercises. He took his students to a nearby Maruichi market, where they could practice speaking English with a cashier.

The teenagers also began building their own résumés, learning the English words and phrases needed to describe their education, activities, work experience, and abilities.

“For teens who may soon be looking for jobs, becoming comfortable with that language can be really helpful,” Dunn said.

Other lessons explored subjects ranging from art and employment to food and outer space, while games helped students build vocabulary and journal writing encouraged them to express themselves in English.

The approach reflects a simple idea: learning the correct words on a worksheet is useful, but having the confidence to use those words in the real world can change what a young person is able to do with them.

A conversation at a grocery store can become a language lesson. A résumé can become an English assignment. And a summer class can potentially give a teenager more confidence when applying for a first job, navigating school or simply talking with someone new.

Justin discovered that some of the workers alongside him at the library had once arrived there for exactly the kind of help his students are receiving today.

“Many of my co-workers are immigrants, and some first came to the library through its English-language programs before later working there,” he said.

“There’s a real sense of community here, and I love that I get to be part of it.”

A poignant reminder that someone can walk through a library’s doors needing help with English—and years later walk through those same doors as an employee helping the next person.

And Justin is one of 40 Brown undergraduates spending the summer working full-time with Providence nonprofits making the world a little brighter—literally.

Bruno Mars performs at Wembley stadium at the first night of six nights

Bruno Mars appeared determined to lift the nation's mood during the first of his six nights at Wembley Stadium.

His last UK performance came in July 2018, shortly after England had been knocked out of the men's World Cup semi-finals. Eight years later, history had repeated itself.

But wearing an England football scarf, Union Jack bucket hat and clutching a Paddington Bear, the showman energised a 75,000-strong, multi-generational crowd.

After nearly a decade away from UK audiences, Mars proved why fans had snapped up tickets in record numbers, external.

The show began with a pre-recorded video of Mars praying in a church for a good performance, before he emerged beneath visuals of a stained-glass window in a red suit bejewelled with roses.

It was a suitably theatrical opening to a two-hour, 15-minute set. But for those who had avoided spoilers, Risk It All, a slow R&B ballad from Mars' latest album, The Romantic, was perhaps an unexpected opener.

Any surprise was short-lived. Within minutes, Mars sat behind a pair of bright red congas for Cha Cha, signalling the start of a set that moved between R&B, funk, Latin influences and pop.

It was an early glimpse of what was to come as he declared: "London, it's time to party."

The crowd quickly accepted the invitation. From then on, neither Mars nor his fans stood still.

24K Magic and Treasure prompted one of the night's biggest singalongs. As Mars sang "put your pinky rings up to the moon", thousands of little fingers rose into the air.

Bruno Mars wears a cape on stage that says 'The Romantic'

The opening run of songs showed why Mars has remained one of pop's most reliable live performers. Rather than relying on one sound, he moved between genres without ever losing the crowd.

Romance has always been at the heart of the singer's music, and it soon became the focus of the show.

"Tonight we sing about love," he told the crowd after Treasure, before introducing the Angel Baby Cam, a segment in which fans' reactions were projected onto the giant screens as he serenaded them.

It was one of several moments that played into his trademark romantic showmanship.

Later, he even emerged wearing a cape emblazoned with the words The Romantic, which appeared to nod to soul legend James Brown.

Anderson .Paak and Bruno Mars of Silk Sonic perform onstage during the 2022 Billboard Music Awards

In the years between his solo releases, Mars has focused on collaborations, most notably Silk Sonic with Anderson .Paak, a partnership he has previously described as "natural and organic"., external

That chemistry was evident as Anderson .Paak joined Mars on stage for a four-song Silk Sonic segment, with the pair delivering tightly choreographed Motown-inspired dance routines and playful banter.

This included their attempts at British accents as they declared the evening to be "absolutely wicked".

Silk Sonic was not the only collaboration to feature. Although Mars has recently enjoyed chart success with Die With a Smile, alongside Lady Gaga, and APT. with RosÃ©, only the former made the setlist.

Performed during the show's ballad section, Die With a Smile prompted one of the evening's biggest singalongs, suggesting the song has earned its place alongside Mars' more established hits.

Paul, 58 and his daughter Alex, 23 and son Thomas, 20 came from Hertfordshire to watch Bruno Mars

Among the crowd were Paul, 58, and his children Alex, 23, and Thomas, 20, who said the eight-year wait had been worth it.

Paul, who jokingly called the singer "Barry Bruno", said the family had grown up listening to his music.

"We've all got little emotional ties to each song," they told BBC News.  "It felt right to come together."

For this family, Wembley hosting Mars' only UK dates was not an issue.

"I think this is the most iconic venue," Alex said.

Bruno Mars performs on stage at Wembley stadium with his backing band 'The Hooligans'

As the show drew to a close, Mars returned to the songs that helped cement his place as one of pop's biggest stars.

For his 2010 hit Just the Way You Are, the singer asked for the stadium lights to be turned up so he could see the crowd, revealing thousands of fans singing every word back to him, before Uptown Funk transformed Wembley into a giant dancefloor complete with fireworks and gold confetti.

The show ended with Dance With Me, a ballad in which Mars yearns for one last slow dance to save a struggling relationship.

Like Risk It All at the start of the evening, it was an unexpected choice to end the concert.

It left the crowd on a reflective note, perhaps hoping they would not have to wait another eight years to see him again.

Bryan Cousins was diagnosed with motor neurone disease a little over a year ago.  (ABC News)

WA football great Bryan Cousins has described how he took inspiration from the late Neale Daniher when he learned he had motor neurone disease, and how his diagnosis had come as a "huge jolt".

Cousins, the father of fellow WA football great Ben Cousins, was diagnosed with the fatal disease just over a year ago.

Daniher, a former AFL footballer and coach, died last month at the age of 65 after a long and courageous battle with the disease.

Since his diagnosis in 2013, Daniher worked to raise awareness of the condition and also helped raise millions of dollars in fundraising for research.

Cousins, who enjoyed a stellar football career with Perth in the WAFL before playing for Geelong in the 1970s, went public with his own MND battle last month.

Speaking to 102.5 ABC Radio Perth, he said the hardest thing about his diagnosis was working out how to tell his family.

"I think anyone that gets diagnosed with an illness that's got a terminal aspect about it and is incurable … it was a huge jolt," Cousins said.

"I knew there was something wrong, but I didn't think it was anything as severe as this.

Bryan Cousins says his diagnosis came as a "huge jolt". (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

"When I got referred to a neurologist, I started looking up on the internet what I might have, and the one thing I didn't want to get was MND.

"I sat in there after all these tests, and the doctor or professor said, 'you've got MND'.

"To be perfectly honest, I got a bit teary, but it was only thinking about how I'm going to tell my children, and that was probably the hardest thing.

On the evening he was diagnosed, Cousins was driving to Fremantle when his thoughts turned to Daniher.

"All I could get my head around was Neale Daniher," he said.

"(I) thought about he had approached it … his courage and his determination.

Neale Daniher showed leadership on and off the field throughout his life, from club captaincy to coaching and as Australian of the Year — but no more so when facing the challenge of an MND diagnosis.

"The word that kept coming into my mind was 'defiance'. He almost defied the fact that MND was going to control his life."

Cousins said Daniher reached out to him when he learned of his diagnosis, and paid tribute to all he did to raise awareness of the disease.

"So many of us now know about MND, so many people support MND (because of Daniher) and unfortunately in Neale's case a cure … that can halt it hasn't been found yet," he said.

Cousins said he was "going OK" since his diagnosis.

"It's affected my legs and my hands a bit," he said.

"Every case of MND takes you in different places. I'm just dealing with it, I'm independent.

"It's something I wouldn't wish on anyone, but I'm trying to approach it the same way Neale did.

"We just hope our wonderful scientists will find a cure for it to save as many people and their families from the hardship on which it puts on us."

Cousins also opened up on the journey of his son, Ben, the 2005 Brownlow Medallist, who battled serious drug problems for years.

"That was a journey in our life that was obviously extremely tough, but it was toughest on him," he said.

"I get asked a lot of times by people … about dealing with someone suffering from addiction, and I'm not making any excuses; he made some poor choices and bad decisions in his life that made him end up where he did.

Bryan Cousins with his son Ben and the 2005 Brownlow Medal.  (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

"But addiction does not discriminate.

"And when people are an addict … they are the ones that are the sick.

"They are the ones that you've got to encourage, they're the ones that you've got to tell them you're proud of them, all be it that they struggle and they relapse and they relapse.

"But he's done a fantastic job … to get his life back in order, and I hope it gives inspiration and hope to other addicts and their families that there is a way out."

Socceroos centre back Cameron Burgess has suffered a possible Achilles injury playing for Swansea City in the League Cup.

Burgess was a key member of Australia's defence at the World Cup, although lost his starting spot to Lucas Herrington during the tournament.

The Asian Cup is to be held in Saudi Arabia from January 7 to February 5, 2027. The Socceroos play Brazil in Townsville on September 25 and in Brisbane on September 29.

Socceroos defender Cameron Burgess's Asian Cup hopes appear in jeopardy following a possible Achilles injury while playing for Swansea City.

The towering central defender played every minute of the gruelling English Championship campaign last season.

That made for 4,140 minutes, plus stoppage time, across all 46 league matches.

But there are fears Burgess's season is over after he limped off late in Swansea's 1-0 League Cup loss to Birmingham City.

In the 87th minute he challenged for a header, landed awkwardly and grabbed at his right lower leg, prompting his Birmingham opponents to check on him.

The 30-year-old, who has 29 Socceroos caps, headed to hospital for scans.

Cameron Burgess played against Türkiye and the USA for the Socceroos at the World Cup. (Getty Images: Richard Heathcote)

"It doesn't look good, but I prefer to wait for the assessment we will do," Swansea head coach Vítor Matos said.

"It could be related to the Achilles, but let's see."

If Burgess has ruptured his Achilles, he faces a significant stint on the sidelines, ending his Asian Cup hopes.

Losing Burgess ahead of tournament, to be held in Saudi Arabia early next year, is a significant blow to Australia's defensive stocks.

Burgess lost his starting spot to teen sensation Lucas Herrington during the World Cup, with coach Tony Popovic preferring a back three involving the teenager, Harry Souttar and Alessandro Circati.

But as a left-footer, Burgess is always a valuable part of Popovic's squad.

Souttar spent more than a year on the sidelines after his own Achilles tear, while wing-back Lewis Miller is on the comeback trail from the same injury, which ruled him out of World Cup contention.

Star wing-back Jordan Bos is sidelined until about October after having surgery on the left knee injured in Australia's round-of-32 loss to Egypt.

The Socceroos are next in action for friendlies against Brazil in Townsville on September 25 and Brisbane four days later.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he told US President Donald Trump he would take a "pragmatic approach" to the issue of North Sea oil and gas.

Trump has long urged the UK to increase drilling and claimed that Burnham had pledged to "open up the North Sea" in their first phone call together.

Asked about the president's comments, the new prime minister said: "There is a resource there. When people are struggling - you can't ignore that and hence me indicating that to the president."

Burnham has faced pressure from some trade unions, industry figures and some of his own Labour MPs to back increased drilling in the North Sea.

In its 2024 general election manifesto, Labour promised not to issue new licences for drilling but said it would honour existing ones.

As energy secretary in Sir Keir Starmer's government, Ed Miliband was a staunch supporter of Labour's manifesto position. He has previously described the licence issued to Rosebank, Britain's largest untapped oil and gas field, as "climate vandalism".

Miliband is now the foreign secretary in Burnham's government.

Is Burnham promising a new dawn for North Sea oil and gas?

To drill or not to drill? Andy Burnham faces North Sea oil dilemma

The city caught in the middle of the big energy shift debate

Although the government has not made any announcements on the issue, Trump has praised what he perceives as a change of stance by the UK government.

In a social media post, published the day before Burnham became prime minister,, external Trump wrote: "The People of Aberdeen, in Scotland, are dancing in the streets because the new Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, has stated that he will be opening up, all the way, the invaluable North Sea Oil!"

This week, when asked about his conversation with Burnham, Trump said: "He said he's going to open up North Sea oil.

"If he does that, you're going to be a wealthy country."

He later added: "You buy a lot of your energy, as you know, from the North Sea. You buy from Norway and Norway gets it from the North Sea... Norway's got trillions of dollars in the bank."

"Scotland has a better part of the North Sea."

Asked about Trump's comments, Burnham said: "I indicated in the phone call that we had a week last Monday that I would take a pragmatic approach when it comes to the North Sea, and that is my intention as we go forward from here."

In response, Green Party leader Zack Polanski said: "Our country is burning. Crops are failing. Thousands have been killed by extreme heat.

"Allowing new oil and gas drilling in the North Sea will worsen the climate breakdown putting more lives at risk and doing untold damage to our economy.

"It's not too late for Burnham to do the right thing and commit to leaving dangerous fossil fuels in the ground."

The Conservatives and Reform have urged the government to approve more drilling in the North Sea, arguing it would reduce energy prices.

Last year, Tory Party leader Kemi Badenoch said it would be "absurd" for the UK to leave "vital resources untapped".

Some Labour MPs have expressed unease about more drilling, with Rachael Maskell urging the government to "follow the climate science because we have got a climate emergency".

Simon Francis, from the End Fuel Poverty Coalition, said: "No household struggling with their energy bills will see a penny come off by drilling more from the North Sea.

"Gas is sold at the global market prices, so whatever is pumped out is sold to the highest bidder, not handed to British billpayers at a discount."

Sir Keir's government had already made concessions, allowing "tie-backs" -  production in unlicensed areas close to or connected to already licensed areas.

Currently, the debate over North Sea drilling has focused on two oil and gas fields - Rosebank and Jackdaw, located in Scotland.

In 2022 and 2023, regulators approved drilling at the sites, but that was overturned in 2025 following a legal challenge.

The legal process is ongoing, but the government will at some point have to decide whether to permit companies to produce oil in the two areas.

Other oil and gas licences have been approved in recent years but remain largely undeveloped.

If he wanted to encourage more drilling in the North Sea, Burnham could also opt to scrap the Energy Profits Levy, also known as the windfall tax.

The levy is due to be replaced in 2030 by another windfall tax, which operators prefer because it's only triggered when prices are high and falls back when they are low.

burnham-prison-pause:
Andy Burnham has announced he is pausing a scheme which would have seen thousands of prisoners in England and Wales eligible to be released early.

It came after criticism of the scheme from survivors and victims' families, including the widow of PC Andrew Harper who described the possibility of his killers' early release as "deplorable".

The Sentencing Act, which was due to come into effect in September, would have seen some offenders let out at varying stages in a bid to ease prison overcrowding.

The new Justice Secretary Alex Norris said the pause aimed to "give victims and survivors certainty" and the government wanted to make sure it got "the implementation of this policy right".

He added a review would also look at the information given to survivors and victims' families as part of the early release process.

Burnham earlier said: "No prisoners will be let out under this policy until we have conducted an urgent review and done everything we can to minimise risk to the public."

He added: "Where changes are needed, we will not hesitate to make them."

Under the act, some offenders would have been let out after serving a third of their sentence, rather than half.

The rest of their sentence would be spent in the community, where they would be monitored and could be returned to prison if they offended again.

More serious offenders would have been released after serving half of their sentence, rather than two-thirds.

The policy was brought in to ease overcrowding in the prison system but has been criticised by opposition parties, as well as victims and their families.

The scheme would have seen around 700 prisoners released in early September, the BBC understands.

The decision to pause the scheme came after criticism from the family of Thames Valley Police officer Andrew Harper, who was killed in Berkshire in 2019 when he was dragged by a car down a country road by three teenagers.

Two of the killers of PC Harper, who were both sentenced to 13 years in prison, would have benefited from the scheme from June 2027, when the longest fixed sentences would have been added to the scheme.

PC Harper's widow, Lissie, called the plans "deplorable" and said politicians were "making decisions from behind a desk that will have real and lasting consequences" for the families of victims.

His mother, meanwhile, said her son had not been given "proper justice" and "every victim will be feeling the same" about the early prison release scheme.

Thousands of letters had been sent to victims in recent weeks, warning them that the early release scheme was coming in September.

Norris, who voted in support of the Sentencing Act under Starmer's government, later said the decision to pause was made after "listening to victims" and he hoped to provide them "certainty as soon as we can".

He said: "The prime minister and I have heard from victims and survivors and from people across the country about their concerns about the implementation of some very important elements of the Sentencing Act."

One element the government needed to get right was the information provided to victims before prisoners were released, Norris added.

Norris refused to be drawn on why he did not raise concerns when the Sentencing Act was first introduced but said Burnham was "quite right" to review the scheme.

Jade Belgrove, a survivor of sexual assault who has been campaigning against the early release scheme, said it was "such a relief that we've been heard".

She told BBC News that when she received a letter informing her that her attacker might be released early "it was horrific".

Belgrove said it even led her to question whether reporting the assault in the first place was worth it.

What could happen to prisoner early release scheme now PM has paused it?

Victims' Commissioner Claire Waxman welcomed the decision, calling the  original form of the early release scheme the "wrong course of action".

"Thousands of victims have already been told the offenders who harmed them could be released early, leaving many living with renewed fear and uncertainty," she said.

"Victims deserve certainty, and their safety and confidence must come first."

Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch said she welcomed the pause but called for killers and rapists to be "permanently" exempt from any future version of the scheme.

In a post on X, she said that the Tories have been "campaigning against this dangerous scheme from day one".

Steve Gillan, general secretary of prison officers' union POA, said he understood concerns about "operational stability" but the government was correct to pause early releases "to ensure there is adequate public protection in place and that victims of crime are put first".

But one prison officer told the BBC Burnham's decision was "bonkers" and warned prisons were close to full capacity.

"We're super overcrowded - this isn't great news," they said.

"If we don't let people out in September we could be at a critical point come November where we're at full capacity."

Another prison officer disagreed, praising the government for "putting public safety first".

The scheme would have started in phases from September and would have meant thousands of prisoners in England and Wales being eligible for earlier release.

Offenders serving standard fixed sentences, who were due to be released after 50% of their term, would leave jail after serving 33%

Serious sexual and violent offenders on fixed terms, who would have been released at 66% of that sentence, would be released after 50%

These offenders would be intensively supervised but could lose the privilege of being out if they don't make progress towards rehabilitation

The most serious offenders - including life prisoners and those who are subjected to extended monitoring - are not eligible under the scheme

In 2024, the Labour government announced separate and temporary emergency measures to release some prisoners early to ease overcrowding.
